Open problem. Whether an odd perfect number exists is unknown. This project does not claim a proof; it formalizes necessary conditions.

Foundations

Definitions, divisor sums of prime powers, valuations, and the divisor sum network.

OddPerfect.Basic

OddPerfect/Basic.lean · 43 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Seed.Starter

The two definitions everything is read against: OddPerfect N (N is odd and perfect, using mathlib's Nat.Perfect) and OddPerfectConjecture, a statement that is never assumed.

Proof idea. No arguments here: six one line projections such as σ 1 N = 2 * N unpack the definition.

OddPerfect.Seed.Starter

OddPerfect/Seed/Starter.lean · 116 lines · 7 public theorems

Exact prime power components of any perfect number: the forcing step and valuation conservation.

Proof idea. By multiplicativity, σ(pe) divides σ(n) = 2n when pe is the full p component of n. So every odd prime dividing σ(pe) divides n (force_prime), and comparing the q exponents of both sides of σ(n) = 2n gives the conservation identity valuation_balance. The examples: σ(3²) = 13 forces 13, σ(13²) = 3·61 forces 61, and the three squares 7², 13², 19² each put a factor 3 into σ(n), which is too many when 3 has exponent exactly 2.

Public theorems

OPNStarter.sigma_eq_two_mul

theorem sigma_eq_two_mul {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) : σ 1 n = 2 * n

OPNStarter.component_sigma_dvd

theorem component_sigma_dvd {n p e : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (hp : p.Prime)
  (he : n.factorization p = e) : σ 1 (p ^ e) ∣ 2 * n

The divisor sum of an entire prime-power component divides the full divisor sum.

OPNStarter.force_prime

theorem force_prime {n p e q : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (hp : p.Prime)
  (he : n.factorization p = e) (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : q ≠ 2)
  (hdiv : q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ e)) : q ∣ n

Any odd prime dividing the divisor sum of an exact component must divide the number.

OPNStarter.valuation_balance

theorem valuation_balance {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (q : ℕ) :
  Nat.factorization 2 q + n.factorization q =
    ∑ p ∈ n.primeFactors, (σ 1 (p ^ n.factorization p)).factorization q

A prime can occur several times among different component sums. This equality counts all incidences, including repeated factors, with the extra factor of two on the left.

OPNStarter.thirteen_dvd_of_three_sq

theorem thirteen_dvd_of_three_sq {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (he : n.factorization 3 = 2) :
  13 ∣ n

A certified first link of a factor chain.

OPNStarter.sixty_one_dvd_of_thirteen_sq

theorem sixty_one_dvd_of_thirteen_sq {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (he : n.factorization 13 = 2) :
  61 ∣ n

The second link requires its own exact-exponent hypothesis.

OPNStarter.exclude_four_exact_squares

theorem exclude_four_exact_squares {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect)
  (h3 : n.factorization 3 = 2) (h7 : n.factorization 7 = 2)
  (h13 : n.factorization 13 = 2) (h19 : n.factorization 19 = 2) : False

Three distinct exact squares each contribute a factor 3. Together they contradict an exponent of exactly two at 3, regardless of which other primes divide the number.

OddPerfect.Seed.Cut

OddPerfect/Seed/Cut.lean · 68 lines · 2 public theorems

For a perfect number split into two coprime factors a and b, some prime of a divides σ(b).

Proof idea. From σ(a)σ(b) = 2ab: if no prime of a divided σ(b), then a would divide σ(a), so σ(a) = ka with k ≥ 2 because σ(a) > a. Then σ(a)σ(b) ≥ 2aσ(b) > 2ab, a contradiction. Splitting σ(b) over the components of b gives one component of b whose divisor sum is divisible by a prime of a.

Public theorems

OPNCut.exists_crossing_prime

theorem exists_crossing_prime {a b : ℕ} (ha : 1 < a) (hb : 1 < b)
  (hc : a.Coprime b) (hperf : (a * b).Perfect) :
  ∃ r : ℕ, r.Prime ∧ r ∣ a ∧ r ∣ σ 1 b

One prime dividing the first factor also divides the divisor sum of the second. Swapping the factors gives the other direction of the cut.

OPNCut.exists_crossing_component

theorem exists_crossing_component {a b : ℕ} (ha : 1 < a) (hb : 1 < b)
  (hc : a.Coprime b) (hperf : (a * b).Perfect) :
  ∃ r ∈ a.primeFactors, ∃ p ∈ b.primeFactors,
    r ∣ σ 1 (p ^ b.factorization p)

A particular prime-power component on the second side supplies a crossing edge. Here the source exponent is its full exponent in the second factor.

OddPerfect.Seed.Example

OddPerfect/Seed/Example.lean · 90 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Seed.Starter

No perfect number has the exponents of both 3 and 5 congruent to 2 modulo 3; also the divisibility of geometric sums used everywhere.

Proof idea. A geometric sum of length d divides one of length any multiple of d, so σ(pa) divides σ(pe) when a + 1 divides e + 1. With exponents ≡ 2 (mod 3), σ(3²) = 13 and σ(5²) = 31 divide the component sums, so 13 and 31 divide n. If 13 has exponent 1, σ(13) = 14 forces 7 and 3²·5²·13·7 is an abundant divisor; otherwise 3²·5²·13²·31 is abundant.

  (∑ i ∈ Finset.range d, p ^ i) ∣ ∑ i ∈ Finset.range m, p ^ i

OddPerfect.Abundancy

OddPerfect/Abundancy.lean · 236 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Basic

The abundancy σ(n)/n as an exact rational: multiplicativity, monotonicity, the bound p/(p − 1), and at least three prime factors.

Proof idea. Abundancy is a product over prime power components, each of which is a geometric sum in 1/p and lies strictly below p/(p − 1). A divisor with abundancy above 2 excludes perfection. For three prime factors: odd primes give p/(p − 1) ≤ 3/2 for p = 3 and ≤ 5/4 for every other prime, so with at most two prime factors the product is at most 15/8 < 2.

theorem abundancy_eq_sum_inv {n : ℕ} (hn : n ≠ 0) :
  abundancy n = ∑ e ∈ n.divisors, (e : ℚ)⁻¹

For n ≠ 0, the abundancy is the sum of the reciprocals of the divisors.

OddPerfect.Cyclotomic

OddPerfect/Cyclotomic.lean · 179 lines · 7 public theorems · imports Basic

σ(pa) as a product of cyclotomic values, its closed form, and the arithmetic of its prime divisors.

Proof idea. σ(pa)·(p − 1) = pa+1 − 1 and the cyclotomic factorization over the divisors of a + 1 other than 1. A prime q dividing σ(pa) differs from p, and either p ≡ 1 (mod q) with q dividing a + 1, or the order of p modulo q exceeds 1 and divides both a + 1 and q − 1. For an odd prime q dividing p − 1, lifting the exponent gives vq(σ(pa)) = vq(a + 1).

Public theorems

OddPerfect.sigma_prime_pow_eq_prod_cyclotomic

theorem sigma_prime_pow_eq_prod_cyclotomic {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  ((σ 1 (p ^ a) : ℕ) : ℤ) =
    ∏ d ∈ (a + 1).divisors.erase 1, (Polynomial.cyclotomic d ℤ).eval (p : ℤ)

The divisor sum of a prime power factors as a product of cyclotomic values.

OddPerfect.sigma_prime_pow_mul_pred

theorem sigma_prime_pow_mul_pred {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  σ 1 (p ^ a) * (p - 1) = p ^ (a + 1) - 1

Closed form of the divisor sum of a prime power.

OddPerfect.prime_dvd_sigma_prime_pow

theorem prime_dvd_sigma_prime_pow {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hdiv : q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ a)) :
  q ≠ p ∧
  ((p % q = 1 ∧ q ∣ a + 1) ∨
   (1 < orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∧ orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1 ∧
     orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ q - 1))

A prime divisor q of σ 1 (p ^ a) differs from p, and either p ≡ 1 (mod q) with q ∣ a + 1, or the order of p modulo q exceeds 1 and divides both a + 1 and q - 1.

OddPerfect.prime_dvd_sigma_prime_pow_of_prime_length

theorem prime_dvd_sigma_prime_pow_of_prime_length {p q l : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hl : l.Prime) (hdiv : q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ (l - 1))) : q = l ∨ q % l = 1

Every prime divisor of σ 1 (p ^ (l - 1)), for a prime length l, is l itself or congruent to 1 modulo l.

OddPerfect.dvd_sigma_prime_pow_of_orderOf_dvd

theorem dvd_sigma_prime_pow_of_orderOf_dvd {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hpq : p ≠ q) (h1 : 1 < orderOf (p : ZMod q)) (hd : orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1) :
  q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ a)

If the order of p modulo a prime q exceeds 1 and divides a + 1, then q divides σ 1 (p ^ a).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_dvd_pred

theorem padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_dvd_pred {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (h : q ∣ p - 1) :
  padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = padicValNat q (a + 1)

Lifting the exponent: for an odd prime q dividing p - 1, the q-adic valuation of σ 1 (p ^ a) equals that of a + 1.

OddPerfect.orderOf_eq_of_dvd_cyclotomic_eval

theorem orderOf_eq_of_dvd_cyclotomic_eval {p q d : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime)
  (hdiv : (q : ℤ) ∣ (Polynomial.cyclotomic d ℤ).eval (p : ℤ)) (hqd : ¬ q ∣ d) :
  orderOf (p : ZMod q) = d ∧ d ∣ q - 1

If a prime q not dividing d divides the dth cyclotomic value at p, then the order of p modulo q is exactly d, and hence d ∣ q - 1.

OddPerfect.Valuation

OddPerfect/Valuation.lean · 282 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Cyclotomic, Network

Exact q-adic valuations of σ(pa) for every prime q and every exponent, and the 2-adic and 3-adic ledgers they give.

Proof idea. Through the order d of p modulo q: if d does not divide a + 1 the valuation is 0; otherwise it is vq(pd − 1) + vq((a + 1)/d). Closed forms at q = 2 (zero for even a, v₂(p + 1) + v₂(a + 1) − 1 for odd a) and at q = 3. Applied to the network, the 2-adic ledger shows the special component alone carries the single factor 2, with v₂(s + 1) = v₂(k + 1) = 1.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_self

theorem padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_self {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  padicValNat p (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = 0

q = p: the prime p never divides σ 1 (p ^ a).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_orderOf_dvd

theorem padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_orderOf_dvd {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (hpq : p ≠ q) (h1 : 1 < orderOf (p : ZMod q))
  (hd : orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1) :
  padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ a)) =
    padicValNat q (p ^ orderOf (p : ZMod q) - 1) +
      padicValNat q ((a + 1) / orderOf (p : ZMod q))

Odd q, general order: if the order d of p modulo q exceeds 1 and divides a + 1, then v_q(σ(p ^ a)) = v_q(p ^ d - 1) + v_q((a + 1) / d).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_not_orderOf_dvd

theorem padicValNat_sigma_prime_pow_of_not_orderOf_dvd {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hd : ¬ orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1) :
  padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = 0

If the order of p modulo a prime q does not divide a + 1, then q does not divide σ 1 (p ^ a).

OddPerfect.dvd_sigma_prime_pow_iff

theorem dvd_sigma_prime_pow_iff {p q a : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) (hpq : p ≠ q) :
  q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ a) ↔
    (if orderOf (p : ZMod q) = 1 then q ∣ a + 1 else orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ a + 1)

Unified divisibility criterion: with d the order of p modulo a prime q ≠ p, q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ a) iff q ∣ a + 1 when d = 1, and iff d ∣ a + 1 otherwise.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_two_sigma_prime_pow

theorem padicValNat_two_sigma_prime_pow {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hp2 : p ≠ 2) (a : ℕ) :
  padicValNat 2 (σ 1 (p ^ a)) =
    if Even a then 0 else padicValNat 2 (p + 1) + padicValNat 2 (a + 1) - 1

q = 2: for an odd prime p, σ 1 (p ^ a) is odd for even a, and for odd a its 2-adic valuation is v_2(p + 1) + v_2(a + 1) - 1.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow_of_mod_one

theorem padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow_of_mod_one {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (h : p % 3 = 1)
  (a : ℕ) : padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = padicValNat 3 (a + 1)

q = 3, p ≡ 1 (mod 3): v_3(σ(p ^ a)) = v_3(a + 1).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow_of_mod_two

theorem padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow_of_mod_two {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (h : p % 3 = 2)
  (a : ℕ) : padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (p ^ a)) =
    if Even a then 0 else padicValNat 3 (p + 1) + padicValNat 3 (a + 1)

q = 3, p ≡ 2 (mod 3): v_3(σ(p ^ a)) is 0 for even a and v_3(p + 1) + v_3(a + 1) for odd a.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_three_sigma_three_pow

theorem padicValNat_three_sigma_three_pow (a : ℕ) : padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (3 ^ a)) = 0

q = 3, p = 3: 3 never divides σ 1 (3 ^ a).

OddPerfect.padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow

theorem padicValNat_three_sigma_prime_pow {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) :
  padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (p ^ a)) = threeWeight p a

v_3(σ(p ^ a)) = threeWeight p a for every prime p and every exponent a.

OddPerfect.sigmaWeight_eq_padicValNat

  sigmaWeight N p q = padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p))

The network weight is the q-adic valuation of the component divisor sum.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_two_special

theorem padicValNat_two_special {N s : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hs : s.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization s)) :
  padicValNat 2 (s + 1) = 1 ∧ padicValNat 2 (N.factorization s + 1) = 1

The special prime s of an odd perfect number, with odd exponent k, satisfies v_2(s + 1) = 1 and v_2(k + 1) = 1: the special component alone supplies the single unit of the 2-adic ledger.

OddPerfect.mod_four_special

theorem mod_four_special {N s : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hs : s.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization s)) : s % 4 = 1 ∧ N.factorization s % 4 = 1

Consistency with Euler: the special prime and its exponent are both ≡ 1 (mod 4), derived from the 2-adic ledger.

OddPerfect.factorization_three_eq_sum_threeWeight

theorem factorization_three_eq_sum_threeWeight {N : ℕ} (hN : N.Perfect) :
  N.factorization 3 = ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, threeWeight p (N.factorization p)

The 3-adic ledger of a perfect number in closed form.

OddPerfect.factorization_eq_sum_erase

theorem factorization_eq_sum_erase {N q : ℕ} (hN : N.Perfect) (hq : q.Prime) (hq2 : q ≠ 2) :
  N.factorization q =
    ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors.erase q, padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p))

The q-adic ledger of a perfect number at an odd prime q, with the vanishing self term removed.

OddPerfect.padicValNat_pow_orderOf_sub_one_le

theorem padicValNat_pow_orderOf_sub_one_le {N p q : ℕ} (hN : N.Perfect) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hq2 : q ≠ 2) (hp : p ∈ N.primeFactors) (hpq : p ≠ q) (h1 : 1 < orderOf (p : ZMod q))
  (hd : orderOf (p : ZMod q) ∣ N.factorization p + 1) :
  padicValNat q (p ^ orderOf (p : ZMod q) - 1) ≤ N.factorization q

Lower bound: if a prime factor p ≠ q has order d > 1 modulo an odd prime q and d ∣ v_p(N) + 1, then v_q(p ^ d - 1) ≤ v_q(N).

OddPerfect.Phi3

OddPerfect/Phi3.lean · 226 lines · 23 public theorems · imports Network, Seed.ThreeFree, Seed.Collision

Arithmetic of σ(p²) = p² + p + 1: parity, coprimality, the exact power of 3, residues of other prime divisors, and roots modulo a prime.

Proof idea. p² + p + 1 is odd, coprime to p and p + 1, divisible by 3 exactly when p ≡ 1 (mod 3) and never by 9. Any other prime divisor has p of order 3, hence is ≡ 1 (mod 6). It lies strictly between p² and (p + 1)², so it is not a square. Modulo a prime there are at most two roots, and two roots below the prime sum to the prime minus 1. Consequence: each exact square prime ≡ 1 (mod 3) sends exactly one factor 3, so their number is at most v₃(N).

OddPerfect.Network

OddPerfect/Network.lean · 224 lines · 9 public theorems · imports Basic, Seed.Cut

The divisor sum network of a perfect number: weights, conservation, no self loops, and strong connectivity.

Proof idea. Conservation at an odd prime q is valuation_balance with vq(2) = 0, and at 2 the incoming weights sum to 1 because N is odd. A prime never divides σ(pe), so there are no self loops. For connectivity, any nonempty proper set S of prime factors splits N into the coprime parts over S and over its complement, and the cut lemma gives an edge from the complement into S; so the set of primes that reach a given prime cannot be proper.

OddPerfect.Reduction

OddPerfect/Reduction.lean · 263 lines · 10 public theorems · imports Euler, Abundancy, Network

Balanced candidates are exactly the factorizations of odd perfect numbers, so the conjecture is equivalent to their nonexistence.

Proof idea. One direction: an odd perfect number's own factorization is balanced by the conservation laws of Network. The other: for a balanced candidate, compare the q exponent of σ(value) with that of 2·value for every q. Multiplicativity turns the left side into the sum of the weights into q, and balance makes this equal to the exponent of q (or 1 at q = 2, or 0 at non primes). Equal factorizations give σ(value) = 2·value. This is a reformulation, not progress toward a proof.

OddPerfect.NetworkCut

OddPerfect/NetworkCut.lean · 198 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Network

The exact balance across a cut of the prime support. For a set A of prime factors of N with M the product of their full prime powers, σ(M)·In = 2^δ·Out·M, where Out and In collect the divisor sum weights leaving and entering A, and δ is 0 or 1. For a nonempty proper A: In < Out < 2·In when δ = 0, and Out < In < 2·Out when δ = 1.

Proof idea. σ is multiplicative, every prime factor of σ(p^e) is 2 or a prime factor of N, and the weights into each prime of A sum to its exponent, so the weights inside A cancel against M. The inequalities are 1 < σ(M)/M < 2 for the two coprime parts of N. The module restates conservation in a form that certificates can use; it is not a new obstruction.

theorem cut_balance {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) {A : Finset ℕ} (hA : A ⊆ N.primeFactors)

  (cutTwo N A = 1 → cutOut N A < cutIn N A ∧ cutIn N A < 2 * cutOut N A)

Two sided balance across a nonempty proper cut. With no weight from A into 2, the weight leaving A exceeds the weight entering it by a factor strictly between 1 and 2; with the single unit of weight into 2 inside A, the roles swap.

Euler's form and the special prime

Consequences of the shape N = qkm².

OddPerfect.Euler

OddPerfect/Euler.lean · 199 lines · 7 public theorems · imports Basic

Euler's form N = qkm² with q ≡ k ≡ 1 (mod 4), N ≡ 1 (mod 4), N not a square, and Touchard's congruence.

Proof idea. The 2-adic ledger: the weights into 2 sum to 1, and σ(pe) is even exactly when e is odd, so exactly one prime q has odd exponent k and v₂(σ(qk)) = 1. If q ≡ 3 (mod 4), pairing terms shows 4 divides σ(qk); with q ≡ 1 (mod 4), σ(qk) ≡ k + 1 (mod 4) forces k ≡ 1 (mod 4). Touchard: if 3 divides N then 9 does (3 ≡ 3 mod 4 is not special), giving N ≡ 9 (mod 36); if N ≡ 2 (mod 3) then q ≡ 2 (mod 3), and 3 divides q + 1, which divides σ(qk), so 3 would divide N.

  ∃ q : ℕ, q.Prime ∧ q ∣ N ∧ q % 4 = 1 ∧ N.factorization q % 4 = 1 ∧

Euler: an odd perfect number has a unique prime q of odd exponent, and q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and its exponent is ≡ 1 (mod 4).

  ∃ q k m : ℕ, q.Prime ∧ N = q ^ k * m ^ 2 ∧ ¬ q ∣ m ∧ q % 4 = 1 ∧ k % 4 = 1

Euler form: N = q ^ k * m ^ 2 with q prime, q ∤ m, and q ≡ k ≡ 1 (mod 4).

Proof idea. The 2-adic ledger. N is odd, so σ(N) = 2N has exactly one factor 2, shared among the components σ(pe). For odd p, σ(pe) has e + 1 odd terms, so it is even exactly when e is odd: one prime q has odd exponent k, and v₂(σ(qk)) = 1. If q ≡ 3 (mod 4), pairing consecutive terms puts q + 1, a multiple of 4, into σ(qk). So q ≡ 1 (mod 4), then σ(qk) ≡ k + 1 (mod 4) forces k ≡ 1 (mod 4).

OddPerfect.SpecialPrime

OddPerfect/SpecialPrime.lean · 289 lines · 17 public theorems · imports Euler, Abundancy, Seed.Example

Facts about the special prime: q + 1 divides σ(qk), (q + 1)/2 divides N, abundancy splits, refined Touchard congruence, and small abundant divisors such as 3²·5·7².

Proof idea. Since k is odd, q + 1 divides σ(qk), which divides 2N. The special component has abundancy below q/(q − 1) ≤ 5/4, so the square part m² has abundancy above 2/(5/4) = 8/5. The refinement of Touchard: if v₃(N) = 2 then σ(3²) = 13 divides N, giving N ≡ 117 (mod 468); otherwise 3⁴ divides N, giving N ≡ 81 (mod 324). For 105: the primes 3 and 7 are ≡ 3 (mod 4), hence squared, and 3²·5·7² has σ = 4446 > 4410 = 2·2205.

  N % 12 = 1 ∨ N % 468 = 117 ∨ N % 324 = 81

Refinement of Touchard's congruence.

Proof idea. From N ≡ 1 (mod 4) and Touchard's N ≡ 1 (mod 12) or N ≡ 9 (mod 36). If 3 divides N, its exponent is even. If it is exactly 2, then σ(3²) = 13 divides N, and N is a multiple of 9·13 = 117 that is ≡ 1 (mod 4), so N ≡ 117 (mod 468). Otherwise 3⁴ divides N and N ≡ 81 (mod 324).

OddPerfect.EulerPart

OddPerfect/EulerPart.lean · 460 lines · 22 public theorems · imports SpecialPrime, ClosedLoop, Valuation

Identities and congruences for Euler's form: the index σ(m²)/qk, the deficiency 2m² − σ(m²), congruences modulo 8, and small bounds.

Proof idea. Multiplicativity turns σ(N) = 2N into σ(qk)σ(m²) = 2qkm². Since qk is coprime to σ(qk), it divides σ(m²), which defines the index i with σ(m²) = qki and σ(qk)i = 2m². The index is odd because σ(m²) is odd: every exponent in m² is even, so each component sum has an odd number of odd terms. The deficiency identity is algebra: 2m² − σ(m²) = i(σ(qk) − qk) = iσ(qk−1). The congruence N ≡ q (mod 8) uses that m² ≡ 1 and, k being odd, qk ≡ q modulo 8.

OddPerfect.ClosedLoop

OddPerfect/ClosedLoop.lean · 321 lines · 5 public theorems · imports Euler, Network, Cyclotomic

The divisor sums of the ordinary components cannot all be powers of the special prime; consequences σ(m²) ≠ qk and 3qk < 2m².

Proof idea. Suppose σ(rer) = qcr for every ordinary r. Then the ordinary primes receive weight only from q, so rer divides σ(qk), which divides qk+1 − 1. Since qcr = 1 + r·σ(rer−1) is 1 modulo r exactly once, lifting the exponent gives rer−1 dividing k + 1, and with k odd, 2∏ rer−1 divides k + 1. Conservation at q gives k = Σ cr, while a size comparison gives cr < rer−1. With tr = rer−1 this gives k + 1 ≤ 1 + Σ (tr − 1) ≤ ∏ tr ≤ (k + 1)/2, a contradiction.

Proof idea. From σ(qk)σ(m²) = 2qkm² and q not dividing σ(qk), write σ(m²) = qkt, so σ(qk)t = 2m². Here t is odd (σ(qk) is even and m is odd), and t ≠ 1 because σ(m²) = qk is excluded by the closed loop argument. So t ≥ 3 and 3qk < 3σ(qk) ≤ 2m².

OddPerfect.Reciprocity

OddPerfect/Reciprocity.lean · 277 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Network, Valuation, Cyclotomic, SpecialPrime contains novelty unverified

Quadratic residue constraints on the network, after Wallace (arXiv 1610.00544): one sign identity per vertex, a reverse edge constraint, and two mutually residual prime factors.

Proof idea. σ(pa) ≡ 1 (mod p), so its Legendre symbol modulo p is 1; expanding over its factorization gives ∏ (r/p)w(p,r) = 1 at an ordinary vertex and (2/q) at the special vertex. In the other direction, if e is even and r divides σ(pe), then pe+1 ≡ 1 (mod r) with e + 1 odd, so p ≡ (pe/2+1)² is a square modulo r. Applied to an edge into the special prime q ≡ 1 (mod 4), reciprocity makes q a square modulo p as well.

Every odd perfect number has two distinct prime factors p and r with p a nonzero square modulo r and r a nonzero square modulo p. One can take r to be the special prime and p any prime factor whose component divisor sum is divisible by r.

Proof idea. The special prime q has positive exponent, so by conservation some prime p ≠ q sends weight to q. Its exponent e is even, so pe+1 ≡ 1 (mod q) with e + 1 odd, which makes p a square modulo q. Since q ≡ 1 (mod 4), quadratic reciprocity makes q a square modulo p.

OddPerfect.RepunitOrder

OddPerfect/RepunitOrder.lean · 211 lines · 3 public theorems

If 1 + w + … + w^(m−1) = k·p^s with p an odd prime, s ≥ 1 and k < p, then w has order exactly m modulo p.

Proof idea. Lemma 2.1 of Zhao and Chen (Front. Math. 2025). Consequences: p does not divide w − 1 and m divides p − 1. With w a prime and m = e + 1 the sum is σ(w^e), so the lemma describes components that are a small multiple of a prime power. Proof: split the sum along the order d of w; the second factor is a geometric sum in a base that is 1 modulo p, and lifting the exponent shows it cannot divide k·p^s unless it has length 1. Known mathematics.

OddPerfect.SpecialSuccSender

OddPerfect/SpecialSuccSender.lean · 61 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Reciprocity

A prime factor r of q + 1 with r ≡ 3 (mod 4) does not send to the special prime q.

Proof idea. If q ≡ 1 (mod 4) divides the divisor sum of an even power of r, then r is a square modulo q; by quadratic reciprocity q is a square modulo r; and q ≡ −1 (mod r), so −1 is a square modulo r and r ≡ 1 (mod 4). Every prime factor of (q + 1)/2 divides N, so this removes edges of the divisor sum network at the special prime. An elementary remark; whether it is stated in the literature has not been checked.

OddPerfect.ParityCount

OddPerfect/ParityCount.lean · 98 lines · 1 public theorem · imports LedgerPrimeThree

The number of prime factors p ≠ q with p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and exponent ≡ 2 (mod 4) is even exactly when q ≡ a (mod 8), where a is the exponent of the special prime q.

Proof idea. For p ≠ q with even exponent e: σ(p^e) ≡ 3 (mod 4) exactly when p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and e ≡ 2 (mod 4), and ≡ 1 otherwise. So the product D of these divisor sums is 1 or 3 modulo 4 according to the parity of the count. Modulo 8, σ(q^a) is 2 when q ≡ a and 6 otherwise, so σ(q^a) = 2s with s ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 4). From s·D = N ≡ 1 (mod 4) the two residues agree.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeParity

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeParity.lean · 147 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Euler

If 3 ∤ N: no prime p ≡ 1 (mod 3) has exponent ≡ 2 (mod 3), every prime p ≡ 2 (mod 3) has an even exponent, and the number of primes p ≡ 1 (mod 3) with exponent ≡ 1 (mod 3) is odd.

Proof idea. Since 3 ∤ N, N ≡ 1 (mod 3) and σ(N) = 2N ≡ 2 (mod 3). For p ≡ 1 (mod 3), σ(p^e) ≡ e + 1 (mod 3). For p ≡ 2 (mod 3), σ(p^e) is 1 for even e and 0 for odd e. No factor σ(p^e) of σ(N) is divisible by 3, which gives the first two statements. The remaining factors are 2 exactly when p ≡ 1 and e ≡ 1 (mod 3), and 1 otherwise, so the product is a power of 2 that is 2 modulo 3: the count is odd.

OddPerfect.EulerIndexPrimePower

OddPerfect/EulerIndexPrimePower.lean · 213 lines · 4 public theorems · imports EulerPart, Cyclotomic

A normal form for odd perfect numbers N = q·m² with special exponent 1 whose Euler index σ(m²)/q is a prime power rb: then m² = rbM² with M odd, M > 1, prime to r and q, and σ(rb) = q = 2M² − 1, σ(M²) = rb, b even, b + 1 prime. The system is not shown to be impossible here. Results on prime power indices exist in the literature; this normal form is elementary.

Proof idea. The two identities σ(m²) = q·i and (q + 1)·i = 2m² hold for the index i. If i = rb then r divides m. Split off the full power of r from m². The value σ(re) is prime to r, exceeds 1 and divides q·rb, so it equals q. Then q ≡ 1 (mod r), so r does not divide q + 1, and comparing powers of r in the second identity gives b = e. A prime value σ(rb) forces b + 1 prime.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelow

OddPerfect/SpecialBelow.lean · 442 lines · 7 public theorems · imports LargePrimes, EulerPart, Cyclotomic, EulerIndexPrimePower

In Euler's form N = qkm², the special prime satisfies q < m whenever k ≠ 1, and for k = 1 unless N has one exceptional shape: a prime p dividing m with exact power pe in N such that σ(pe) = q and σ((q + 1)/2) = pe. In that shape m < q holds, so q < m for all odd perfect numbers is equivalent to the impossibility of the shape, which is not decided here. The inequality q < m is claimed in the literature (Brown, 2016 preprint); the module does not use that claim, and how the literature treats the shape was not checked.

Proof idea. An extension of the size argument of Acquaah and Konyagin. Some prime p of m has q dividing σ(pe). Write σ(pe) = qu and x = gcd(q + 1, pe); perfection gives exact identities between q, u, x and the divisor sum of the rest of m². They force q² < m² except when x = u = 1 and the rest contributes nothing extra, which is the shape, and in one case with p = 3 that is impossible modulo 5.

theorem special_lt_or_shape_of_exponent_one {N q m : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hN : N = q ^ 1 * m ^ 2) (hqm : ¬ q ∣ m) :
  q < m ∨ ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ p ∣ m ∧ 2 * m ^ 2 = p ^ N.factorization p * (q + 1) ∧
    σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = q ∧ σ 1 ((q + 1) / 2) = p ^ N.factorization p

Exponent one: either q < m, or N = q * p ^ e * ((q + 1) / 2) for a prime p ∣ m with exponent e in N, σ(p ^ e) = q and σ((q + 1) / 2) = p ^ e. This proves q < m for k = 1 apart from that one exceptional shape.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowParity

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowParity.lean · 162 lines · 4 public theorems · imports SpecialBelow, SquareRow

Let N = qkm2 be an odd perfect number with special prime q not dividing m. If m ≤ q, then N has an even number of distinct prime factors. So an odd number of distinct prime factors gives q < m.

Proof idea. The module SpecialBelow leaves one shape: N = q·pe·t2 with σ(pe) = q, q + 1 = 2t2 and σ(t2) = pe, with e even. Each component σ(r2c) for a prime r dividing t is a power pw, and the exponents w add up to e. An even w makes the component a square, which happens only for σ(34) = 112; then p = 11 and 3 divides t, so q ≡ 2 (mod 3), while q = σ(11e) ≡ 1 (mod 3). So every w is odd, t has an even number of prime factors, and N has two more. This does not prove q < m: the parity of the number of prime factors of an odd perfect number is not known.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowRows

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowRows.lean · 288 lines · 4 public theorems · imports SpecialBelow, PureRows, SpecialBelowParity

In the one open shape of q < m, every prime of (q + 1)/2 has a divisor sum that is a power of p, and one of these powers has an odd exponent at least 3. So q < m follows from one explicit hypothesis on σ(r^g) = p^w.

Proof idea. The shape is N = q·p^e·W with W = (q + 1)/2 an odd square, σ(p^e) = q and σ(W) = p^e. For a prime r dividing W, σ(r^g) divides σ(W) = p^e, so σ(r^g) = p^w, and the exponents w add up to e. A row with w = 1 gives p ≡ 1 (mod r), so q = σ(p^e) ≡ e + 1 (mod r), and r divides q + 1, hence r divides e + 2. If every w were 1, W would have e distinct odd prime factors, all dividing e + 2, so 3^e ≤ e + 2, which is false for e ≥ 2. So some w is at least 2. Such a w is odd, hence at least 3, except for σ(3⁴) = 11², and that case contradicts q = σ(11^e) ≡ 1 (mod 3) with 3 dividing q + 1. The theorem special_lt_of_noHighPureRow takes the absence of such rows as its hypothesis and returns q < m for every odd perfect number.

OddPerfect.ShapeSeries

OddPerfect/ShapeSeries.lean · 192 lines · 2 public theorems

A solution of 2t² = 1 + σ(p^(2h)) in a prime p has p ≤ max(7, 2D), where D comes from a truncated power series certificate.

Proof idea. A certificate is a number D and coefficients c₀ = D, c₁, …, c_h, which are D times the first coefficients of the power series of √((1 − X/2)/(1 − X)). With A = Σ cᵢ pⁱ and U = D·t, the certificate identities give that p^(h + 1) divides (U − A)(U + A). If p > 2D, then p divides at most one factor, so p^(h + 1) divides one of them; but both lie strictly between 0 and p^(h + 1). Hence p ≤ max(7, 2D). The certificate conditions are finitely many integer identities.

OddPerfect.pow_succ_dvd_cert_sq_sub

theorem pow_succ_dvd_cert_sq_sub (c : ℕ → ℕ) {h D : ℕ} (hc0 : c 0 = D)
  (hck : ∀ k, 1 ≤ k → k ≤ h → 2 * ∑ ij ∈ antidiagonal k, c ij.1 * c ij.2 = D ^ 2) (x : ℤ) :
  x ^ (h + 1) ∣ 2 * (∑ i ∈ range (h + 1), (c i : ℤ) * x ^ i) ^ 2 -
    (D : ℤ) ^ 2 * (1 + ∑ i ∈ range (h + 1), x ^ i)

The certificate congruence: if c_0 = D and 2 ∑_{i + j = k} c_i c_j = D ^ 2 for 1 ≤ k ≤ h, then x ^ (h + 1) divides 2 A ^ 2 - D ^ 2 (1 + ∑_{i ≤ h} x ^ i) for every integer x, where A = ∑_{i ≤ h} c_i x ^ i.

theorem prime_le_of_two_sq_eq_succ_sigma {h D p t : ℕ} (c : ℕ → ℕ) (hD : 0 < D) (hc0 : c 0 = D)
  (hck : ∀ k, 1 ≤ k → k ≤ h → 2 * ∑ ij ∈ antidiagonal k, c ij.1 * c ij.2 = D ^ 2)
  (hsmall : ∀ i, 1 ≤ i → i ≤ h → 2 * c i ≤ D) (hh : 1 ≤ h) (hp : p.Prime)
  (ht : 2 * t ^ 2 = 1 + ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (2 * h + 1), p ^ i) : p ≤ max 7 (2 * D)

Bound on the prime base: if p is a prime with 2 t ^ 2 = 1 + ∑_{i ≤ 2 h} p ^ i = 1 + σ(p ^ (2 h)) and h ≥ 1, then p ≤ max 7 (2 D) for every certificate D, c of degree h (see the module docstring); p = 2 needs no separate hypothesis since p > 7 is assumed in the proof by contradiction. Only this equation is used; the shape of the inequality q < m is not excluded.

OddPerfect.ShapeSmall

OddPerfect/ShapeSmall.lean · 412 lines · 29 public theorems · imports ShapeSeries, SpecialBelow

In Euler’s form with m ≤ q, the prime p with σ(p^e) = q has e ≥ 16. The equation 2t² = 1 + σ(p^e) has no solution with e < 16 and e + 1 prime.

Proof idea. For each exponent below 16 with e + 1 prime, a certificate for ShapeSeries bounds p, and the finite range below the bound is checked in the kernel with residue masks and an exact square test. The certificates and masks were produced by a script and each is verified here, so the script is not trusted. The shape with e ≥ 16 is not excluded.

  ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ p ∣ m ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = q ∧ 16 ≤ N.factorization p

In Euler's form N = q ^ k * m ^ 2 of an odd perfect number with q ∤ m, if m ≤ q (the open shape of the inequality q < m), then some prime p ∣ m has σ(p ^ v_p(N)) = q and exponent v_p(N) ≥ 16. Only the equation 2 t ^ 2 = 1 + σ(p ^ e) of the shape is used. The shape is not excluded: exponents e ≥ 16 remain open. Novelty was not verified.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowOrder

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowOrder.lean · 340 lines · 8 public theorems · imports SpecialBelowRows, EqualExponentsBound

In the open shape of q < m, a row σ(r^g) = p^w has w odd, the order d of p modulo r odd and dividing w, r not dividing w, and r dividing e + 2 when p ≡ 1 (mod r); otherwise d ≥ 3, d does not divide e and w ≥ 3. Derived from a step of Dandapat, Hunsucker and Pomerance (1975).

Proof idea. Reducing σ(r^g) = p^w modulo r gives p^w ≡ 1, so d divides w. The weight w is odd by the earlier parity lemma, hence d is odd. If d = 1 then q = σ(p^e) ≡ e + 1 (mod r) and r divides q + 1, so r divides e + 2. If d divided e, then q ≡ 1 (mod r), against r dividing q + 1. Lifting the exponent, with r² not dividing σ(r^g) − 1, gives that r divides p^d − 1 exactly once and that r does not divide w.

OddPerfect.SpecialBelowRadical

OddPerfect/SpecialBelowRadical.lean · 362 lines · 6 public theorems · imports SpecialBelowOrder

In the open shape of q < m, with W = (q + 1)/2: the product of the primes of W is 1 modulo p, hence at least 2p + 1, and some row prime r ≥ 7 has p not 1 modulo r, order of p modulo r at least 3 and weight at least 3. Hence q < m under the hypothesis NoOrderPureRow, which asks less than NoHighPureRow; neither is proved.

Proof idea. Every prime r of W has σ(r^g) = p^w with g the exponent of r in W, and (r − 1)σ(r^g) = r^(g + 1) − 1, so r^(g + 1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Multiplying over the primes of W gives W·rad(W) ≡ 1 (mod p). Also q = σ(p^e) ≡ 1 (mod p) and 2W = q + 1, so W ≡ 1 and rad(W) ≡ 1 (mod p). If every prime r of W had p ≡ 1 (mod r), then rad(W) would divide p − 1 and lie strictly between 1 and p, which is impossible. For a row prime with p not 1 modulo r, the order of p is odd, at least 3, and divides the even number r − 1.

Prime factor counts, size and exponents

Lower bounds on ω, inequalities between ω and Ω, upper bounds on N, and caps on exponents.

OddPerfect.OmegaFour

OddPerfect/OmegaFour.lean · 268 lines · 1 public theorem · imports Abundancy, Euler, Cyclotomic, Seed.Example

At least four distinct prime factors.

Proof idea. With exactly three prime factors the bound 2 < ∏ p/(p − 1) forces the support {3, 5, s} with s ∈ {7, 11, 13}. In each case some prime with even exponent has a component sum larger than 1 whose prime factors must lie among the other two primes; multiplicative orders, and in one case the extra prime 3221 or 61, rule out every candidate exponent.

OddPerfect.OmegaFive

OddPerfect/OmegaFive.lean · 515 lines · 1 public theorem · imports Certificate, OmegaFour, SmallestPrime, SpecialPrime, Zsigmondy

At least five distinct prime factors, closed by a kernel computation over 104 explicit supports.

Proof idea. With four prime factors, 3 divides N and the product bound leaves the supports {3, 5, r, s} with 17 ≤ r ≤ 31 and s < 256, {3, 7, r, s} with r ∈ {11, 13} and s ≤ 26, and the families {3, 5, 11, s} and {3, 5, 13, s}, cut to s ≤ 100 and s ≤ 46 ({3, 5, 7, s} is out since 105 does not divide N). That is 70 + 6 + 20 + 8 = 104 supports. For each, a Boolean function lists the candidate exponents of each prime (from Euler's form and primitive divisors: e = 1 for the special prime, or e + 1 dividing y − 1 for some y in the support) and checks that σ(xe) always has a prime factor outside the support and 2; decide +kernel evaluates it.

OddPerfect.SmallestPrime

OddPerfect/SmallestPrime.lean · 288 lines · 9 public theorems · imports Abundancy

Bounds on the smallest prime factor p₁: p₁ ≤ ω and 3p₁ < 2ω + 6, and ω ≥ 7 without 3, ω ≥ 15 without 3 and 5.

Proof idea. Everything rests on 2 < ∏ p/(p − 1) over the prime factors. If all elements of a set are at least m, the product telescopes to at most 1 + |S|/(m − 1), giving p₁ ≤ ω; over odd numbers the squared product is at most 1 + 2|S|/(m − 2), giving 3p₁ < 2ω + 6. The bounds without 3 or 5 compare the product with an explicit set of small primes.

OddPerfect.LeastPrimeSeven

OddPerfect/LeastPrimeSeven.lean · 148 lines · 1 public theorem · imports SmallestPrime contains novelty unverified

The least prime factor p₁ of an odd perfect number with ω distinct prime factors satisfies 7p₁ < 3ω + 21. Published comparison: Zelinsky (INTEGERS 21 (2021), A76, Corollary 4) proves ω ≥ 2p₁ + 2, which is stronger than this bound for p₁ ≤ 23; this bound is stronger from p₁ = 29 on.

Proof idea. The method of the bound 3p₁ < 2ω + 6 with cubes: the prime factors are at least p₁ ≥ 5 and coprime to 6, so the i-th of them is at least p₁ + 3i − 1, and (u/(u − 1))³ < (u + 1)/(u − 2) telescopes to ∏ (p/(p − 1))³ ≤ (p₁ + 3ω − 3)/(p₁ − 3). The left side exceeds 8.

OddPerfect.PerfectRigidity

OddPerfect/PerfectRigidity.lean · 160 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Basic

A unitary divisor B of a perfect number N with 1 < B < N forces a prime into N/B. Two perfect numbers with a common prime factor and equal exponents at all common primes are equal.

Proof idea. Write N = B·C with gcd(B, C) = 1. From σ(B)σ(C) = 2BC and σ(C) > C: B < σ(B) < 2B. So σ(B) does not divide 2B, and some prime r divides σ(B) to a higher power than 2B. Since σ(B) divides 2BC, such a prime divides C. For two perfect numbers N and N′ that agree at their common primes, B = gcd(N, N′) is a unitary divisor of both. If B is smaller than both, a forced prime of B divides both cofactors, hence B: contradiction. If B = N, then N is a proper unitary divisor of N′ with σ(N) = 2N, against σ(B) < 2B.

OddPerfect.PerfectCount

OddPerfect/PerfectCount.lean · 429 lines · 18 public theorems · imports PerfectRigidity, UpperBound, SmallestPrime, UnconditionalSupport contains novelty unverified

At most 4^(k²) odd perfect numbers have at most k distinct prime factors; at most 4^((5T+7)²) have total excess at most T.

Proof idea. Start with the full power of the least prime factor of N. As long as the current unitary divisor B is smaller than N, multiply by the full power of the least forced prime of B, which depends on B alone. The chain gains one prime per step and stops at N, so N is determined by its least prime factor and the exponents along the chain. For ω(N) ≤ k the least prime p₁ satisfies 3p₁ < 2k + 6 and every exponent is below 3·4^(k−1), because 3^e ≤ N < 2^(4^k). Counting the possible data gives 4^(k²). The second bound uses ω(N) ≤ 5T + 7.

OddPerfect.CountBelow

OddPerfect/CountBelow.lean · 67 lines · 2 public theorems · imports EulerPart

At most √(x/5) odd perfect numbers are at most x.

Proof idea. In Euler's form N = q^k·m² the number m determines N (Hornfeck's lemma, in EulerPart). The special prime q is at least 5, so 5m² ≤ N ≤ x and m lies between 1 and the integer square root of x/5. Distinct odd perfect numbers have distinct m.

OddPerfect.Counting

OddPerfect/Counting.lean · 251 lines · 12 public theorems · imports Euler, Network, Seed.ThreeFree

Linear inequalities between Ω and ω: 2ω ≤ Ω + 1 and 12ω ≤ 5Ω + 6v₃(N) + 9.

Proof idea. Every ordinary exponent is even, hence at least 2, which gives 2ω ≤ Ω + 1. Exponent 2 primes ≡ 1 (mod 3) each spend one unit of v₃(N). For the set A₂ of exponent 2 primes not ≡ 1 (mod 3), every prime factor of σ(p²) is ≡ 1 (mod 3) and so outside A₂; conservation at those receivers gives |A₂| ≤ Ω − 2|A₂|. Combining the two counts gives the inequality.

OddPerfect.CountingZelinsky

OddPerfect/CountingZelinsky.lean · 434 lines · 10 public theorems · imports Counting

8ω ≤ 3Ω + 7 when 3 does not divide N, and 21ω ≤ 8Ω + 39 in general, after Zelinsky (arXiv 1706.07009).

Proof idea. A ledger of the exponent 2 primes, split by residue modulo 3, with conservation of the 3-free parts of σ(p²). The new input over Counting is injectivity: when σ(p²) has at most two prime factors its largest prime factor determines p, because a prime shared by σ(a²) and σ(b²) with b < a is at most a; and when the 3-free part of σ(p²) is prime it determines p, using that 3(x² + x + 1) = y² + y + 1 has no solution with x an odd prime (it forces y = 3a + 1 and x(x + 1) = 3a(a + 1)). Linear arithmetic on the resulting relations gives both bounds.

OddPerfect.zelinsky_ledger

theorem zelinsky_ledger {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) :
  ∃ a b x y W ρ F : ℕ,
    (∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, N.factorization p) = 2 * a + F + N.factorization 3 ∧
    N.primeFactors.card = a + ρ + (if 3 ∣ N then 1 else 0) ∧
    4 * ρ ≤ F + 3 + 2 * b ∧ W ≤ F ∧ 3 * a + 2 * b ≤ W + x + y ∧
    x ≤ a ∧ y ≤ x + b ∧ x ≤ ρ ∧ y ≤ ρ ∧ b ≤ N.factorization 3 ∧
    (3 ∣ N → 2 ≤ N.factorization 3)

With S₂ the exponent 2 primes that are 2 (mod 3) (a of them), S₁ those that are 1 (mod 3) (b of them), R the remaining prime factors other than 3 (ρ of them, total exponent F), W the number of prime factors with multiplicity of the 3-free parts of σ(p ^ 2) over p ∈ S₁ ∪ S₂, X the primes of S₂ whose σ(p ^ 2) has at most two prime factors, and Y the primes of S₁ ∪ S₂ whose 3-free part of σ(p ^ 2) is prime, the listed linear relations hold. The bounds x ≤ ρ and y ≤ ρ are the two injectivity statements (largest prime factor, and the 3-free part itself).

OddPerfect.RadicalBound

OddPerfect/RadicalBound.lean · 662 lines · 18 public theorems · imports Abundancy, SmallestPrime, Euler, SpecialPrime

Identities linking abundancy to the radical R and to φ(R), with consequences such as 2φ(R) < R for perfect numbers and linear bounds on the second, third and fourth smallest prime factors.

Proof idea. Each component contributes σ(pe)/pe = (p/(p − 1))(1 − p−(e+1)), so the abundancy of N is H(N) = R/φ(R) times a product of factors below 1. For a perfect N the abundancy is 2, hence R/φ(R) > 2, and since R and 2φ(R) are integers, R − 2φ(R) ≥ 1, which gives H(N) − 2 ≥ 1/φ(R). Keeping one factor 1 − p−(e+1) and bounding the others by 1 gives the component bound R ≤ pe+1(R − 2φ(R)).

OddPerfect.third_prime_le

OddPerfect.UpperBound

OddPerfect/UpperBound.lean · 773 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Abundancy

N < 24k for an odd perfect number with k distinct prime factors, from the general bound dN < (d + 1)4k for odd N with σ(N)/N = n/d.

Proof idea. The key lemma (cook_lemma in the source): for integers 2 ≤ x₁ < ⋯ < xr with ∏ (1 − 1/xi) ≤ a/b below the same product without xr, one has a∏ xi < (a + 1)2r, proved by strong induction on r with a majorization comparison against the extremal sequence (a + 1)2i + 1. The theorem then grows a set of known primes: the lemma is applied first to new primes and then to prime power components, which splits off a coprime factor V of N; the cofactor N/V is again odd with rational abundancy of denominator dσ(V), and the induction runs on the number of prime factors.

  (hlt : (a : ℚ) / b < ∏ x ∈ G.erase m, (1 - 1 / (x : ℚ))) :
  a * ∏ x ∈ G, x < (a + 1) ^ (2 ^ G.card)

Let G be a finset of integers x ≥ 2 with largest element m, and let a > 0. If ∏_{x ∈ G} (1 - 1/x) ≤ a/b < ∏_{x ∈ G, x ≠ m} (1 - 1/x) then a ∏_{x ∈ G} x < (a + 1)^(2^|G|).

OddPerfect.Zsigmondy

OddPerfect/Zsigmondy.lean · 249 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Cyclotomic

Primitive prime divisors for bases a ≥ 3: for every n ≥ 3 some prime q has a of order exactly n modulo q.

Proof idea. Through the cyclotomic value Φn(a). A prime factor of Φn(a) not dividing n is primitive. Otherwise every prime factor q divides n, the order of a modulo q is the part of n prime to q, which forces a single such prime, and lifting the exponent shows it divides Φn(a) only once. Then Φn(a) = q, contradicting Φn(a) > (a − 1)φ(n) ≥ 2q−1 ≥ q. Consequence: each divisor d ≥ 3 of e + 1 yields a prime factor of N congruent to 1 modulo d.

OddPerfect.ExponentCap

OddPerfect/ExponentCap.lean · 298 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, Euler, SpecialPrime, UpperBound

Exponents are capped by the largest prime factor (2e + 3 ≤ R), the divisors of e + 1 inject into the prime factors, and finiteness for fixed ω or bounded primes.

Proof idea. For an ordinary prime with exponent e, a primitive prime of order e + 1 divides σ(pe), hence N, and is ≡ 1 (mod 2(e + 1)), so it is at least 2e + 3. For the special prime with exponent k ≥ 5, the primitive primes of orders k + 1 and (k + 1)/2 are distinct and both ≡ 1 (mod k + 1); for k = 1 the special prime itself is at least 5. Distinct divisors d ≥ 3 of e + 1 give distinct primes since p has order exactly d at each. Finiteness for fixed ω uses the bound N < 24ω.

OddPerfect.ValuationBounds

OddPerfect/ValuationBounds.lean · 377 lines · 9 public theorems · imports Valuation, ExponentCap contains novelty unverified

Bounds on the exponent of a prime q in terms of ω(N): the q-adic ledger bounded term by term, with special forms for primes q with q − 1 a power of two and for q = 3. The main formula factorization_le_sq_add_sum_orderWeight is an analogue of a corollary of Thackeray, proved here directly and under different hypotheses: his statement concerns odd squares.

Proof idea. The q-adic ledger vq(N) = Σ vq(σ(pep)) is bounded term by term. A component with p ≡ 1 (mod q) contributes vq(ep + 1), and q, q², …, qj are distinct divisors at least 3 of ep + 1, so the injection of divisors into prime factors gives vq(ep + 1) ≤ ω − 1. A component of order d > 1 contributes vq(pd − 1) + vq((ep + 1)/d), and the second summand is bounded the same way.

OddPerfect.FermatSpecial

OddPerfect/FermatSpecial.lean · 84 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Valuation, ValuationBounds contains novelty unverified

Special prime q = 2^k + 1 ≥ 5: (q − 3)/2 · a ≤ T, where a is the special exponent and T the total excess. For q = 5: a ≤ T.

Proof idea. For a prime p ≠ q with even exponent e, the order of p modulo q divides the odd number e + 1 and the power of two q − 1, so q divides σ(p^e) only if p ≡ 1 (mod q), and then v_q(σ(p^e)) = v_q(e + 1). If this valuation is h ≥ 1 then e + 1 ≥ q^h ≥ 3 + h(q − 3), so h·(q − 3)/2 ≤ e/2 − 1. Sum over the ledger for q. Whether this is stated in the literature has not been checked.

OddPerfect.FermatFactor

OddPerfect/FermatFactor.lean · 148 lines · 3 public theorems · imports FermatSpecial contains novelty unverified

A Fermat prime F ≥ 5 that divides N, is not the special prime q, with q ≢ ±1 (mod F): T ≥ (F − 2)·t + (F − 3), where t is the excess of F.

Proof idea. The special component sends nothing to F: the order of q modulo F would divide a + 1 ≡ 2 (mod 4) and a power of two, so it would be 1 or 2. The other components send at most v_F(e + 1) each, as in FermatSpecial, so (F − 3)/2 times the exponent of F is at most the excess of the remaining primes. Whether this is stated in the literature has not been checked.

(F - 3) / 2 times the exponent of F is at most the excess of the remaining primes.

OddPerfect.LeastOddFactor

OddPerfect/LeastOddFactor.lean · 69 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Valuation, SpecialPrime contains novelty unverified

If L bounds q and every odd prime factor of q − 1 from below, then (L − 3)/2 ≤ T.

Proof idea. Some prime r ≠ q sends to q. The order of r modulo q divides e + 1 (odd) and q − 1, or r ≡ 1 (mod q) and q divides e + 1. So e + 1 has an odd prime factor that divides q − 1 or equals q, and e + 1 ≥ L. Whether this is stated in the literature has not been checked.

  ∃ d, d.Prime ∧ d ≠ 2 ∧ d ∣ e + 1 ∧ (d ∣ q - 1 ∨ d = q)

If a prime q divides the divisor sum of an even power r ^ e of another prime, then e + 1 has an odd prime factor that divides q - 1 or equals q.

  (hLq : L ≤ q) :

Let L be a lower bound for the special prime q of an odd perfect number and for every odd prime factor of q - 1. Then (L - 3) / 2 is at most the total excess.

OddPerfect.AttackPrimality

OddPerfect/AttackPrimality.lean · 344 lines · 12 public theorems · imports Network, Valuation, Zsigmondy, SpecialPrime, Spoof

Order data on the edges of the network: an edge from a smaller prime to a larger one has order at least 3, and if the largest prime factor P has even exponent e then 2e + 5 ≤ P. The decidable statement MaxReceives asks for a divisor d ≥ 3 of e + 1 with bd ≡ 1 (mod P); it does not require d to be the exact order. Descartes' spoof violates it, while every odd perfect number satisfies it.

Proof idea. For an edge p → r the order d of p modulo r divides both ep + 1 and r − 1. Orders 1 and 2 would force r to divide p − 1 or p + 1, which is impossible for an odd prime r > p, so an upward edge has d ≥ 3. By conservation the largest prime factor receives an edge, necessarily upward.

Descartes' spoof violates MaxReceives: no base divides geom b (e b) by 22021. The cause is that 22021 = 19² · 61 is not prime, and the formal divisor sums deliver its factors 19, 19, 61 from three different components (7², 11², 13²).

OddPerfect.Phi3Algebra

OddPerfect/Phi3Algebra.lean · 1088 lines · 43 public theorems · imports Phi3

Reusable algebra of φ₃(x) = x² + x + 1, and of x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1, for the inequalities between Ω and ω: factorization identities such as φ₃(b²) = φ₃(b)(b² − b + 1) and φ₃((a + 1)²) = φ₃(a)φ₃(a + 1), the solutions of φ₃(x) = m·φ₃(b) when φ₃(b) is prime, and the fact that for a prime c at most two residues x modulo c have c dividing x² + x + 1.

Proof idea. The identities are polynomial identities checked by ring after casting to the integers. For the equation φ₃(x) = m·φ₃(b) with p = φ₃(b) prime and 1 < m ≤ p: x² < φ₃(x) ≤ p² gives x < p, and x ≠ b because m > 1. Then x and b are two distinct roots of t² + t + 1 modulo p below p, and two such roots add up to p − 1, so x + b + 1 = b² + b + 1 and x = b². The counting statement follows because a quadratic has at most two roots modulo a prime.

theorem ch_factorization1 {a b c d e : ℕ} (hc : c.Prime) (ha : phi3 a = c * d)
  (hb : phi3 b = c * e) (hcd : d < c) (hde : e < d) :

If c is prime, a ^ 2 + a + 1 = c d, b ^ 2 + b + 1 = c e and c > d > e, then c = a + b + 1 and a - b = d - e (stated additively as a + e = b + d). The paper's positivity hypotheses are not needed. Compared with phi3_roots_sum, the size condition a, b < c is derived from c > d > e, and the cofactor relation is added.

Φ₃(Φ₅(x)) = (x ^ 2 - x + 1)(x ^ 6 + 3 x ^ 5 + 5 x ^ 4 + 6 x ^ 3 + 7 x ^ 2 + 6 x + 3). Natural subtraction is harmless since x ≤ x ^ 2.

OddPerfect.ch_factorization3

theorem ch_factorization3 {a b d e f : ℕ} (hd : d.Prime) (hA : phi3 a = 3 * d * e)
  (hB : phi3 b = 3 * d * f) (hde : e ≤ d) (hef : f < e) :
  3 * d = a + b + 1 ∧ a + f = b + e

If d is prime, a ^ 2 + a + 1 = 3 d e, b ^ 2 + b + 1 = 3 d f and d ≥ e > f, then 3 d = a + b + 1 and a - b = e - f (stated as a + f = b + e). The paper also assumes a, b prime; this is not needed.

OddPerfect.ch_factorization2

theorem ch_factorization2 {a b d e f : ℕ} (ha : a.Prime) (hb : b.Prime) (hd : d.Prime)
  (hA : phi3 a = 3 * d * e) (hB : phi3 b = d * f) (hde : e ≤ d) (hef : f < e) :
  d = a + b + 1 ∧ a + f = b + 3 * e

If a, b, d are prime, a ^ 2 + a + 1 = 3 d e, b ^ 2 + b + 1 = d f and d ≥ e > f, then d = a + b + 1 and a - b = 3 e - f (stated as a + f = b + 3 e). The paper assumes d > e; d ≥ e suffices. The paper's mod 3 step tacitly assumes b ≡ 2 (mod 3); the cases b = 3 and b ≡ 1 (mod 3) are handled here separately (the latter by a size argument).

OddPerfect.yamada_gap

theorem yamada_gap {l q x₁ x₂ : ℕ} (hl : Odd l) (hq : q.Prime)
  (h1 : (x₁ : ZMod q) ^ l = 1) (h2 : (x₂ : ZMod q) ^ l = 1)
  (hq1 : x₁ ^ ((l - 1) / 2) < q)
  (hind : ∀ i j : ℕ, x₁ ^ i = x₂ ^ j → i = 0 ∧ j = 0) :
  x₁ ^ ((l + 1) / 6) < x₂

Let q be prime, let x₁, x₂ satisfy x₁ ^ l ≡ x₂ ^ l ≡ 1 (mod q), let x₁ and x₂ be multiplicatively independent (x₁ ^ i = x₂ ^ j only for i = j = 0), and let x₁ ^ ((l - 1) / 2) < q. Then x₂ > x₁ ^ ⌊(l + 1) / 6⌋. In the paper q is the common large prime of Φ_l(x₁) = p ^ {m₁} q and Φ_l(x₂) = p ^ {m₂} q with p ^ {m₁} < q, which gives the size hypothesis. For l = 3 the conclusion is only x₂ > 1; for l = 5 it is x₂ > x₁. The proof counts the l + 1 or more distinct residues x₁ ^ i x₂ ^ j < q that are l-th roots of unity modulo q.

theorem ch_unique_S1_S2 {a b c d g h : ℕ} (ha : a.Prime) (hb : b.Prime) (hc : c.Prime)

  (hA : phi3 a = c * d) (hB : phi3 b = 3 * c) (hg : g.Prime) (hg2 : g ≠ 2)
  (hG : phi3 g = d * h) (hdh : h < d) (hh : h = 1 ∨ (h.Prime ∧ h ≠ 2)) : False

Let a, b, c, d be odd primes with c > d, d ≠ 3, a ^ 2 + a + 1 = c d and b ^ 2 + b + 1 = 3 c. Then there is no odd prime g with g ^ 2 + g + 1 = d h, d > h, where h = 1 or h is an odd prime.

OddPerfect.LargePrimes

OddPerfect/LargePrimes.lean · 614 lines · 18 public theorems · imports SpecialPrime, Network, Phi3 contains novelty unverified

Upper bounds for prime factors in terms of N. Every prime factor p satisfies p³ < 3N, and p⁴ < 2N when its exponent is at least 2; any two prime factors p < q satisfy p⁴q < 2N; every prime factor other than the largest satisfies p⁵ < 2N; and any two distinct prime factors satisfy (pq)⁴ < 6N². Along the way: no two odd primes satisfy both q | p² + p + 1 and p | q + 1, while 13 divides 3² + 3 + 1 and 3 divides 13² + 13 + 1.

Proof idea. The basic tool: if p has exact exponent e in N, then pe and σ(pe) are coprime divisors of 2N, so their product divides 2N, and pe < σ(pe) gives p2e < 2N. With e ≥ 2 this is p⁴ < 2N. Bounds involving two primes use that the divisor sums of two distinct components together divide 2N, and add a further prime factor q to the product whenever q does not divide σ(pe). For a prime with exponent 1, the cubic bound takes a component rc whose divisor sum is a multiple of p and compares its size with the part of p + 1 that it shares with rc.

OddPerfect.pow_three_lt_three_mul

theorem pow_three_lt_three_mul (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hpN : p ∣ N) :
  p ^ 3 < 3 * N

Every prime factor p of an odd perfect number satisfies p ^ 3 < 3 * N. For exponent at least two this follows from p ^ 4 < 2 * N. For p ∥ N, take a component r ^ c with p ∣ σ(r ^ c) = p * s, let r ^ e = gcd(p + 1, r ^ c); then r ^ c * σ(r ^ c) * (p + 1) ≤ 2 N r ^ e, and r ^ e ∣ s + (1 + r + ... + r ^ (e - 1)) forces s large enough.

OddPerfect.CountingClaytonHansen

OddPerfect/CountingClaytonHansen.lean · 1478 lines · 58 public theorems · imports CountingZelinsky, Phi3Algebra

99ω ≤ 37Ω + 187 for every odd perfect number, and 51ω ≤ 19Ω + 46 when 3 does not divide N, after Clayton and Hansen (arXiv 2303.11974).

Proof idea. The primes with exponent exactly 2, other than 3, are sorted by the number of prime factors of p² + p + 1 and by p modulo 3. Each class contributes to, and receives from, the others through the factors of p² + p + 1, and each such relation is one linear inequality, proved as its own lemma. A linking map sends a prime of the small classes to a prime factor of its p² + p + 1; it is injective on one union of classes and at most two to one on a larger one. One lemma of the printed argument, whose proof applies an earlier lemma without its size hypotheses, is replaced by two direct lemmas. Some rows of the printed system are used in a merged form with the same optimum. A cited result, that no prime is the largest factor of three values of x² + x + 1 in the required configuration, is proved here by unique factorization in the Eisenstein integers, carried out by hand on integer pairs. The final ledger of linear relations is closed by integer linear arithmetic.

theorem ch_ledger {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) :
  ∃ s t G f s1 a2 b2 a3 b3 a4 b4 s1s s1t xs xt sone : ℕ,
    N.primeFactors.card = s + t + (if 3 ∣ N then 1 else 0) ∧
    ∑ p ∈ N.primeFactors, N.factorization p = 2 * s + G + f ∧
    f = N.factorization 3 ∧ 4 * t ≤ G + 3 ∧
    s = s1 + a2 + b2 + a3 + b3 + a4 + b4 ∧ sone = a2 + a3 + a4 ∧
    s1 ≤ s1s + s1t + 1 ∧ a3 + b3 ≤ xs + xt ∧ sone ≤ f ∧
    s1 + 2 * b2 + 3 * b3 + a4 + 4 * b4 ≤ G + a2 ∧
    s1 + a2 + b2 ≤ sone + t ∧ 2 * (s1 + a2) + b2 + a3 ≤ 2 * (sone + t) ∧
    2 * s1s + xs ≤ 2 * sone ∧ 4 * s1t + xt ≤ G

With s = |S|, t = |T ∪ {p₀}|, G = g₄ + e₀, f = v₃(N), s1 = |S₁|, a2, a3, a4 the sizes of S_{2,1}, S_{3,1}, S_{≥4,1}, b2, b3, b4 those of S_{2,2}, S_{3,2}, S_{≥4,2}, sone = |S_{·,1}|, s1s = |S₁^S|, s1t = |S₁^T|, xs = |X_S|, xt = |X_T|, the listed linear relations hold.

OddPerfect.DivisorCount

OddPerfect/DivisorCount.lean · 222 lines · 8 public theorems · imports ExponentCap, ThreeFreeCert, RadicalBound

For every prime factor p of N with exponent e, the number of divisors of e + 1 is at most ω(N); this includes the special prime. Also two exclusions of exact square patterns without the hypothesis that 3 does not divide N, and identities for the radical R, the product F of p − 1, and the least component pe + 1.

Proof idea. Each divisor d ≥ 3 of e + 1 has a prime factor of N, other than p, modulo which p has order exactly d; different divisors give different primes. The divisor 1 is matched with p itself. For the special prime the divisor 2 is matched with an odd prime factor of (p + 1)/2, which divides N and modulo which p has order at most 2, so it is none of the primes used for d ≥ 3. Counting gives the bound.

OddPerfect.SmallPrimes

OddPerfect/SmallPrimes.lean · 1008 lines · 28 public theorems · imports RadicalBound, ExponentCap

Bounds for the small prime factors. A general inequality bounds the smallest prime outside a set S of prime factors through the exact abundancy of the components in S, with corollaries for the second, third and fourth smallest prime factors. An exchange lemma gives a lower bound on ω(N) for each lower bound on the smallest prime factor: at least 7, 15, 27, 41, 62, 85, 115 prime factors when the smallest is at least 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. If 3 does not divide N, then ω(N) ≥ 8.

Proof idea. Split the prime factors into S and the rest T, with p the smallest prime of T. From 2 = HS·HT and a telescoped bound for HT over |T| primes that are at least p one gets a linear inequality for p. The exchange lemma compares a set of integers with the primes of an interval: replacing each element by a smaller prime not yet used can only increase the product of s/(s − 1), so if the first k primes from the lower bound on do not reach abundancy 2, no set of k prime factors does. The kernel computes these products. For ω(N) ≥ 8 without 3, only four supports of seven primes pass the product test, and each is excluded with the exponent restrictions that hold when 3 does not divide N.

theorem eight_le_card_primeFactors_of_not_three_dvd (h : OddPerfect N) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) :
  8 ≤ N.primeFactors.card

If 3 ∤ N for an odd perfect number N, then N has at least eight distinct prime factors. With seven prime factors the support would be {5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, q} with q ∈ {23, 29, 31, 37} (the only supports with ∏ p/(p-1) > 2); each is excluded by the exponent restrictions for 3 ∤ N (the special prime is ≡ 1 (mod 12), primes ≡ 1 (mod 3) have exponent ≢ 2 (mod 3), all other exponents are even) and a short branch and bound on the exponents of 5, 11, 13, 17, 37 with abundancy bounds only.

OddPerfect.RadicalDefect

OddPerfect/RadicalDefect.lean · 593 lines · 15 public theorems · imports RadicalBound contains novelty unverified

Write R for the product of the prime factors of N and F for the product of p − 1 over them. If every component pe + 1 is at least B³ for an odd B, then 4B³(R − 2F) < (3B + 2)R. Consequences: for every odd perfect number, 3² exactly divides N, or 5 exactly divides N, or 500(R − 2F) < 17R; analogous statements for B = 7, 9, 11; the last inequality whenever 3 does not divide N; and a certificate rule that forces a small component from a subset of the support.

Proof idea. Perfection gives 1 − 2F/R = 1 − ∏(1 − 1/y) ≤ ∑ 1/y over the components y = pe + 1. An ordinary prime above B has e ≥ 2, so its term is at most 1/p³, and the sum of 1/n³ over odd n from B + 2 on telescopes below 1/(4B²). The odd primes up to B number at most (B − 1)/2 and each contributes at most 1/B³ by hypothesis, and the special prime contributes at most 1/B³. The three parts add up to (3B + 2)/(4B³), which bounds the defect uniformly in the unknown primes. The trichotomy then lists the components below B³: for B = 5 these are 3² and 5¹.

OddPerfect.RadicalExponent

OddPerfect/RadicalExponent.lean · 663 lines · 6 public theorems · imports LargePrimes, SpecialBelow, OmegaFive

The radical R of an odd perfect number N (the product of its distinct prime factors) satisfies R < 2 N17/26, stated as R26 < 226 N17: the theorem of Luca and Pomerance (2010) for odd perfect numbers. Also R2 < N when the special exponent is not 1, and R3 < N2 outside one exceptional shape. Known mathematics.

Proof idea. Compare R2 qk with q2 N prime by prime. Then three ranges for the special prime q: small q, large q (with q3 < 3N), and a middle range where the part of N with exponents at least four is small; there the prime p with q dividing σ(p2) and the primes that feed p would make N a product of at most four prime powers, against five distinct prime factors.

OddPerfect.RadicalExponentTwo

OddPerfect/RadicalExponentTwo.lean · 606 lines · 3 public theorems · imports LargePrimes, OmegaFive, Cyclotomic

The radical R of an odd perfect number N satisfies R < 2 N9/14, stated as R14 < 214 N9. Known mathematics: the exponent 9/14 is due to Klurman (2016); his paper was not read, the proof here modifies the argument of Luca and Pomerance.

Proof idea. Same skeleton as RadicalExponent with sharper thresholds. Two new steps: σ(ue) < 2ue for the components of exponent at least four, and, when two primes t > s both feed the prime p, the difference σ(t2) − σ(s2) = (t − s)(t + s + 1) gives p ≤ 2t.

OddPerfect.OmegaSix

OddPerfect/OmegaSix.lean · 946 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Certificate, OmegaFour, SmallestPrime

An odd perfect number has at least six distinct prime factors. The proof is a search over the prime factors in increasing order, run by the kernel, with a soundness theorem for the search.

Proof idea. If 3 does not divide N there are at least seven prime factors, so 3 divides N. A state lists primes with exponents that are exact or bounded below, the number j of further primes, and a lower bound for them. Lower and upper bounds L and U for the abundancy of the listed part use σ(pk)/pk and p/(p − 1). A state closes by an abundant divisor (L > 2), by two exact odd exponents, by a factor chain (the part of an exact σ(pk) coprime to the listed primes needs unlisted prime factors, impossible when none remain or when it is too small), or, with the support fully listed, when 2 is outside the reachable range. Otherwise the smallest unlisted prime lies in a finite window, because the remaining j primes must lift U above 2, and the search tries each prime in it, or it splits one exponent into an exact value and a larger lower bound. Exact exponents force the remaining primes through their divisor sums, which also closes the families where the largest prime is not bounded in advance.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeOrder

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeOrder.lean · 746 lines · 11 public theorems · imports AttackPrimality, ExponentCap contains novelty unverified

The largest prime factor P and the multiplicative orders of the primes that send a factor P. Results: P is not 3·4t + 1 for any t ≥ 2; P − 1 is not a power of 2; if a prime q = 3·4t + 1 with t ≥ 2 divides N, some prime factor is at least q + 3·2t(2t − 1)/2; and if P − 1 = 3·2j, every sender has order 3 and weight 1, and the exponent of P is 1, or it is 2 and both roots of x² + x + 1 below P are prime factors of N.

Proof idea. A prime p that sends a factor P has an order d modulo P with d ≥ 3, d dividing P − 1 and dividing ep + 1, and ep + 1 is not a multiple of 4. For P = 3·4t + 1 this leaves d = 3 or d = 6. With x = 2t, the two roots of z² + z + 1 modulo P are 3x(x − 1)/2 and 3x(x + 1)/2, both even for t ≥ 2, so no odd prime below P has order 3. An order 6 sender has an odd exponent, so it is the special prime, and its weight is the valuation of P in p² − p + 1, which is 1 by size. Then the exponent of P would be 1, making P special as well, a contradiction. When P − 1 is a power of 2 no order d ≥ 3 that is odd or twice odd exists at all. The exponent t = 1 is a real exception: 3 has order 3 modulo 13.

theorem false_of_senders_odd (h : OddPerfect N) {q : ℕ} (hq : q ∈ N.primeFactors)
  (hsend : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) →
    Odd (N.factorization p) ∧ padicValNat q (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)) ≤ 1) :
  False

A column with only odd exponent senders of weight at most one is impossible. Let q be a prime factor of the odd perfect number N such that every sender p (a prime factor p ≠ q with q ∣ σ(p ^ e_p)) has odd exponent and v_q(σ(p ^ e_p)) ≤ 1. If q is special, nothing sends into it and e_q = 0; otherwise only the special prime sends, so e_q ≤ 1, against e_q even and positive.

Senders have order 3 or 6; order 3 would make the sender a root, so all senders have order 6, odd exponent, and weight v_P(p ^ 2 - p + 1) ≤ 1 (as p < P); false_of_senders_odd ends it.

Target A. For t ≥ 2, the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number is not 3 · 4 ^ t + 1. With y = 2 ^ (t - 1) the roots of X ^ 2 + X + 1 modulo P = 12 y ^ 2 + 1 are 3 y (2 y - 1) and 3 y (2 y + 1), both even since y is even.

Target B. If q = 3 · 4 ^ t + 1 with t ≥ 2 is a prime factor of an odd perfect number, then the largest prime factor P satisfies P ≥ q + 3 · 2 ^ t (2 ^ t - 1) / 2. Otherwise every sender into q lies below q + a with a = 3 · 2 ^ t (2 ^ t - 1) / 2: order 2 would give p = q - 1, order 3 gives p ∈ {a, b} (even), and order 6 gives p ∈ {a + 1, b + 1}, so p < q and the weight is at most one.

OddPerfect.factorization_largest_le_two

theorem factorization_largest_le_two (h : OddPerfect N) {P j : ℕ}
  (hP : P ∈ N.primeFactors) (hmax : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ P) (hj : P - 1 = 3 * 2 ^ j) :
  N.factorization P ≤ 2

Capacity of the largest prime factor when P - 1 = 3 · 2 ^ j: e_P ≤ 2. Each sender has order 3 or 6 and weight at most one; sending an order 3 sender p to p and an order 6 sender to -p maps the senders injectively into the roots of X ^ 2 + X + 1 modulo P (two odd numbers below P do not add up to P), and there are at most two roots.

OddPerfect.largest_cube_roots_odd

theorem largest_cube_roots_odd (h : OddPerfect N) {P j : ℕ}
  (hP : P ∈ N.primeFactors) (hmax : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ P) (hj : P - 1 = 3 * 2 ^ j)
  (hodd : ∀ r < P, P ∣ r ^ 2 + r + 1 → Odd r) :
  (∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ P → P ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) →
    orderOf (p : ZMod P) = 3 ∧ 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1 ∧
      padicValNat P (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)) = 1) ∧
  (N.factorization P = 1 ∨ (N.factorization P = 2 ∧
    ∀ r < P, P ∣ r ^ 2 + r + 1 → r ∈ N.primeFactors ∧ 3 ∣ N.factorization r + 1))

The odd root case. Let P be the largest prime factor, P - 1 = 3 · 2 ^ j, and suppose every root r < P of X ^ 2 + X + 1 modulo P is odd. Then every sender into P has order 3, 3 ∣ e_p + 1 and weight exactly 1 (an order 6 sender p would make the even number P - p a root); and either e_P = 1, so P is the special prime, or e_P = 2 and every root r < P is a prime factor of N with 3 ∣ e_r + 1. A sender may be the special prime when e_P = 2 (its exponent can be ≡ 5 (mod 12)).

    orderOf (p : ZMod P) = 3 ∧ 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1 ∧
      padicValNat P (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)) = 1) ∧

    ∀ r < P, P ∣ r ^ 2 + r + 1 → r ∈ N.primeFactors ∧ 3 ∣ N.factorization r + 1))

Structure of the largest prime factor P with P - 1 = 3 · 2 ^ j, with no parity hypothesis. The roots below P of X ^ 2 + X + 1 modulo P share one parity (roots_same_parity); an even root is excluded by false_of_largest_of_cube_roots_even, so they are all odd and largest_cube_roots_odd applies: every sender has order 3 and weight 1, and either e_P = 1 or e_P = 2 and every root is a prime factor r with 3 ∣ e_r + 1.

OddPerfect.SupportBridges

OddPerfect/SupportBridges.lean · 310 lines · 12 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, ClosedLoop, ValuationBounds, Reciprocity, SpecialPrime, Pratt, Cyclotomic contains novelty unverified

Consequences of existing theorems about the set of prime factors. Call a prime of Fermat type when p − 1 is a power of 2. Every prime with even exponent has a receiver that is not of Fermat type, and at least two prime factors of N are not of Fermat type. Every prime factor has exponent 1 or a receiver modulo which its order is the exponent plus one. If the special prime s divides the component divisor sum of a prime q ≡ 3 (mod 4), then q does not divide s + 1; for q = 3 this bounds the exponent of 3 by (ω − 1)². A control set of six primes shows how small the gap R − 2F can be.

Proof idea. For an even exponent e, a primitive prime factor r of σ(pe) has p of order e + 1 modulo r, an odd number at least 3 dividing r − 1, so r is not of Fermat type. If only one prime t were not of Fermat type, t would be the special prime, and an ordinary p of Fermat type would have odd order above 1 modulo every prime factor r of σ(pe), so r would not be of Fermat type and r = t. Every ordinary component divisor sum would then be a power of t, which the closed loop theorem excludes. For the direct edge: q is a square modulo s, reciprocity with s ≡ 1 (mod 4) makes s a square modulo q, and −1 is not a square modulo q ≡ 3 (mod 4), so s ≢ −1 (mod q).

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeFactor

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeFactor.lean · 687 lines · 3 public theorems · imports ExponentCap, Abundancy

An odd perfect number has a prime factor above 10000. The proof is a search with a soundness theorem valid for every bound B, run by the kernel for B = 10000.

Proof idea. Suppose every prime factor is at most B. A prime known to divide N branches on its exponent e, which must satisfy 2e + 3 ≤ B and Euler's parity rule, and σ(pe) must have only prime factors up to B that are not excluded. An odd exponent is rejected when another prime already has one. The odd prime factors of σ(pe) are then forced to divide N. When no forced prime is left to treat, the smallest undecided prime is split into dividing and not dividing. A branch closes when the recorded exponents alone give an abundant divisor, or when the product of the abundancy bounds over all primes up to B that are not excluded is below 2, with σ(qe)/qe for a prime with exact exponent and q/(q − 1) otherwise. That product is computed from two fixed products over all primes up to B, corrected at the recorded and the excluded primes.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeFactorTwo

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeFactorTwo.lean · 881 lines · 4 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeFactor

A cheaper way for the kernel to accept the table of the largest prime factor search: each row of the table is proved correct from a certificate that passes a cheap check, in place of recomputing the row. Proves that an accepted search with certified rows gives a prime factor above the bound B.

Proof idea. A row lists the exponents e of a prime p for which σ(pe) may have only prime factors up to B. For every other exponent the certificate gives data from which the check shows that σ(pe) has a prime factor above B. The list of odd primes up to B is checked by trial division up to the square root of B.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeFactorThree

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeFactorThree.lean · 801 lines · 7 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeFactorTwo

A cheaper row certificate for the largest prime factor search: for each odd prime r a product Mr of the primes q up to the bound with q ≡ 1 (mod 2r) is fixed once, and a row is accepted from σ(pr−1) modulo Mr together with a size bound. Also three step lemmas that join a search from separately checked subtrees.

Proof idea. A prime factor of σ(pr−1) is r or is 1 modulo 2r, so only the primes in Mr matter below the bound; one modular power replaces the full number.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSum

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSum.lean · 538 lines · 16 public theorems · imports Abundancy, SpecialPrime

Bounds for the sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors: 23/40 < ∑ 1/p < 347/500, and log 2 < ∑ 1/(p − 1). The upper bound is the rational form of ∑ 1/p < log 2 + 1/29 − log(30/29).

Proof idea. For the lower bound, 2 = σ(N)/N is below the product of p/(p − 1), so log 2 is below the sum of log(p/(p − 1)). The difference log(p/(p − 1)) − 1/p is bounded explicitly at the primes up to 19 and by a telescoping sum over odd numbers from 23 on, and 3, 5 and 7 cannot all divide N. For the upper bound, an ordinary prime has exponent at least 2, so its component is at least 1 + 1/p + 1/p², whose logarithm exceeds 1/p; the special prime q gives 1 + 1/q. Hence ∑ 1/p is at most log 2 plus 1/q − log(1 + 1/q), minus the slack of the ordinary primes. The term for q decreases in q. For q = 5 and q = 17 the prime 3 divides N and its slack is larger, for q = 13 the prime 7 divides N, and otherwise q ≥ 29.

OddPerfect.LowerBound

OddPerfect/LowerBound.lean · 10585 lines · 43 public theorems · imports Euler, Seed.Example, Seed.Starter, Pratt, OmegaFive, SmallestPrime

Every odd perfect number exceeds 1079. The module defines a proof tree language for lower bounds on N with a soundness theorem, and the kernel checks three trees. A bound that needs no search is also proved: N ≥ 4002075.

Proof idea. A state is a list of facts about N: a prime power divides N, a number divides an exponent plus one, an exponent is exact, or a prime does not divide N. A branch splits the exponent of a prime, forces a prime power qk that divides the product of the known component divisor sums (using σ(N) = 2N and that σ(pa) divides σ(pe) when a + 1 divides e + 1), or passes from an odd exponent to the next even one. A leaf closes when the least common multiple of the recorded prime powers and half the product of the divisor sums, which divides N, exceeds the bound; or by a contradiction: an excluded prime divides N, an exact exponent is exceeded, two primes have odd exponent, or a divisor is abundant. The trees cover the cases 3 divides N; 5 divides N and 3 does not; 7 divides N and 3, 5 do not. If no prime below 11 divides N, the product of t/(t − 1) over the primes from 11 to 127 is below 2, so N has at least 27 prime factors, which gives the bound directly. All primes used for forcing come from one table of primality certificates that is checked once.
