OddPerfect.LowerBound.compP_sound

theorem compP_sound {p a : ℕ} {f : Fact} (hf : f.Holds N) (h : compP p a f = true) :
  p.Prime ∧ a + 1 ∣ N.factorization p + 1

A fact accepted by compP p a gives a + 1 ∣ N.factorization p + 1 with p prime.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.oddP_sound

theorem oddP_sound {f : Fact} (hf : f.Holds N) (h : oddP f = true) :
  f.prime.Prime ∧ Odd (N.factorization f.prime)

A fact accepted by oddP records a prime with odd exponent.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.special_of_odd

theorem special_of_odd (h : OddPerfect N) {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (ho : Odd (N.factorization p)) :
  p % 4 = 1 ∧ N.factorization p % 4 = 1 ∧
    ∀ r, r.Prime → Odd (N.factorization r) → r = p

An odd exponent forces the special prime of Euler's form.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.gs_eq

theorem gs_eq {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (a : ℕ) : σ 1 (p ^ a) = gs p a

For prime p, σ (p ^ a) = gs p a.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.nodupB_cons

theorem nodupB_cons {x : ℕ} {l : List ℕ} (h : nodupB (x :: l) = true) :
  (∀ y ∈ l, y ≠ x) ∧ nodupB l = true

Unpacks nodupB on a cons.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.Dv_dvd_sigma

theorem Dv_dvd_sigma : ∀ (cs : List (ℕ × ℕ)) (M : ℕ), M ≠ 0 → nodupB (cs.map Prod.fst) = true →
  (∀ c ∈ cs, c.1.Prime ∧ c.2 + 1 ∣ M.factorization c.1 + 1) → Dv cs ∣ σ 1 M

The product of component divisor sums divides σ M.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.compsOK_sound

theorem compsOK_sound {s : List Fact} {cs : List (ℕ × ℕ)} (h : OddPerfect N) (hs : Holds N s)
  (hc : compsOK s cs = true) : Dv cs ∣ 2 * N

Accepted components give ∏ σ(p ^ a) ∣ 2 N.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.half_dvd

theorem half_dvd {D : ℕ} (hD : D ∣ 2 * N) : half D ∣ N

If D ∣ 2 N then half D ∣ N.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.base_dvd

theorem base_dvd {f : Fact} (hf : f.Holds N) : base f ∣ N

The prime power recorded by a fact divides N.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.Av_dvd

theorem Av_dvd : ∀ {s : List Fact}, Holds N s → Av s ∣ N

The least common multiple of the recorded prime powers divides N.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.tdAux_sound

theorem tdAux_sound {n : ℕ} : ∀ fuel d, tdAux n fuel d = true →
  ∀ m, d ≤ m → m * m ≤ n → ¬ m ∣ n

Soundness of the trial division loop.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.tdPrime_sound

theorem tdPrime_sound {n : ℕ} (h : tdPrime n = true) : n.Prime

Soundness of trial division.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.tdAux_complete

theorem tdAux_complete {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Prime) : ∀ fuel d, 2 ≤ d → n < fuel + d →
  tdAux n fuel d = true

The trial division loop accepts primes when the fuel suffices.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.tdPrime_complete

theorem tdPrime_complete {n : ℕ} (hn : n.Prime) : tdPrime n = true

Trial division accepts every prime.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.smallPrimes_check

theorem smallPrimes_check :
  (List.range 1000).all (fun r => !tdPrime r || smallPrimes.contains r) = true

smallPrimes contains every prime below 1000.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.mem_smallPrimes

theorem mem_smallPrimes {r : ℕ} (hr : r.Prime) (h : r < 1000) : r ∈ smallPrimes

Every prime below 1000 is in smallPrimes.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.mem_primesBelow

theorem mem_primesBelow {r R : ℕ} (hr : r.Prime) (hR : r < R) : r ∈ primesBelow R

Every prime below R is listed by primesBelow R.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.PT.allOK_mem

theorem PT.allOK_mem (T : PT) : ∀ {U : PT} {q : ℕ}, PT.allOK T U = true → U.mem q = true →
  ∃ a fs, entryOK T q a fs = true

A key found in a table has an entry passing entryOK.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.pm_eq_powModAux

theorem pm_eq_powModAux (n : ℕ) :
  ∀ fuel b e acc, pm n fuel b e acc = Pratt.powModAux n fuel b e acc

pm agrees with the project's binary modular exponentiation.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.pm_eq

theorem pm_eq (n a e : ℕ) (h : e < n) : pm n n a e 1 = a ^ e % n

Correctness of pm with the fuel used by entryOK.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.mem_of_dvd_ppow

theorem mem_of_dvd_ppow {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) : ∀ {fs : List (ℕ × ℕ)},
  (∀ c ∈ fs, c.1.Prime) → q ∣ ppow fs → ∃ c ∈ fs, c.1 = q

A prime dividing ∏ f ^ k, where every f is prime, is one of the f.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.PT.prime_of_mem

theorem PT.prime_of_mem {T : PT} (hT : T.allOK T = true) : ∀ q, T.mem q = true → q.Prime

Every key of a table whose entries all pass entryOK against the table itself is prime.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.coprime_dprod

theorem coprime_dprod {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) : ∀ {l : List (ℕ × ℕ)},
  (∀ c ∈ l, c.1.Prime) → (∀ c ∈ l, c.1 ≠ p) → Nat.Coprime p (dprod l)

A prime outside the list is coprime to the recorded product.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.dprod_sound

theorem dprod_sound : ∀ {l : List (ℕ × ℕ)}, nodupB (l.map Prod.fst) = true →
  (∀ c ∈ l, c.1.Prime ∧ c.1 ^ c.2 ∣ N) → dprod l ∣ N ∧ σ 1 (dprod l) = sprod l

The recorded product divides N, and its divisor sum is sprod.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.holds_cons

theorem holds_cons (f : Fact) {s : List Fact} (hf : f.Holds N) (hs : Holds N s) :
  Holds N (f :: s)

Adding a valid fact keeps a state valid.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.step_sound

theorem step_sound {L : ℕ} {T : PT} (hT : ∀ x, T.mem x = true → x.Prime) {i : Ins}
  {s : List Fact} {cs : List (List Fact)} (hst : step L T i s = some cs) (hcs : ∀ c ∈ cs, Good L c) : Good L s

Soundness of one step: if all children are good, the state is good.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.run_sound

theorem run_sound {L : ℕ} {T : PT} (hT : ∀ x, T.mem x = true → x.Prime) :
  ∀ (is : List Ins) (stk : List (List Fact)), run L T is stk = true → ∀ s ∈ stk, Good L s

Soundness of the runner: every state on an accepted stack is good.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.prod_range_le_prod

theorem prod_range_le_prod (S : Finset ℕ) : ∀ {m k : ℕ}, (∀ s ∈ S, Odd s ∧ m ≤ s) →
  k ≤ S.card → ∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (m + 2 * i) ≤ ∏ s ∈ S, s

A finite set of odd numbers, all at least m, with at least k elements has product at least m (m + 2) ⋯ (m + 2 (k - 1)).

OddPerfect.LowerBound.prod_consec_le_prod

theorem prod_consec_le_prod : ∀ (l : List ℕ) (S : Finset ℕ) {m : ℕ}, consec m l = true →
  (∀ s ∈ S, s.Prime ∧ m ≤ s) → l.length ≤ S.card → l.prod ≤ ∏ s ∈ S, s

A finite set of primes, all at least m, with at least |l| elements has product at least ∏ l when l lists the consecutive primes from m.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.le_of_card_primeFactors_consec

theorem le_of_card_primeFactors_consec (h : OddPerfect N) {m : ℕ} (l : List ℕ)
  (hl : consec m l = true) (hm : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, m ≤ p)
  (hk : l.length + 1 ≤ N.primeFactors.card) : m * l.prod ^ 2 ≤ N

If every prime factor of an odd perfect number is at least m, there are more than |l| of them, and l lists the consecutive primes from m, then N ≥ m (∏ l) ^ 2.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.structural_lower_bound

theorem structural_lower_bound {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) : 4002075 ≤ N

Structural bound with no search: an odd perfect number has at least five distinct prime factors, all odd, and all but the special one have exponent at least two, so N ≥ 3 (3 · 5 · 7 · 11) ^ 2.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.le_of_card_primeFactors

theorem le_of_card_primeFactors (h : OddPerfect N) {m k : ℕ}
  (hm : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, m ≤ p) (hk : k + 1 ≤ N.primeFactors.card) :
  m * (∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (m + 2 * i)) ^ 2 ≤ N

If every prime factor of an odd perfect number is at least m and there are more than k of them, then N ≥ m (m (m + 2) ⋯ (m + 2 (k - 1))) ^ 2: all prime factors but the special one have exponent at least two.

OddPerfect.LowerBound.length_le_card_primeFactors

theorem length_le_card_primeFactors (h : OddPerfect N) {P L : ℕ} (T : List ℕ) (hnd : T.Nodup)
  (hP : ∀ p, p.Prime → p < P → ¬ p ∣ N) (hT : ∀ t ∈ T, 2 ≤ t ∧ t ≤ L)
  (hcover : (List.range (L + 1)).all
    (fun p => !tdPrime p || Nat.blt p P || T.contains p) = true)
  (hval : (T.map fun t : ℕ => (t : ℚ) / (t - 1)).prod < 2 * ((L : ℚ) / (L - 1))) :
  T.length ≤ N.primeFactors.card

If no prime below P divides an odd perfect number N, and T is a list of distinct numbers in [2, L] containing every prime in [P, L] with ∏ t/(t-1) < 2 L/(L-1), then N has at least |T| distinct prime factors.

OddPerfect.LowerBoundTwoTablePrime

OddPerfect/LowerBoundTwoTablePrime.lean · 796 lines · 129 public theorems · imports LowerBoundTwoTableOk1, LowerBoundTwoTableOk2

Part of the kernel checked lower bound 10150. The statement that every entry of the table is prime, assembled from the two halves.

Proof idea. Combines the chunk checks into one lemma used by the tree runner.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.LowerBoundTwo.allOK_node

theorem allOK_node {T l r : PT} {p a : ℕ} {fs : List (ℕ × ℕ)} (h : entryOK T p a fs = true)
  (hl : PT.allOK T l = true) (hr : PT.allOK T r = true) :
  PT.allOK T (PT.node l p a fs r) = true

A node of the table is valid when its entry and both subtrees are.

OddPerfect.LowerBoundTwoTree1

OddPerfect/LowerBoundTwoTree1.lean · 10913 lines · 11 public theorems · imports LowerBoundTwoTablePrime

Part of the kernel checked lower bound 10150. Proof trees, part 1.

Proof idea. A tree branches on the exponent of a prime and follows forced prime factors of component divisor sums until the product of the known prime powers exceeds 10150.

OddPerfect.LowerBoundTwo

OddPerfect/LowerBoundTwo.lean · 268 lines · 6 public theorems · imports LowerBoundTwoTree1, LowerBoundTwoTree2, LowerBoundTwoTree3, LowerBoundTwoTree4

Every odd perfect number exceeds 10150. Also: an odd perfect number with no prime factor below 13 has at least 41 distinct prime factors. Known mathematics; the literature reaches 101500 (Ochem and Rao, 2012).

Proof idea. The factor chain method with the proof tree checker of LowerBound: roots 3, 5, 7 and 11 are closed by trees with 40986 instructions in all; an odd perfect number with none of these primes has so many prime factors that it exceeds the bound by counting.

OddPerfect.OmegaSeven

OddPerfect/OmegaSeven.lean · 637 lines · 9 public theorems · imports OmegaSix, SpecialPrime

Partial results for exactly six distinct prime factors, used by the final theorem in OmegaSevenFinal: if an odd perfect number has exactly six distinct prime factors, then 3 and 5 divide it, and its third smallest prime factor is one of 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31.

Proof idea. The search of OmegaSix is reused. A state is called closed when no odd perfect number satisfies it. A state is closed when the search closes it, or when every candidate for the next prime in its finite window gives a closed state. This splits one large search into separate leaves, each checked by the kernel on its own. The leaves cover the cases without 5, with 3 and 7, and with 3 and 5 and third prime above 31. The cases with third prime from 11 to 31 need far more search than the kernel can run here, and the case 3, 5, 17 does not close by this search at all, because the abundancy bound for Fermat primes stays below 2 for every exponent.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenFermat

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenFermat.lean · 111 lines · 3 public theorems · imports OmegaSeven

One more case for exactly six prime factors: if 17 divides N and 11 and 13 do not, some prime factor lies strictly between 17 and 601. So when 3, 5, 17 are the three smallest prime factors, the fourth smallest is below 601. The case is not excluded.

Proof idea. The state with 3, 5, 17 and a fourth prime above 600 has a finite window for that prime, the primes from 601 to 761, because three more primes must lift the abundancy to 2. The kernel checks one search per prime of the window.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalLogTwo

OddPerfect/ReciprocalLogTwo.lean · 157 lines · 6 public theorems · imports ReciprocalSum, SpecialPrime, SupportBridges

The sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors of an odd perfect number is below log 2. This is a classical result. The module proves a sharper form that keeps correction terms: with q the special prime and U any set of ordinary prime factors, the sum is at most log 2 + 1/(2q²) minus a quarter of the sum of 1/p² over U.

Proof idea. Take logarithms in σ(N) = 2N. An ordinary prime p contributes at least log(1 + 1/p + 1/p²), which is at least 1/p + 1/(4p²). The special prime contributes at least log(1 + 1/q), which is at least 1/q minus 1/(2q²). Some ordinary prime r divides (q + 1)/2, so its correction 1/(4r²) is at least 1/(q + 1)², which exceeds the loss 1/(2q²).

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeCapacity

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeCapacity.lean · 413 lines · 8 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeOrder contains novelty unverified

A bound for the exponent of the largest prime factor P in terms of the odd part m of P − 1: the exponent is at most the sum of φ(d)(φ(d) − 1) over the divisors d > 1 of m, and at most m − 1 primes p have P dividing σ(pe). The cases m = 1 and m = 3 recover the two results of LargestPrimeOrder. For large m the bound is weaker than the general exponent cap. Whether this statement is in the literature was not checked.

Proof idea. A prime p that sends a factor P has order t modulo P with t ≥ 3, t not divisible by 4 and t below P. So t is d or 2d with d odd, and p or −p has order exactly d. This signed residue determines p, because two odd numbers below P never add up to P, and there are φ(d) residues of order d. The power of P in σ(pe) equals the power of P in the cyclotomic value Φt(p), which lies below (p + 1)φ(t) ≤ Pφ(t), so it is at most φ(d) − 1.

OddPerfect.SecondLargestPrime

OddPerfect/SecondLargestPrime.lean · 1227 lines · 5 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeFactor

The search engine for two distinct prime factors above a bound B, with its soundness proof. The bounds themselves (72, and 58 as a corollary) are proved in SecondLargestPrimeTwo. Much larger bounds for the second largest prime factor are known in the literature; this is the range the kernel checks here.

Proof idea. Let P₀ be a prime factor above 3000, which exists by LargestPrimeFactor, and suppose every other prime factor is at most B. Each prime up to B is undecided, excluded, has an exponent bounded below, or has an exact exponent. Upper and lower bounds for the abundancy of the small part confine P₀ to a window, since the factor contributed by P₀ lies between 1 + 1/P₀ and P₀/(P₀ − 1). For an exact exponent k of p, the part of σ(pk) coprime to the small primes is a power of P₀, which determines P₀. A short window is enumerated. Once P₀ is fixed, the remaining conditions are finite: every σ(pk) is supported on the small primes and P₀, and σ of the power of P₀ is supported on the small primes. The search is a stack machine with a soundness theorem, and the kernel runs it in nine chunks with the intermediate stacks as literals.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenEngine

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenEngine.lean · 1296 lines · 7 public theorems · imports OmegaSeven

A second verified search engine for odd perfect numbers with exactly six distinct prime factors, with a soundness theorem against the same states as OmegaSix. It needs far fewer search nodes than the first engine and each node is cheaper for the kernel. It is the tool for the theorem that an odd perfect number has at least seven distinct prime factors, proved in OmegaSevenFinal.

Proof idea. A state lists some prime factors with exact or minimal exponents and says how many further prime factors there are, all above a bound. New rules: if an exponent is exact, the part of σ(pk) not made of listed primes consists of unlisted prime factors of N, so the state dies when that part has a small prime factor or is itself below the bound, and when that part must be prime it is added to the list; the next unlisted prime is bounded from below for any number of missing primes; small exponents are split before the next prime is enumerated; exact exponents that fail a local test are skipped. The definitions use structural recursors and closed forms for the geometric sums, which the kernel evaluates several times faster.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenSplit

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenSplit.lean · 152 lines · 5 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenEngine

Lemmas that cut one search of the engine into several smaller kernel runs: a split of an exponent into exactly k or at least the next admissible value, and a cover of the range of the next prime by contiguous intervals, each closed by one kernel run.

Proof idea. Kernel memory grows with the size of a single run, not with the number of runs in a file. Cutting at the split points the engine itself would choose keeps every run below 6000 search nodes.

A single closed child covers a range of length one.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenSplit.cover_join

theorem cover_join {P : ℕ → Prop} {a b c : ℕ} (h1 : ∀ q, a ≤ q → q < b → P q)
  (h2 : ∀ q, b ≤ q → q < c → P q) : ∀ q, a ≤ q → q < c → P q

Two adjacent ranges cover their union.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenSplit.closed_of_cover

theorem closed_of_cover {l : List Ent} {j m a c : ℕ} (hj : j ≠ 0) (hb : bounds l j m ≠ [])
  (ha : a ≤ lowB l j m) (hc : minB (bounds l j m) < c)
  (h : ∀ q, a ≤ q → q < c → Closed (l ++ [⟨q, kmin q, false⟩]) (j - 1) q) : Closed l j m

A state is closed when every child with next prime in a range around its window is closed.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenRootsA

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenRootsA.lean · 692 lines · 38 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenSplit

Kernel runs of the search engine for exactly six distinct prime factors: the prefixes 3, 5, p for p in 11, 19, 23, 29, 31, 37 to 61 and 3, 5, 17, q for q from 19 to 137. Each statement says that no odd perfect number with exactly six prime factors has the listed primes as its smallest prime factors (with the listed exponent information).

Proof idea. Generated by a script from a cut plan computed with an exact mirror of the engine. The four files hold 280 kernel runs and more than 200,000 search nodes in total.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenRootsC

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenRootsC.lean · 447 lines · 16 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenRootsB

Kernel runs of the search engine for exactly six distinct prime factors: the rest of the prefix 3, 5, 17, 257 and the prefix 3, 5, 17, 263. Each statement says that no odd perfect number with exactly six prime factors has the listed primes as its smallest prime factors (with the listed exponent information).

Proof idea. Generated by a script from a cut plan computed with an exact mirror of the engine. The four files hold 280 kernel runs and more than 200,000 search nodes in total.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenFinal

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenFinal.lean · 132 lines · 3 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenRootsD, OmegaSevenPilot

An odd perfect number has at least seven distinct prime factors. This is the theorem of Pomerance (Acta Arith. 25, 1973/74). The bound eight (Chein 1979, Hagis 1980) is not proved here.

Proof idea. By OmegaSix there are at least six. If there are exactly six, then 3 and 5 divide N and 7 does not (105 ∤ N), so the remaining four primes exceed 7. Enumerating the third prime (11 to 61) and, after 3, 5, 17, the fourth prime (19 to 761) reduces everything to the runs in OmegaSevenRootsA to OmegaSevenRootsD and OmegaSevenPilot.

Six prime factors with 3, 5, 17 the three smallest is impossible.

OddPerfect.OmegaSevenFiveSeven

OddPerfect/OmegaSevenFiveSeven.lean · 148 lines · 6 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenSplit, SmallPrimes

An odd perfect number with exactly seven distinct prime factors is divisible by 5 or by 7. This is a known consequence of the theorem of Chein and Hagis that an odd perfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors, which the library does not prove. The cases where 5 or 7 divides N are not treated.

Proof idea. By the three free theorem 3 divides N. If neither 5 nor 7 divides N, the six further primes all exceed 7, and the abundancy window leaves 11, 13, 17 or 19 for the least of them. Each of the four cases is closed by the verified engine of the seven prime theorem, cut into kernel checks of at most 6000 search nodes; the case 11 needs 6 checks, the others one each.

OddPerfect.NotThreeNine

OddPerfect/NotThreeNine.lean · 170 lines · 2 public theorems · imports OmegaSevenEngine, SmallPrimes

An odd perfect number not divisible by 3 has at least nine distinct prime factors. Known mathematics: Hagis and Kishore (1983) proved eleven and Nielsen (2007) twelve; only nine is proved here.

Proof idea. At least eight is already in SmallPrimes, so only exactly eight prime factors, all above 4, must be excluded. The abundancy window leaves 5, 7 or 11 for the least prime; windows of the next prime are applied until every case is small, and each case is closed by one kernel check of the verified search engine of the seven prime theorem. No fact beyond the cuts of that engine is used.

  Closed [] 8 4

  9 ≤ N.primeFactors.card

If 3 ∤ N for an odd perfect number N, then N has at least nine distinct prime factors.

OddPerfect.NotThreeTenForce

OddPerfect/NotThreeTenForce.lean · 48 lines · 1 public theorem · imports OmegaSevenSplit

One soundness lemma for the search states of the seven prime theorem: a prime that divides the divisor sum of an exact prime power component may be added to the state.

Proof idea. The divisor sum of an exact component p^k divides 2N, so each of its odd prime factors divides N. The verified engine already uses this step inside a check; stating it as a lemma lets a plan cut a large state at a forced prime.

theorem closed_of_force {l : List Ent} {j m p k c : ℕ} (hj : j ≠ 0) (hc : c.Prime)
  (hc2 : c ≠ 2) (he : (⟨p, k, true⟩ : Ent) ∈ l) (hd : c ∣ geom p k) (hn : c ∉ l.map Ent.p)
  (h : Closed (⟨c, kmin c, false⟩ :: l) (j - 1) m) : Closed l j m

A forced prime: an odd prime c, not listed, dividing the divisor sum geom p k of an exact entry p ^ k, may be added to the state.

OddPerfect.NotFifteenSixteen

OddPerfect/NotFifteenSixteen.lean · 68 lines · 2 public theorems · imports NotFifteenSixteenD, SmallestPrime

An odd perfect number divisible by neither 3 nor 5 has at least sixteen distinct prime factors. Fifteen is classical (Norton 1960); whether sixteen is in the literature was not verified.

Proof idea. At least fifteen is in SmallestPrime, so only exactly fifteen prime factors, all above 6, must be excluded. With fifteen primes from 7 on, the abundancy barely reaches 2, so the small primes are almost forced; the remaining cases are closed by kernel checks of the verified search engine with the forcing step of NotThreeTenForce: 240 checks, 122294 search nodes in all.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumTwo

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumTwo.lean · 212 lines · 7 public theorems · imports ReciprocalSum

Sharper lower bounds for the sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors: ∑ 1/p > 29/50 and ∑ 1/p > 581/1000. Bounds of this kind are classical (Suryanarayana; Suryanarayana and Hagis; Cohen), and the published constants by cases on 3 and 5 are stronger.

Proof idea. Write c(p) = log(p/(p − 1)) − 1/p, so log 2 < ∑ 1/p + ∑ c(p). The primes at least B contribute at most 1/(4(B − 2)) to ∑ c(p) by a telescoping bound. Each odd prime below B gets an explicit rational bound from the series of −log(1 − 1/p), and one of 3, 5, 7 is absent since 105 ∤ N. The cutoffs B = 101 and B = 1009 give the two constants; the kernel checks the rational inequality and the list of primes below B.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumThree

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumThree.lean · 354 lines · 1 public theorem · imports ReciprocalSumTwo

The sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors of an odd perfect number exceeds 59/100. Classical mathematics, and weaker than the published bound near 0.596 (Cohen, 1980).

Proof idea. As in ReciprocalSumTwo, log 2 < ∑ 1/p + ∑ c(p) with c(p) = log(p/(p − 1)) − 1/p. The thirteen smallest odd primes are treated jointly: for the subset of them dividing N, the product of 1 + 1/q at the special prime and 1 + 1/p + 1/p² at the others is at most the abundancy 2. A kernel check over all subsets and all roles of the special prime bounds the total correction weight of any subset that passes this test. The remaining primes below the cutoff are bounded by their weights and the tail by the telescoping bound; the kernel checks each weight against the series bound and the final rational inequality.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumFour

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumFour.lean · 493 lines · 5 public theorems · imports ReciprocalSumThree

The sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors of an odd perfect number exceeds 0.5960631, with separate bounds for the four cases on whether 3 and 5 divide N. Classical mathematics (Cohen, 1980); the constants were not compared digit by digit with the published ones.

Proof idea. The thirteen smallest odd primes are treated exactly: a kernel check runs over every subset of them that can divide N and every role of the special prime. For the remaining prime factors, log 2 < ∑ log(p/(p − 1)) and log(p/(p − 1)) ≤ (1 + 1/(2(m − 2)))/p for p ≥ m give a lower bound for their reciprocal sum; either all of them are at least 257, or one of them is at most 255 and contributes at least 1/255. The extremal case is 3, 5 and 17 together with one prime near 256.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumUpper

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumUpper.lean · 737 lines · 9 public theorems · imports ReciprocalSumFour, ReciprocalLogTwo

Upper bounds for the sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors of an odd perfect number by cases on 3 and 5: below 0.673634, 0.657304 and 0.677637 in the three cases where 3 or 5 divides N. With the lower bounds of ReciprocalSumFour each case has a window. Classical mathematics (Suryanarayana; Suryanarayana and Hagis; Cohen); the constants were not compared digit by digit with the published ones.

Proof idea. For a prime with exact exponent e the factor σ(p^e)/p^e has logarithm above 1/p, and the logarithms add up to log 2, so each small prime known to divide N lowers the bound log 2 by its gap; the special prime costs a little instead. A branch and stop check walks through the small odd primes and decides for each whether it divides N and in which role: exponent exactly 2, exponent at least 4, special with exponent 1, special with larger exponent. Exact components force the odd prime factors of their divisor sums into N, and when 3 has exponent exactly 2 the exact components may carry only two factors 3 in all.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumFive

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumFive.lean · 534 lines · 1 public theorem · imports ReciprocalSumFour

If neither 3 nor 5 divides N, the sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors exceeds 0.66747288. Cohen (1980) proves about 0.66747275 and shows that the bound cannot pass about 0.66747289 without new restrictions; this bound uses none and stays below that limit. The module header compares all eight constants of the library with Cohen's tables.

Proof idea. Every prime factor is at least 7 and log 2 < ∑ log(p/(p − 1)). A kernel check decides every prime below 5000 in increasing order and stops a branch by a tail estimate from the next prime.

OddPerfect.ReciprocalSumSeven

OddPerfect/ReciprocalSumSeven.lean · 410 lines · 7 public theorems · imports ReciprocalSum

Upper bounds in terms of the smallest prime factor p1 of an odd perfect number, for p1 ≥ 7: the sum of the reciprocals of the prime factors is below log 2 − 11/(50 p12), and the product of p/(p − 1) is at most 2 + 9/(4 p12). Known mathematics: Corollary 16 and Proposition 6 of Zelinsky (arXiv 2402.14234), stated there for p1 ≥ 11 and for every odd perfect number respectively; the product bound is proved here only for p1 ≥ 7.

Proof idea. The special prime q satisfies q ≥ 2 p1 − 1 because (q + 1)/2 divides N. The inequality x + 2x2/5 ≤ log(1 + x + x2) is proved for x ≤ 1/7 from truncated logarithm series, independently of the source, and the product bound by a telescoping sum.

  x + 2 * x ^ 2 / 5 ≤ Real.log (1 + x + x ^ 2)

For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1/7, x + 2x²/5 ≤ log(1 + x + x²).

  ∑ p ∈ T, (1 / ((p : ℝ) - 2) ^ 2 - 1 / (p : ℝ) ^ 2) ≤ 1 / ((M : ℝ) - 2) ^ 2

OddPerfect.prod_div_sub_one_le_two_add_of_seven_le

theorem prod_div_sub_one_le_two_add_of_seven_le {N p₁ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hp₁ : p₁ ∈ N.primeFactors) (hmin : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p₁ ≤ p) (h7 : 7 ≤ p₁) :
  ∏ p ∈ N.primeFactors, ((p : ℝ) / (p - 1)) ≤ 2 + 9 / (4 * (p₁ : ℝ) ^ 2)

For an odd perfect number N whose smallest prime factor p₁ is at least 7, ∏_{p ∣ N} p/(p-1) ≤ 2 + 9/(4 p₁²). Its Equation (25) replaces 1/(p_j² - 1) by the smaller 1/p_j² and 1/(p_i³ - 1) by 1/p_i³, which loses the upper bound; it passes from log H ≤ log h + 3/(4 p₁²) to H ≤ h (1 + 3/(4 p₁²)), which does not follow (since exp t ≥ 1 + t); and it calls 1/p_j² + ∑ 1/p_i³ ≤ 3/(4 p₁²) not hard to see. Here: ∏ p/(p-1) = 2 ∏ (p/(p-1))/A_p with A_p = σ(p^e)/p^e; each factor is at most q²/(q² - 1) (special prime q) or p³/(p³ - 1); so the product is at most 2 exp δ with δ = 1/(q² - 1) + ∑ 1/(p³ - 1) ≤ 1/(4 p₁ (p₁ - 1)) + 1/(4 (p₁ - 2)²) (using q ≥ 2 p₁ - 1 and a telescoping sum), and 2 exp δ ≤ 2 + 2 δ (1 + δ) ≤ 2 + 9/(4 p₁²) for p₁ ≥ 7.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeCapacityTwo

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeCapacityTwo.lean · 253 lines · 4 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeCapacity

Two isolated exclusions: the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number is neither 40961 nor 18433. Both values lie below published lower bounds for the largest prime factor, so the statements are known; they are proved here by the sender argument, not by a search.

Proof idea. A prime p of N whose σ(p^e) is divisible by the largest prime P has order t modulo P with t ≥ 3 and 4 ∤ t. For P = 40961 = 2¹³·5 + 1 this forces p¹⁰ ≡ 1, and the four odd candidates below P are composite, so nothing sends a factor P. For P = 18433 = 2¹¹·9 + 1 the only prime candidate is 4481; its order is even, so it would be the special prime, and it contributes at most one factor P, which contradicts Euler's form. The lists of roots are covered by a kernel check over all residues.

OddPerfect.false_of_largest_40961

theorem false_of_largest_40961 {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hP : 40961 ∈ N.primeFactors)
  (hmax : ∀ r ∈ N.primeFactors, r ≤ 40961) : False

40961 is not the largest prime factor of an odd perfect number: if it divides N and every prime factor of N is at most 40961, there is no sender into 40961, so its exponent is 0. This excludes one value only; it does not say the largest prime factor exceeds 40961.

OddPerfect.LargestPrimeRoots

OddPerfect/LargestPrimeRoots.lean · 196 lines · 6 public theorems · imports LargestPrimeCapacity, Pratt

A root table criterion and two isolated exclusions: 167772161 = 5·2²⁵ + 1 and 12289 = 3·2¹² + 1 can divide an odd perfect number only together with a larger prime factor. The method is elementary and of a known type; 167772161 lies above 10⁸, the published lower bound for the largest prime factor (Goto and Ohno), so that bound does not decide it. The theorems exclude single values and do not bound the largest prime factor in general.

Proof idea. If P = 2am + 1 is the largest prime factor, some smaller prime p of N has σ(pe) divisible by P. The order of p modulo P is not divisible by 4, so p2m ≡ 1 (mod P). In an integral domain, n distinct n-th roots of unity are all of them, so a table of 2m residues lists every candidate. For 167772161 the ten tenth roots are 1, 124765, 2596626, 36505748, 38977608, 128794553, 131266413, 165175535, 167647396 and 167772160; none is prime. For 13 the method rightly declines: 3 is a root and σ(3²) = 13.

OddPerfect.exists_primeFactor_gt_of_no_prime_root

theorem exists_primeFactor_gt_of_no_prime_root {N P a m : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hPp : P.Prime) (hd : P ∣ N) (hm : P - 1 = 2 ^ a * m)
  (hno : ∀ p, p.Prime → p < P → (p : ZMod P) ^ (2 * m) ≠ 1) :
  ∃ r ∈ N.primeFactors, P < r

Root criterion. Let N be an odd perfect number and P a prime dividing N, with P - 1 = 2 ^ a · m. If no prime p < P satisfies p ^ (2 m) ≡ 1 (mod P), then N has a prime factor larger than P.

OddPerfect.SecondLargestPrimeFast

OddPerfect/SecondLargestPrimeFast.lean · 368 lines · 3 public theorems · imports SecondLargestPrime

A faster form of the step function of the second largest prime search. It computes exactly the same values as the original step, proved by expandF_eq and runF_eq, so a run checked with it certifies its stack exactly as before. No new statement about odd perfect numbers.

Proof idea. Most of the cost of a step was reading the entries of the state in several separate passes. The fast step gathers everything it needs in one pass.

OddPerfect.SecondLargestPrimeTwo

OddPerfect/SecondLargestPrimeTwo.lean · 71 lines · 3 public theorems · imports SecondLargestPrimeFastData1, SecondLargestPrimeFastData2, SecondLargestPrimeFastData3, SecondLargestPrimeFastData4, SecondLargestPrimeFastData5, SecondLargestPrimeFastData6, SecondLargestPrimeFastData7, SecondLargestPrimeFastData8, SecondLargestPrimeFastData9

An odd perfect number has two distinct prime factors above 72. The earlier bound 58 follows as a corollary. Much larger bounds for the second largest prime factor are known in the literature; this is the range the kernel checks here.

Proof idea. The search engine of SecondLargestPrime, unchanged, started from a prime factor above 10000 (from LargestPrimeFactor) in place of 3000. The search for the bound 72 takes 101315 steps, about seven times the search for 58: the number of steps roughly doubles with each new small prime, which is what stops this method well below the bounds in the literature. This module assembles the checks of the nine data modules.

Exponent patterns

Exclusions of families of exponent patterns for the ordinary primes.

OddPerfect.Seed.ThreeFree

OddPerfect/Seed/ThreeFree.lean · 89 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Seed.Starter

When 3 does not divide a perfect number, exact square primes are ≡ 2 (mod 3), and every prime of σ(p²) is ≡ 1 (mod 3) and not itself an exact square.

Proof idea. If p ≡ 1 (mod 3) then 3 divides 1 + p + p², which would force 3. A prime q ≠ 3 dividing 1 + p + p² gives p³ ≡ 1 with p ≢ 1 modulo q, so p has order 3 and 3 divides q − 1.

  (hp : p.Prime) (he : n.factorization p = 2) : p % 3 = 2

An exact-square prime in a perfect number coprime to 3 has residue 2 modulo 3.

theorem exact_square_transfer {n p q : ℕ} (hn : n.Perfect) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ n)
  (hp : p.Prime) (he : n.factorization p = 2) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hdiv : q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ 2)) :
  p % 3 = 2 ∧ q ∣ n ∧ q ≠ 3 ∧ q % 3 = 1 ∧ n.factorization q ≠ 2

Every prime forced by an exact square belongs to the support of the perfect number, is 1 modulo 3, and cannot itself be an exact-square component.

OddPerfect.SteuerwaldThree

OddPerfect/SteuerwaldThree.lean · 140 lines · 1 public theorem · imports Euler

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 2 when 3 divides N.

Proof idea. 3 is ≡ 3 (mod 4), so it is ordinary with exponent 2 and the 3-adic ledger has budget exactly 2. A forcing chain starting at σ(3²) = 13 always produces three distinct non special primes p ≡ 1 (mod 3), each contributing a factor 3 through σ(p²) = 1 + p + p², which overflows the budget. The case split follows the primes 13, 61, 97 of the chain and whether each is special.

OddPerfect.Steuerwald

OddPerfect/Steuerwald.lean · 159 lines · 6 public theorems · imports ClosedLoop, SteuerwaldThree, Seed.Example

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 2; more generally, for an odd prime l not dividing N they cannot all equal l − 1. Hence some prime has an even exponent at least 4.

Proof idea. With l not dividing N and l dividing every ordinary e + 1: no ordinary prime is ≡ 1 (mod l), since such a prime would put a factor l into σ(pl−1). Every prime divisor of σ(pl−1) is l or ≡ 1 (mod l), so it must be the special prime q, and σ(pl−1) is a positive power of q. When all ordinary exponents equal l − 1 this is the situation excluded by ClosedLoop. For l = 3 this is the case where 3 does not divide N; the other case is SteuerwaldThree.

OddPerfect.steuerwald

theorem steuerwald {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → N.factorization p = 2) : False

Steuerwald: the primes other than the special prime cannot all have exponent two.

Proof idea. If 3 does not divide N, every σ(p²) of an ordinary p is a power of the special prime, which the closed loop argument excludes. If 3 divides N, the 3-adic budget is exactly 2, and a forcing chain from σ(3²) = 13 produces three ordinary primes ≡ 1 (mod 3), each adding a factor 3.

OddPerfect.McDaniel

OddPerfect/McDaniel.lean · 664 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Euler, Abundancy, Seed.Example, Seed.ThreeFree

The ordinary exponents cannot all be ≡ 2 (mod 3).

Proof idea. Case 3 divides N: each ordinary prime t has exponent at least 2 and forces every odd divisor of t² + t + 1, the special prime q forces every odd divisor of q + 1, and primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) are never special. A finite tree starting from 3 and 13 branches on whether each forced prime (13, 61, 97, 3169, 3348577, 3737657091169) is special, and every leaf exhibits an abundant divisor; large primes carry certified primality witnesses. Case 3 does not divide N: every ordinary p has p² + p + 1 = qc with c ≥ 1, q ≥ 13 and p ≥ 5 give 3c < p, distinct p give distinct c, and the abundancy stays below (13/12)·∏ (1 + 3−c) ≤ (13/12)(8/5) < 2.

OddPerfect.KanoldFour

OddPerfect/KanoldFour.lean · 151 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Certificate, Steuerwald, Valuation, SpecialPrime

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 4.

Proof idea. If 5 does not divide N, the prime length argument of Steuerwald applies with l = 5. If 5 is ordinary, the 5-adic budget is 4, and the chain σ(5⁴) = 11·71, σ(11⁴) = 5·3221, σ(71⁴) = 5·11·211·2221, σ(211⁴) = 5·1361·292661 yields 11, 71, 211 (all ≡ 3 mod 4, so ordinary) and 1361, 2221, 3221, at most one of which is special; five ordinary primes ≡ 1 (mod 5) each contribute a factor 5, which overflows. If 5 is special with exponent k, then 6 divides σ(5k), so 3 divides N; no σ(p⁴) is divisible by 3, and the 3-adic ledger gives 6 dividing k + 1, so σ(5⁵) = 2·3²·7·31 divides σ(5k), 7 divides N, and 3⁴·5·7⁴ is abundant.

OddPerfect.ExponentSix

OddPerfect/ExponentSix.lean · 206 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Certificate, Steuerwald, SpecialPrime

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 6.

Proof idea. If 7 does not divide N, the prime length argument applies with l = 7. If 7 divides N, it is ordinary (7 ≡ 3 mod 4) with 7-adic budget 6, and each ordinary prime p ≡ 1 (mod 7) puts a factor 7 into σ(p⁶), so seven such primes overflow. Forcing chains supply them: σ(7⁶) = 29·4733, then 4733 → 70001 → 50359 → 71 → 883 → 379 → 43 when neither 4733 nor 70001 is special. If 4733 is special, 4734 = 2·3²·263 forces 3 and 263, with chains 3 → 1093 → 14939 → 197, 263 → 239, 7211, and 7 → 29 → 88009573. If 70001 is special, 70002 = 2·3²·3889 forces 3, with chains through 1093, 14939, 197, then 29, 88009573 and 4733, 69655517.

OddPerfect.EqualExponents

OddPerfect/EqualExponents.lean · 531 lines · 20 public theorems · imports Steuerwald, Valuation, McDaniel, SpecialPrime

Odd perfect numbers whose ordinary exponents all equal 2β, and general forms: an l-adic counting bound, divisibility by l when every ordinary e + 1 is a power of l, and l⁴ dividing N. The count near the end of the module bounds only the ordinary primes whose σ(p2β) is not a power of the special prime; it does not bound the total number of prime factors.

Proof idea. The counting bound is the l-adic ledger: a prime factor p ≡ 1 (mod l) with exponent e has vl(σ(pe)) = vl(e + 1) by lifting the exponent, and these contributions add up to at most vl(N). Residue avoidance is the forcing step: if p has order l modulo a prime r and l divides e + 1, then r divides σ(pl−1), which divides σ(pe) and hence N.

OddPerfect.EqualExponentsBound

OddPerfect/EqualExponentsBound.lean · 467 lines · 9 public theorems · imports KanoldGeneral

If every ordinary exponent of an odd perfect number equals 2β, the number has at most 4β2 + 2β + 3 distinct prime factors. Known mathematics: Theorem 1.1, part (1), of Yamada, Colloq. Math. 103 (2005). Part (2) of that theorem (a bound for the size of N) and the later improvement of the bound are not proved here.

Proof idea. When 2β + 1 = l is prime, l is an ordinary prime factor; at most 2β(2β + 1) ordinary primes p have σ(p2β) not a power of the special prime q. For any other p ≠ l the whole power p2β divides σ of the special component, which forces p2β − 1 to divide the special exponent plus one; the divisors of that number each give a different prime factor of N, so at most one such p exists. When 2β + 1 is not prime, every ordinary prime sends to a prime that is 1 modulo a prime divisor l of 2β + 1, and there are at most 2β of those.

OddPerfect/EqualExponentsSize.lean · 39 lines · 2 public theorems · imports EqualExponentsBound, UpperBound

If every ordinary exponent of an odd perfect number N equals 2β, then N < 244β² + 2β + 3, so for each β only finitely many numbers are candidates. Known mathematics: Theorem 1.1, part (2), of Yamada, Colloq. Math. 103 (2005).

Proof idea. Combine the bound on the number of prime factors from EqualExponentsBound with Nielsen's bound N < 24k for k distinct prime factors (UpperBound).

OddPerfect.PrimePowerIndexBound

OddPerfect/PrimePowerIndexBound.lean · 327 lines · 4 public theorems · imports EqualExponentsBound, UpperBound

Let l be an odd prime. If every ordinary exponent e of an odd perfect number N has e + 1 a power of l and e ≤ E, then N has at most E2 + 2E + 3 distinct prime factors, so N < 24E² + 2E + 3 and the family is finite for each E. Also: l is then not the special prime, for any exponents. The family is empty for l = 3 (McDaniel) and l = 5 (Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem); the statement has content for l ≥ 7. Whether it is new was not verified.

Proof idea. The argument for equal exponents (Yamada) run with varying exponents. Every prime factor of an ordinary divisor sum is l or 1 modulo l; at most E ordinary primes are 1 modulo l and each receives from at most E senders; every other prime p has σ of its component a power of the special prime q, which forces pl − 2 to divide the special exponent plus one, and the divisors of that number each give a different prime factor.

If every exponent e_p of the odd perfect number N at a prime p ≠ l has e_p + 1 a power of the prime l, then l is not the special prime. Write N = l ^ k Y with Y = ∏ p ^ e_p. Every prime factor of X = ∏ σ(p ^ e_p) is l or ≡ 1 (mod l), so the part U of X prime to l is ≡ 1 (mod l); removing the powers of l from σ(l ^ k) X = 2 l ^ k Y gives σ(l ^ k) U = 2 Y, which reads 1 = 2 modulo l since p ^ (l ^ γ) ≡ p.

OddPerfect.CommonIndexCapacity

OddPerfect/CommonIndexCapacity.lean · 122 lines · 3 public theorems · imports EqualExponentsBound, UpperBound

Let an odd prime l divide every ordinary index e + 1 of an odd perfect number N, with arbitrary other factors in the indices. Then N has at most 1 + S distinct prime factors, where S is the sum of the exponents of the prime factors that are 1 modulo l. If also the special prime is not 1 modulo l, and the exponents of l and of those prime factors are at most E, then N has at most E2 + 1 distinct prime factors and N < 2^(4^(E2 + 1)).

Proof idea. For an ordinary prime p the value 1 + p + … + p^(l−1) divides σ(p^e), and by Bang's theorem it has a prime factor r that is 1 modulo l. That prime divides N and is not p. A receiver r takes at most e_r senders, by the exact count of the factors r in σ(N) = 2N. So the ordinary primes are counted by the exponents of the receivers. When the special prime is not 1 modulo l every such receiver is ordinary, so each sends one factor l, and there are at most e_l of them. The result bounds the number of prime factors and excludes nothing; the case where the special prime is 1 modulo l is open here.

OddPerfect.PrimePowerIndexCapacity

OddPerfect/PrimePowerIndexCapacity.lean · 265 lines · 4 public theorems · imports PrimePowerIndexBound

Let every ordinary index of an odd perfect number N be a power of one odd prime l. If the exponent of l and the exponents of the ordinary prime factors that are 1 modulo l are at most B, then N has at most B2 + 2B + 2 distinct prime factors and N < 2^(4^(B2 + 2B + 2)). No condition on the special prime modulo l and no cap on the other exponents.

Proof idea. Let S be the ordinary prime factors that are 1 modulo l and C the exponent of l plus the sum of the exponents over S. An ordinary prime outside S and different from l sends only to primes that are 1 modulo l. So either its σ value is a power of the special prime q (call these sources U), or it sends to a member of S, and a receiver s takes at most e_s senders. Also |S| ≤ e_l. This gives ω(N) ≤ C + |U| + 2. No ordinary row feeds a member of U, so its whole exponent comes from σ(qα), and the lemma of Dandapat, Hunsucker and Pomerance puts pl−2 into α + 1 for each p in U. Bang's theorem at q bounds the number of divisors of α + 1 by ω(N) + 1, so 2(l − 1)|U| ≤ C + |U| + 3, and |U| ≤ B under the caps. The cap B is a hypothesis; nothing is excluded.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeException

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeException.lean · 617 lines · 1 public theorem · imports Abundancy, Euler, Seed.ThreeFree, Seed.Example contains novelty unverified

If every prime other than q and one further prime r has exponent exactly 2, then 3 divides N.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Then q ≡ 1 (mod 12), so q ≥ 13, and for every other ordinary p, σ(p²) = qarb with a, b not both even, since 1 + p + p² lies strictly between consecutive squares. If r divides no σ(p²), the σ(p²) are odd powers of q, consecutive ordinary primes grow by a factor at least 13, and the abundancy is below (13/12)(5/4)(7/5) = 91/48 < 2. Otherwise r ≡ 1 (mod 3), the map p ↦ (a, b) is injective with (p + 1)² > 13arb, and a box count for small (a, b) plus a geometric tail bound the abundancy below 2. The argument uses only elementary size bounds.

A restrained odd perfect number is divisible by 3.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Then q ≡ 1 (mod 12), and for every other ordinary p, σ(p²) = qarb. Size comparisons on these values, split by whether r divides some σ(p²), bound the abundancy below 2. No computer search is used.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeCert

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeCert.lean · 159 lines · 8 public theorems · imports Certificate

Certificates excluding exponent 2 at 5, 11, 29 and a fourth prime x: outright for x ∈ {17, 23, 47}, and for x ∈ {41, 53} when 3 does not divide N.

Proof idea. Each certificate forces primes from the exact squares (σ(5²) = 31, σ(11²) = 7·19, σ(29²) = 13·67, and for example σ(17²) = 307 or σ(23²) = 7·79) and closes with an abundant divisor that takes every forced prime to the first power. OddPerfect.AttackSize

OddPerfect/AttackSize.lean · 542 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Abundancy, Euler, Network, ExponentCap, Steuerwald, Seed.ThreeFree contains novelty unverified

Results that mix exact arithmetic with size. When 3 does not divide N, primes p with p² exactly dividing N and σ(p²) a power of the special prime carry little abundancy, so 3 divides N if every ordinary exponent is 2 except for at most twelve primes ≡ 2 (mod 3), or except for at most four primes that divide no σ(p²) of the exponent two primes. For every odd perfect number, a proper set S of prime factors that are all at least p gives 2p2|S| < 3N, and if every prime factor is at least p then p2ω(N)+1 ≤ N.

Proof idea. For the first part, call p a pure square when p² exactly divides N and 1 + p + p² is a power qa of the special prime. Then q ≡ 1 (mod 12), and p ≡ 2 (mod 3) and p ≡ 3 (mod 4), so p ≡ 11 (mod 12); 11, 23 and 47 fail because 133 = 7·19, 553 = 7·79 and 2257 = 37·61, so p ≥ 59. The exponent a is odd since 1 + p + p² lies strictly between two squares, so two pure squares p < p' satisfy 13p ≤ p'. The pure squares therefore contribute at most 61/59 to the abundancy, and the remaining primes must have ∏ p/(p − 1) > 1416/793. For the second part, the components over S multiply to at least p2|S|−1, because at most one exponent is odd. Strong connectivity of the network gives an edge from some component lb outside S into S, so σ(lb) ≥ p, while σ(lb) < (3/2)lb. Multiplying gives 2p2|S| < 3N.

OddPerfect.ExponentTenTwelve

OddPerfect/ExponentTenTwelve.lean · 659 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Certificate, Steuerwald, Valuation, SpecialPrime, Pratt contains novelty unverified

The ordinary exponents cannot all equal 10 and cannot all equal 12. Also, for every prime l, the special prime cannot be l when every ordinary exponent equals l − 1.

Proof idea. Write l for 11 or 13. If l does not divide N, the prime length argument of Steuerwald applies. If l is the special prime, write N = lkRl − 1; every prime factor of the product of the ordinary component divisor sums is l or ≡ 1 (mod l), and removing the powers of l from σ(N) = 2N leaves an identity that reads 1 = 2 modulo l. If l is ordinary, its budget is l − 1, and every ordinary prime ≡ 1 (mod l) spends one unit, so at most l such primes divide N. Forcing chains then exhibit l + 1 of them, starting from σ(11¹⁰) = 15797·1806113 and σ(13¹²) = 53·264031·1803647, after a case split on which forced prime ≡ 1 (mod 4) is special. Large primes carry certificates checked by Pratt.

OddPerfect.UniformExponents

OddPerfect/UniformExponents.lean · 812 lines · 21 public theorems · imports EqualExponents, SmallestPrime contains novelty unverified

Structure of a hypothetical odd perfect number whose ordinary exponents all equal l − 1, for every odd prime l at once. The ordinary primes split into S (those ≡ 1 mod l) and W (the others, apart from l). Results: every prime of W receives its whole budget from the special component, so 2(∏W)l − 1 divides σ(qk); the size of S is bounded; W is nonempty, with at least two elements for l ≥ 53; and the exact l-adic ledger |S| + vl(k + 1) = l − 1 holds when l is ordinary.

Proof idea. No ordinary component divisor sum is divisible by a prime w of W, because an ordinary σ(pl − 1) only has prime factors equal to l or ≡ 1 (mod l). So the w-adic ledger has a single term, vw(σ(qk)) = l − 1. Each prime of S spends one unit of the budget of l, which bounds |S| and hence the product of s/(s − 1) over S. Abundancy 2 must then be supplied by q, l and the primes of W, which forces W to be nonempty and gives the lower bounds on |W|. Lifting the exponent turns vw(σ(qk)) = l − 1 into exact statements about vw(k + 1) and the order of q modulo w.

OddPerfect.KanoldGeneral

OddPerfect/KanoldGeneral.lean · 503 lines · 10 public theorems · imports EqualExponents, Zsigmondy, Abundancy contains novelty unverified

If t divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then t⁴ divides N. Also: if an odd prime l divides every e + 1 then l divides N, the prime power form l4a | N, and two cases of the stronger fifth power statement.

Proof idea. Suppose an odd prime l divides every ordinary e + 1 but not N. Then every Φl(p) = 1 + p + … + pl − 1 with p ordinary is a power of the special prime q. A growth lemma shows that such primes are sparse: for ordinary p < p′, both are l-th roots of unity modulo M = Φl(p), the unit group modulo a power of q is cyclic, so p′ is congruent to a power pj with j < l, and p′ < M would force p′ = pj. Hence Φl(p) < p′, the ordinary primes grow faster than squaring, and the abundancy stays below 2. For the fourth power: if l is ordinary its exponent is at least la − 1; if l = q, primitive prime factors of the cyclotomic values at q, q², …, qa of one ordinary prime give a + 1 primes ≡ 1 (mod q), each of which spends a units, and the residue of the special exponent modulo 4 finishes.

Growth of primes whose Φ_l values are powers of one odd prime. Let l be a prime, q an odd prime, and p < p' primes with p' ≠ q such that 1 + p + ... + p ^ (l - 1) and 1 + p' + ... + p' ^ (l - 1) are both powers of q. Then 1 + p + ... + p ^ (l - 1) < p'.

OddPerfect.ForcingClosed

OddPerfect/ForcingClosed.lean · 527 lines · 15 public theorems · imports Euler, Abundancy, Zsigmondy, Pratt contains novelty unverified

A relaxation of the problem. A forcing closed configuration is a finite set of odd primes with exponents that satisfies Euler's parity pattern, closure (every odd prime factor of a component divisor sum is in the set), and total abundancy at most 2. The exact valuation ledger is dropped. Every odd perfect number gives a configuration, so nonexistence of configurations (the statement C1, a definition that is never assumed and may be false) would imply the conjecture. Proved for configurations: every exponent is below the largest prime of the set, the exponents can be reduced to 1 for the special prime and l − 1 with l prime for the others, and the ordinary exponents e cannot all satisfy 3 | e + 1.

Proof idea. Closure and a primitive prime factor give, for each exponent e ≥ 2, a prime r ≡ 1 (mod e + 1) in the set, so e + 2 ≤ r. Reduction uses that σ(pa) divides σ(pb) when a + 1 divides b + 1, so closure and the size bound survive when exponents shrink. If every ordinary e has 3 | e + 1, then p² + p + 1 divides every ordinary component divisor sum; closure and parity force 3 into the set, and a finite forcing tree starting at 3 produces a subset whose abundancy already exceeds 2. No valuation count is used, only closure, parity and size.

OddPerfect.ExceptionCount

OddPerfect/ExceptionCount.lean · 827 lines · 4 public theorems · imports AttackSize contains novelty unverified

Let E be a finite set such that every prime factor outside E and other than the special prime q has exponent exactly 2. Then 3 divides N if E has at most 29 elements, all ≡ 2 (mod 3), or if E has at most 5 elements, none of which divides a σ(p²) with p outside E. With q ≠ 109 the first count rises to 31, and with q ≥ 61 the second rises to 6. These sharpen the counts 12 and 4 of AttackSize.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Then every exponent 2 prime p outside E has σ(p²) equal to a power of q, is ≡ 11 (mod 12), is at least 59, and two such primes s < t satisfy 13s ≤ t. So their abundancies multiply to little more than that of the smallest one. The abundancy 2 must then come from q and the primes of E, and the product of r/(r − 1) over the smallest admissible primes is compared with the bound. Small values of q are removed by forcing through the odd prime factors of q + 1, which must divide N and must lie in the allowed residue class. The module docstring records the values of q at which the comparison stops, which is why the counts 29 and 5 are the limits of this method without a condition on q.

OddPerfect.EqualExponentChain

OddPerfect/EqualExponentChain.lean · 2050 lines · 25 public theorems · imports Pratt, Steuerwald, SpecialPrime, Valuation, Cyclotomic contains novelty unverified

A certificate checker for the case where every ordinary exponent equals l − 1 with l an odd prime, with a soundness theorem, and certificates checked by the kernel that exclude the common exponents 4, 6, 10, 12, 16, 18, 22 and 28. The exponents 4, 6, 10, 12, 16, 22 and 28 are known results. For the exponent 18 we did not find a published proof; an independent computer assisted claim by another author exists and is not peer reviewed. The case l = 31 is not covered.

Proof idea. If l does not divide N the prime length argument applies. Otherwise l is ordinary or special, and a certificate tree is checked in each case. A state records primes proved to be ordinary prime factors, primes proved to differ from q, the value of q once fixed, and a number M proved to divide k + 1 for the special exponent k. Steps: a prime factor r of σ(pl − 1) for a known p divides N, and is ordinary when it is not ≡ 1 (mod 4) or is known to differ from q; a prime factor of σ(qm − 1) with m | M is ordinary; a branch decides whether a given prime is q; and for a known prime s with s ≠ l and s ≢ 1 (mod l), the whole budget l − 1 of s comes from σ(qk), so lifting the exponent forces a new divisor of k + 1. A branch closes when a prime receives more than l − 1 factors or when the fixed q is not ≡ 1 (mod 4). Divisibility is checked by Horner evaluation modulo the divisor and primality by Pratt certificates.

OddPerfect.Restrained

OddPerfect/Restrained.lean · 1498 lines · 3 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeException, Steuerwald, Phi3, Valuation, ValuationBounds, SpecialPrime, Reciprocity, Certificate

The restrained case: every prime factor other than the special prime q and one further prime r has exponent exactly 2. The module proves a case map and excludes nothing outright. If r ≠ 3, then 3² exactly divides N and only four explicit cases remain: r = 13; q = 13 with r = 7; r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N; r = 97 with 13² and 61² exactly dividing N. If r = 3, the exponent of 3 is even and at least 4, q ≡ 1 (mod 3), and neither 5 nor 7 divides N. The four cases with r ≠ 3 are excluded in the modules RestrainedTwo to RestrainedFive, so r = 3.

Proof idea. With 3² exactly dividing N, each ordinary prime ≡ 1 (mod 3) spends one unit of the budget 2 of the prime 3. Forcing from σ(3²) = 13 gives nine leaves according to which forced primes equal q or r; every other branch has three ordinary primes ≡ 1 (mod 3). In five leaves the budget is spent or nearly spent, so every further ordinary prime t has σ(t²) supported on known primes. An exact search checked by the kernel lists the t with σ(t²) below a bound, the small survivors are removed by abundant divisors, and for the rest a weighted sum bound keeps the abundancy below 2. For r = 3, quadratic reciprocity gives q ≡ 1 (mod 3), and factor chains from 5 and from 7 end in abundant divisors or in an overflow of a budget.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeTwo

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeTwo.lean · 1698 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Abundancy, Euler, Seed.ThreeFree, Seed.Example, ThreeFreeException contains novelty unverified

If every prime factor other than the special prime q and two further primes r₁, r₂ has exponent exactly 2, then 3 divides N. No condition is placed on r₁ and r₂. This extends the one exception theorem.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Every ordinary prime s then has σ(s²) = qar₁br₂c, and s determines the exponent vector. For s ≥ 300 the excess σ(s²)/s² − 1 is bounded by a weight that decays geometrically in (a, b, c), so the sum over all vectors is a small box evaluated exactly plus a geometric tail. For s < 300 a table of the prime factors of 1 + s + s² confines the ordinary primes to an explicit finite set once the classes of r₁ and r₂ are fixed. For each of 41 pairs of classes the resulting upper bound for the abundancy is below 2.

OddPerfect.ForcingClosedBound

OddPerfect/ForcingClosedBound.lean · 275 lines · 7 public theorems · imports ForcingClosed, Pratt, Cyclotomic

Every forcing closed configuration has a node above 1000. In particular this holds for the set of prime factors of an odd perfect number, where it is weaker than the bound in LargestPrimeFactor; the point is that it uses only parity and closure under forcing, and none of the size information.

Proof idea. A greatest fixed point computation. Start from the odd primes up to 1000 and delete every prime p that has no move inside the current list: a special move (p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and every prime factor of p + 1 in the list, apart from 2) or an ordinary move (an odd prime l with 2l + 1 ≤ 1000 such that every prime factor of σ(pl−1) is in the list). By the reduction theorem of ForcingClosed, the special exponent may be taken to be 1 and each ordinary exponent to be l − 1 for a prime l, so the nodes of a configuration with all nodes at most 1000 survive every round. Smoothness of n over the list is tested exactly as n dividing a power of the product of the list. The kernel checks nine rounds, one lemma per round, and the list becomes empty.

OddPerfect.EqualExponentChainMore

OddPerfect/EqualExponentChainMore.lean · 2656 lines · 8 public theorems · imports EqualExponentChain contains novelty unverified

Four more excluded patterns: the ordinary prime factors of an odd perfect number cannot all have exponent 30, 36, 40 or 42. These are the instances l = 31, 37, 41, 43 of the checker in EqualExponentChain. The exponent 36 is a known result (Cohen and Williams, 1985). For 30, 40 and 42 we did not find a published proof; the surveys we read list the equal exponent case as settled only for other values, so these three carry the tag novelty unverified. The case l = 47 is not covered: its certificate search did not finish.

Proof idea. Same method as EqualExponentChain: a search outside Lean builds a tree of forced prime factors, with Pratt certificates for every prime used, and the kernel checks the tree with the checker and its soundness theorem. The largest prime in these certificates has 121 digits.

OddPerfect.KanoldFive

OddPerfect/KanoldFive.lean · 422 lines · 10 public theorems · imports KanoldGeneral

Boundary cases of the fifth power form of Kanold's theorem. If a prime power la divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then l5a divides N whenever l is an ordinary prime. For the special prime q the same holds when a is not 2. The case a = 2 with the exponent of q equal to 9 stays open here in general; it is excluded for q = 5. These are known results; the general statement t⁵ divides N for every t is in the literature and is not fully proved here.

Proof idea. Count the power of q through the exact ledger: the exponent of q is the sum of the powers of q in σ(pe) over the other primes p. Primes p ≡ 1 (mod q) contribute the power of q in e + 1, at least a each, and a prime of this class with qb dividing e + 1 brings b more primes of the class through primitive prime factors. Primes outside the class contribute nothing or at least a + 1. The exponent a(a + 1) + 1 fits neither count. For the ordinary prime 5 with exponent 4, the factors forced by σ(5⁴) = 11 · 71 give at least five ordinary primes ≡ 1 (mod 5), more than the exponent 4 allows.

OddPerfect.KanoldSquare

OddPerfect/KanoldSquare.lean · 316 lines · 3 public theorems · imports KanoldFive

The last case of the fifth power theorem, reduced to a normal form; the normal form is excluded in KanoldSquareFinal. Let q be the special prime and let q² divide e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e. Then q¹⁰ divides N, or the exponent of q is 9 and: only primes ≡ 1 (mod q) contribute to the power of q, exactly four prime factors are ≡ 1 (mod q), three of them have e + 1 = q² and one has e + 1 = q³. The known proof excludes this configuration with a further Diophantine argument, which is not formalized here.

Proof idea. The exponent 9 of q is the sum of the powers of q in σ(pe) over the other primes. A contributing prime outside the class ≡ 1 (mod q) would bring four primes of the class through the orders q, q², dq, dq², for a total of at least 11. So the class carries all 9, with at least 2 from each member. A member with qb dividing e + 1 forces b + 1 members, which leaves only four members with powers 3, 2, 2, 2. A further prime factor of a length e + 1 would bring a fifth member.

OddPerfect.kanold_square_normal_form

theorem kanold_square_normal_form {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → q ^ 2 ∣ N.factorization p + 1)
  (h9 : N.factorization q = 9) :
  (∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) →
      p ∈ N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => p % q = 1)) ∧
    (N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => p % q = 1)).card = 4 ∧
    ∃ r ∈ N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => p % q = 1), N.factorization r + 1 = q ^ 3 ∧
      ∀ s ∈ N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => p % q = 1), s ≠ r →
        N.factorization s + 1 = q ^ 2

The normal form of the square case with exponent 9. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q, suppose q ^ 2 ∣ e_p + 1 for every ordinary prime p, and v_q(N) = 9. Let S be the set of prime factors ≡ 1 (mod q). Then (a) every ordinary prime p with q ∣ σ(p ^ e_p) lies in S; (b) |S| = 4; (c) one member r of S has e_r + 1 = q ^ 3 and every other member s has e_s + 1 = q ^ 2. This is the normal form preceding the last step of the known proof of the fifth power theorem q ^ 10 ∣ N; that last step is not formalized here.

The remaining gap in the square case of the fifth power theorem. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q and q ^ 2 ∣ e_p + 1 for every ordinary prime p. Then either q ^ 10 ∣ N, or v_q(N) = 9 and the normal form of kanold_square_normal_form holds. The known proof excludes the second alternative by a further Diophantine step that is not formalized here.

OddPerfect.ExponentTwentyFour

OddPerfect/ExponentTwentyFour.lean · 180 lines · 1 public theorem · imports KanoldFive

The ordinary prime factors of an odd perfect number cannot all have exponent 24. This is a known result (Hagis and McDaniel, 1975). The checker of EqualExponentChain needs a prime length and 25 is not prime, so this case has its own short proof.

Proof idea. Since 25 divides every ordinary e + 1, the fourth power theorem gives 5 ∣ N. If 5 is ordinary, σ(5²⁴) has the prime factors 11, 71, 101, 251, 401 and 9384251, and the values 1 + p + p² + p³ + p⁴ at 11, 71, 251, 9384251 and 211 give eight more, fourteen primes ≡ 1 (mod 5) in all. At most one is special, and each ordinary one contributes exactly 2 to the power of 5 in σ(N), so that power is at least 26, above 24. If 5 is special, its exponent is at least 13, 3 divides 5 + 1 and 11 divides σ(3²⁴), and 3⁴·5⁵·11² is an abundant divisor of N.

OddPerfect.CommonPrimeChain

OddPerfect/CommonPrimeChain.lean · 1394 lines · 31 public theorems · imports KanoldFive, EqualExponentChain contains novelty unverified

Families where one prime divides every ordinary e + 1. If 5 divides every ordinary e + 1, then 5 is not the special prime and 5186 divides N. If 7 divides every ordinary e + 1, then 7124 divides N. So the ordinary exponents cannot all equal E when 5 divides E + 1 and E < 186, or 7 divides E + 1 and E < 124; this includes 34, 48, 54, 64, 76, 84, 90 and 94. The method is the classical one of forced prime chains. Of the excluded exponents, 34 and 48 are results of Hagis and McDaniel (1975). The family of 5 is empty by published results: the Main Theorem of Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem (Math. Comp. 81, 2012) excludes the prime factor 5 when 3 or 5 divides every ordinary e + 1, and Kanold's theorem forces it; a preprint of 2015 also claims this, by a computation with about 960 thousand forced primes. Both are far beyond the tables checked here, and the library does not prove the general statement. For the family of 7 we did not find published statements of this kind (novelty unverified). The families themselves are not excluded here.

Proof idea. Let r divide every ordinary e + 1. For an ordinary prime p, every odd prime factor of 1 + p + … + pr−1 divides N, and it is r or ≡ 1 (mod r). Each ordinary prime ≡ 1 (mod r) contributes at least 1 to the exponent of r. A table of forced primes, starting from r, is checked by the kernel. The special prime is unknown and cannot be used as a source, so the checker removes each possible node in turn and counts the primes that are still forced; the smallest count is the bound. For r = 5 the special case is excluded first: 5 special would force 3 and 11 and the abundant divisor 3⁴·5⁵·11².

OddPerfect.CommonFamily

OddPerfect/CommonFamily.lean · 375 lines · 16 public theorems · imports CommonPrimeChain

A whole family excluded: if 35 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. This is a theorem of Hagis and McDaniel (1975). In particular the ordinary exponents cannot all equal E when 35 divides E + 1, with no bound on E. The module also proves two facts of Evans and Pearlman (2007) for the family where 5 divides every ordinary e + 1: 3 does not divide N, and the special prime is ≡ 1 (mod 12).

Proof idea. In the family of 35, the primes 5 and 7 divide N and are ordinary, and for an ordinary prime s every odd prime factor of 1 + s + … + s³⁴ divides N. A kernel checked table forces the 22 primes 5, 7, 11, 29, 31, 41, 43, 61, 71, 101, 113, 127, 131, 151, 181, 191, 197, 211, 239, 241, 251 and 271, whichever prime is special: the special prime is ≡ 1 (mod 12), and the checker never uses such a node as a source. Every ordinary exponent is at least 4, so the fourth powers of these primes divide N; if one of 61, 181, 241 is the special prime, only its first power is used. In each of the four cases the divisor is abundant, which is impossible. For 3 ∤ N in the family of 5: otherwise 3⁴·5⁴·11⁴ would be an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.ForcingClosedBoundTwo

OddPerfect/ForcingClosedBoundTwo.lean · 285 lines · 3 public theorems · imports ForcingClosedBound

Every forcing closed configuration has a node above 2000, up from 1000 in ForcingClosedBound. As there, this uses only parity and closure under forcing, and none of the size information of an odd perfect number.

Proof idea. The same greatest fixed point iteration: start from the odd numbers up to 2000 that pass a cheap sieve and repeatedly delete every entry with no move inside the current list. The step is faster: an ordinary move of length l at p needs a node r with r ≡ 1 (mod l) and pl ≡ 1 (mod r), so the expensive smoothness test of a row runs only when such an r is present. The list empties in ten rounds, one kernel check per round.

OddPerfect.CommonFiveSeven

OddPerfect/CommonFiveSeven.lean · 1272 lines · 39 public theorems · imports CommonFamily

In the family where 5 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, 7 does not divide N. This is a theorem of Evans and Pearlman (2007). With 3 ∤ N from CommonFamily it gives gcd(N, 21) = 1 in that family. The module also holds the general tools used for the larger tables: a reach checker with an arbitrary test for the special prime, primality by trial division to the square root, and an abundancy check for all cases at once.

Proof idea. Suppose 7 ∣ N. Then 7 is ordinary with exponent at least 4, and the forcing table starts from 5 and 7: for an ordinary prime s, every odd prime factor of 1 + s + s² + s³ + s⁴ divides N. A table of 358 rows, checked by the kernel, forces 110 primes up to 3911 whichever prime is special (the special prime is ≡ 1 (mod 12), and each such source is switched off in turn). The fourth powers of these primes, with only the first power for the special one, form an abundant divisor in every case; the smallest margin is 2.00048, when 61 is special.

OddPerfect.dvd_of_reach

theorem dvd_of_reach {N q d ns passes tm : ℕ} {cand : ℕ → Bool} {nodes : List ℕ}
  {rows : List (List ℕ)} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → d ∣ N.factorization p + 1) (hd : 1 ≤ d)
  (hcq : cand q = true) (hP : ∀ t ∈ nodes, t.Prime) (h2 : ∀ t ∈ nodes, t ≠ 2)
  (hseed : ∀ t ∈ nodes.take ns, t ∣ N) (hns : ns ≤ nodes.length)
  (hrows : ∀ e ∈ nodes.zip rows, rowChk d nodes e = true)
  (hcand : ∀ b ∈ nodes.take rows.length, cand b = true →
    reach nodes rows ns tm passes b = true)
  (h0 : reach nodes rows ns tm passes 0 = true) :
  ∀ k, tm.testBit k = true → nodes.getD k 0 ∣ N

Soundness of the reach checks. Let N be an odd perfect number and q a number such that d ∣ v_p(N) + 1 for every prime factor p ≠ q, where d ≥ 1, with cand q. Take a table with odd prime nodes nodes, whose first ns nodes divide N (with ns at most the number of nodes), and whose rows pass rowChk. If all bits of tm are reached for every blocked source node b (one of the first rows.length nodes) with cand b, and for the blocked value 0, then every node whose index is a bit of tm divides N.

OddPerfect.not_seven_dvd_of_common_five

theorem not_seven_dvd_of_common_five {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → 5 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : ¬ 7 ∣ N

In the common 5 family, 7 ∤ N. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q and 5 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 for every ordinary prime p. Then 5 ∣ N and q ≡ 1 (mod 12); if 7 ∣ N, the forcing table from the seeds 5, 7 reaches all target primes whichever source node ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special, and they give an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.CommonSixtyFive

OddPerfect/CommonSixtyFive.lean · 696 lines · 33 public theorems · imports CommonFiveSeven

A second family excluded as a whole: if 65 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. This is a theorem of Evans and Pearlman (2007). In particular the ordinary exponents cannot all equal E when 65 divides E + 1.

Proof idea. The seeds are 5 and 13, which divide N. For an ordinary prime s every odd prime factor of 1 + s + … + s⁶⁴ divides N. The prime 13 is ≡ 1 (mod 12) and may itself be special, so the proof splits. If 13 is special, 7 = (13 + 1)/2 divides N and joins the seeds, and the rows of 13 are not used. Otherwise 13 is ordinary and every other source ≡ 1 (mod 12) is switched off in turn. In both branches a kernel checked table of 361 rows forces 315 primes, and their fourth powers (first power for the special prime) form an abundant divisor; the smallest margin is 2.0000666.

OddPerfect.not_common_sixty_five

theorem not_common_sixty_five {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → 65 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : False

The common 65 family is impossible. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q. Then 65 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 cannot hold for every ordinary prime p. Here 5 ∣ N, 13 ∣ N and q ≡ 1 (mod 12). If q = 13, then 7 ∣ 13 + 1 divides N and the seeds are 5, 13, 7 with the rows of 13 blocked; otherwise 13 is ordinary, the seeds are 5, 13, and every source node ≡ 1 (mod 12) other than 13 is blocked in turn. In both cases the target primes give an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.CommonFiftyFive

OddPerfect/CommonFiftyFive.lean · 1364 lines · 44 public theorems · imports CommonFastChecks

A third family excluded as a whole: if 55 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. Known mathematics: every family whose common divisor is a multiple of 5 follows from the Main Theorem of Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem (Math. Comp. 81, 2012) together with Kanold's theorem that a common prime divisor of all ordinary e + 1 divides N. The module gives an independent certificate checked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The same method as for 35 and 65, with a larger table. The seeds are 5 and 11, both ordinary. A kernel checked table of 911 rows forces 936 primes whichever source ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special (186 sources are switched off in turn), and their fourth powers, with the first power for the special prime, form an abundant divisor in every case. The smallest margin is 2.0000034, when 61 is special. The table was found by a search outside Lean; the kernel rechecks every primality, every divisibility, every reach computation and every inequality.

OddPerfect.not_common_eighty_five

theorem not_common_eighty_five {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → 85 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : False

The common 85 family is impossible. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q. Then 85 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 cannot hold for every ordinary prime p. Here 5 ∣ N, 17 ∣ N and q ≡ 1 (mod 12); the forcing table from the seeds 5, 17 reaches all target primes whichever source node ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special, and they give an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.not_all_exponents_eq_of_eighty_five_dvd_succ

theorem not_all_exponents_eq_of_eighty_five_dvd_succ {N q E : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hE : 85 ∣ E + 1)
  (hexp : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → N.factorization p = E) : False

The ordinary exponents of an odd perfect number cannot all equal one E with 85 ∣ E + 1.

OddPerfect.CommonOneFifteenData

OddPerfect/CommonOneFifteenData.lean · 2540 lines · 48 public theorems · imports CommonFastChecks

Data for the family of 115: the forcing table of 1958 rows on 2728 primes, the kernel checks that every listed receiver divides 1 + s + … + s¹¹⁴ for its source s, the 1521 targets, and the two full products used in the abundance check.

Proof idea. The divisibility checks are split into 40 kernel runs to keep memory low. The table was found by a search outside Lean and is fully rechecked here.

OddPerfect.CommonOneFifteenPrime

OddPerfect/CommonOneFifteenPrime.lean · 157 lines · 29 public theorems · imports CommonOneFifteenData

Primality of all 2728 nodes of the table for the family of 115, by trial division over a fixed list of odd primes, in 28 kernel runs.

Proof idea. The largest node is 15352501, below 4201², so trial division by the odd primes up to 4201 suffices for each node.

OddPerfect.CommonOneFifteen

OddPerfect/CommonOneFifteen.lean · 163 lines · 11 public theorems · imports CommonOneFifteenPrime

A fifth family excluded as a whole: if 115 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. Known mathematics: every family whose common divisor is a multiple of 5 follows from the Main Theorem of Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem (Math. Comp. 81, 2012) together with Kanold's theorem that a common prime divisor of all ordinary e + 1 divides N. The module gives an independent certificate checked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The method of CommonFiftyFive with the seeds 5 and 23. A kernel checked table of 1958 rows forces 1521 primes whichever source ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special (391 cases), and their fourth powers, with the first power for the special prime, form an abundant divisor in every case. The smallest margin is 2.0000023. This module holds the reach checks, the abundance check and the final theorem; the table and the primality proofs are in the two modules it imports.

OddPerfect.KanoldObstruction

OddPerfect/KanoldObstruction.lean · 614 lines · 17 public theorems

Kanold's obstruction: for an odd prime p, primes r, s and positive a, b, the equations G(r^(p^u)) = p·s^a and G(s^(p^v)) = p·r^b cannot both hold, where G(X) = 1 + X + … + X^(p−1). A special case of a theorem of H.-J. Kanold (J. reine angew. Math. 189, pages 243 to 245).

Proof idea. Both equations force r ≡ s ≡ 1 (mod p). If one exponent is small (a ≤ p^v), a size comparison forces v = 0, a = 1 and then s < r^(p^u), against p·s = G(r^(p^u)). Otherwise u = v, and with r < s the residue of b modulo p·p^u is pinned down, which forces u = 0, a = 2 and p(s − 1) = s² − r², impossible since p divides s − r. The lemma is the Diophantine input for the last case of the fifth power divisibility theorem, proved in KanoldSquareFinal.

OddPerfect.KanoldSquareFinal

OddPerfect/KanoldSquareFinal.lean · 1158 lines · 24 public theorems · imports KanoldSquare, KanoldObstruction

The fifth power theorem in full: if t divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then t⁵ divides N. The theorem is due to Kanold (fourth power) and Yamada (fifth power). This module settles the last case, the special prime q ≥ 13 with q² dividing every ordinary e + 1 and exponent 9 at q.

Proof idea. In the last case exactly four primes ≡ 1 (mod q) carry all of q⁹: three with e + 1 = q² and one with e + 1 = q³. The cyclotomic blocks 1 + Y + … + Y^(q−1) of these primes are q times products of powers of the other three, and blocks at different levels share no prime. Kanold's obstruction rules out two blocks that are q times a prime power of each other; order arguments force one prime above q², and size comparisons with real logarithms then contradict q ≥ 13.

theorem core (st : KSetup N q D) {A B E : ℕ} (hA : A ∈ kS N q) (hB : B ∈ kS N q)

  (hBE : B ≠ E) {h : ℕ} (hh0 : 0 < h) (hh : kC q 2 D = q * A ^ h)
  (hDBp : ∃ i ≤ 1, ∃ k, 0 < k ∧ kC q i D = q * B ^ k)
  (hDEp : ∃ i ≤ 1, ∃ k, 0 < k ∧ kC q i D = q * E ^ k)
  (hD0 : ∃ k, 0 < k ∧ (kC q 0 D = q * B ^ k ∨ kC q 0 D = q * E ^ k))
  {γ e2 e3 e4 : ℕ} (hγ : γ ≤ 1) (he3 : 0 < e3) (he4 : 0 < e4)
