OddPerfect.CommonFastChecks

OddPerfect/CommonFastChecks.lean · 358 lines · 15 public theorems · imports CommonFiveSeven

Three cheaper forms of the forcing table checks, each with a proof that it implies the original check: primality by trial division over a fixed list of odd primes, row checks through a node list cut into parts, and reach checks with a whole set of source nodes blocked at once.

Proof idea. The kernel evaluates the same facts with far less work. Each fast check comes with a soundness lemma, so the theorems that use them state exactly what they stated before.

  (hg : ∀ f ∈ bls, reachS nodes rows ns tm passes f = true)
  (hc : (nodes.take rows.length).all (fun b => !cand b || bls.any fun f => f b) = true) :
  ∀ b ∈ nodes.take rows.length, cand b = true → reach nodes rows ns tm passes b = true

Reach checks for all blocked candidates from a few blocked sets: every source node b with cand b lies in one of the sets of bls, and each set passes the reach check.

OddPerfect.CommonNinetyFiveData

OddPerfect/CommonNinetyFiveData.lean · 4296 lines · 0 public theorems · imports CommonFastChecks

Data for the family of 95: the forcing table of 3200 rows on 4480 primes (largest 17607871), and the 2700 targets.

Proof idea. The table was found by a search outside Lean and is fully rechecked by the kernel in the modules that import this one. The node list is defined as the concatenation of its parts so that the parts can be checked separately.

OddPerfect.CommonNinetyFiveFacts

OddPerfect/CommonNinetyFiveFacts.lean · 104 lines · 9 public theorems · imports CommonNinetyFiveData

List facts for the family of 95: the equations between the table and its parts, no node is 2, the target primes are selected and distinct, and the two full products of the abundance check.

Proof idea. Kept apart from the heavy check modules so that each of those needs only the data.

OddPerfect.CommonNinetyFiveReach1

OddPerfect/CommonNinetyFiveReach1.lean · 48 lines · 5 public theorems · imports CommonNinetyFiveData

Reach checks for the family of 95: four kernel checks, each with a whole set of candidate special primes blocked at once, which together cover every candidate.

Proof idea. One closure computation per candidate, run in the kernel; 639 candidates in all.

OddPerfect.CommonNinetyFive

OddPerfect/CommonNinetyFive.lean · 218 lines · 6 public theorems · imports CommonNinetyFiveFacts, CommonNinetyFiveRows1, CommonNinetyFiveRows2, CommonNinetyFiveRows3, CommonNinetyFiveRows4, CommonNinetyFiveRows5, CommonNinetyFivePrime1, CommonNinetyFivePrime2, CommonNinetyFivePrime3, CommonNinetyFivePrime4, CommonNinetyFiveReach1

A sixth family excluded as a whole: if 95 divides e + 1 for every ordinary exponent e, then N is not an odd perfect number. Known mathematics: every family whose common divisor is a multiple of 5 follows from the Main Theorem of Fletcher, Nielsen and Ochem (Math. Comp. 81, 2012) together with Kanold's theorem that a common prime divisor of all ordinary e + 1 divides N. The module gives an independent certificate checked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The method of CommonFiftyFive with the seeds 5 and 19; 19 is ≡ 3 (mod 4), so it is not the special prime. A kernel checked table of 3200 rows on 4480 primes forces 2700 primes whichever source ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special (639 cases), and their fourth powers, with the first power for the special prime, form an abundant divisor in every case. The smallest margin is 2.0000015. This module assembles the checks of the modules it imports and states the final theorem.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.FamInst.hrows95

theorem hrows95 : ∀ e ∈ nodes95.zip rows95, rowChk 95 nodes95 e = true

The divisibility checks of all rows.

OddPerfect.FamInst.hcand95

theorem hcand95 : ∀ b ∈ nodes95.take rows95.length, cand95 b = true →
  reach nodes95 rows95 2 tm95 3 b = true

Every blocked source node passes the reach check.

OddPerfect.FamInst.nodes95_prime

theorem nodes95_prime : ∀ t ∈ nodes95, t.Prime

The common 95 family is impossible. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q. Then 95 ∣ v_p(N) + 1 cannot hold for every ordinary prime p. Here 5 ∣ N, 19 ∣ N and q ≡ 1 (mod 12); the forcing table from the seeds 5, 19 reaches all target primes whichever source node ≡ 1 (mod 12) is special, and they give an abundant divisor.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeThreeCore

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeThreeCore.lean · 908 lines · 21 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeTwo, OmegaFour

The setting for three exceptional primes: the core configuration of an odd perfect number not divisible by 3 with special prime q and three exceptional primes, the facts about its ordinary primes, whose exponents e satisfy 3 ∣ e + 1, and the closing inequality with an abstract bound per exponent vector.

Proof idea. For an ordinary prime s with exponent e, 3 ∣ e + 1 makes 1 + s + s² divide σ(se), so s ≡ 2 (mod 3) and 1 + s + s² = qar₁br₂cr₃d, and s determines the vector (a, b, c, d). Each ordinary component is below s/(s − 1), which is the bound for exponent 2 times s³/(s³ − 1); the product of these factors over all s from a cap on is bounded by a constant close to 1, which the checker fixes. The excess σ(s²)/s² − 1 is bounded by the product of four weights raised to these exponents, so the sum over all ordinary primes is a finite box sum plus a geometric tail. Labels that are not distinct prime factors of N are replaced by three distinct prime factors other than q, which only weakens the hypothesis.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeThreeChecker

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeThreeChecker.lean · 1113 lines · 9 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeThreeCore

A Boolean certificate checker for the three exception theorem, in natural number arithmetic, with its soundness proof, and the proof that 102 sorted class triples cover every configuration. It contains no certificate data.

Proof idea. A node constrains each of q, r₁, r₂, r₃ to a pinned value or to a residue class with a lower bound and a list of excluded values. A leaf check computes the least possible values, the small ordinary primes that the constraints allow (from a table of the prime factors of 1 + s + s² for s below 300), the box sum, the tail and the closing inequality, which carries the factor s/(s − 1) for each small ordinary prime and the tail factor 178802/178801. Exponent vectors supported on pinned primes are decided exactly: 4n − 3 must be an odd square for a prime s with 1 + s + s² = n to exist, and the checker tests a computed integer square root. A tree is sound by induction: a split pins a free slot to a value or excludes that value.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeThree.three_dvd_of_three_exceptions_of_check

theorem three_dvd_of_three_exceptions_of_check (trees : List (ClassTriple × Tree))
  (hcheck : allOK trees = true) {N q r₁ r₂ r₃ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hmod : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → p ≠ r₃ → 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) :
  3 ∣ N

The statement with three exceptional primes, conditional on the check allOK trees = true. This theorem proves nothing by itself: the three exception statement is proved only once a data module supplies trees and establishes the check. If N is an odd perfect number, q its special prime, and every prime factor p of N other than q, r₁, r₂, r₃ has an exponent e with 3 ∣ e + 1, then 3 ∣ N.

Case data for the three exception theorem, part 11 of 11: 85 leaves of the case trees, each rechecked by the kernel.

Proof idea. The leaves were found by a search outside Lean. Each group of five leaf checks is one kernel evaluation of the checker, and the subtree lemmas combine them with the split rule. Grouping by five keeps the memory of the module below 10 GB.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeThree

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeThree.lean · 1031 lines · 106 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeThreeData01, ThreeFreeThreeData02, ThreeFreeThreeData03, ThreeFreeThreeData04, ThreeFreeThreeData05, ThreeFreeThreeData06, ThreeFreeThreeData07, ThreeFreeThreeData08, ThreeFreeThreeData09, ThreeFreeThreeData10, ThreeFreeThreeData11 contains novelty unverified

If every prime factor other than the special prime q and three further primes r₁, r₂, r₃ has an exponent e with 3 dividing e + 1 (for example e = 2), then 3 divides N. No condition is placed on r₁, r₂, r₃. Counting form: if 3 does not divide N, at least four prime factors other than q have an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1. This extends the two exception theorem and the earlier version for exponents exactly 2. Whether the statement is new has not been checked (novelty unverified, literature not screened).

Proof idea. The method of ThreeFreeTwo with four target primes. Assume 3 does not divide N. The three exceptional primes are sorted into classes (the fixed primes 5, 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43, other primes ≡ 2 (mod 3), and primes ≡ 1 (mod 3) from 61 on), which gives 102 class triples. For each triple a tree of cases pins the special prime or an exceptional prime to explicit values or excludes them, and at each of the 1223 leaves the abundancy is bounded below 2: an exact part of the box sum is decided by an integer square root test, the rest by geometric weights and a tail. This module assembles the checks of the data modules and states the final theorem.

OddPerfect.three_dvd_of_three_mod_exceptionsnovelty unverified

theorem three_dvd_of_three_mod_exceptions {N q r₁ r₂ r₃ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hmod : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → p ≠ r₃ → 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) :
  3 ∣ N

An odd perfect number N with special prime q, in which every prime factor p other than q and three further numbers r₁, r₂, r₃ has an exponent e = N.factorization p with 3 ∣ e + 1, is divisible by 3. Here r₁, r₂, r₃ are arbitrary natural numbers: they need not be distinct, prime, or divisors of N, so the cases of fewer exceptional primes are included. The case analysis behind the proof was found by a search outside Lean and is rechecked by the kernel.

OddPerfect.three_dvd_of_three_exceptionsnovelty unverified

theorem three_dvd_of_three_exceptions {N q r₁ r₂ r₃ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → p ≠ r₃ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  3 ∣ N

An odd perfect number in which every prime factor other than the special prime q and three further primes r₁, r₂, r₃ has exponent exactly 2 is divisible by 3. Here r₁, r₂, r₃ are arbitrary natural numbers: they need not be distinct, prime, or divisors of N, so the cases of fewer exceptional primes are included. This is the case e = 2 of three_dvd_of_three_mod_exceptions.

OddPerfect.four_le_card_mod_exceptionsnovelty unverified

theorem four_le_card_mod_exceptions {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) :
  4 ≤ ((N.primeFactors.erase q).filter fun p => ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1).card

The counting form of three_dvd_of_three_mod_exceptions: if N is an odd perfect number with special prime q and 3 ∤ N, then at least four prime factors p ≠ q of N have an exponent e = N.factorization p with 3 ∤ e + 1.

OddPerfect.ThreeFreeCount

OddPerfect/ThreeFreeCount.lean · 95 lines · 3 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeThree, Counting, SpecialPrime

Counting corollaries of the modular three exception theorem: if 3 does not divide N, at least four prime factors other than the special prime have exponent at least 4, and 2 ω(N) + 7 ≤ Ω(N). Formal consequences inside this library; the literature has much stronger results when 3 does not divide N.

Proof idea. The modular theorem gives four ordinary primes whose exponent e has 3 not dividing e + 1. Such an exponent is even, positive and not 2, so it is at least 4. Summing the exponents (at least 1 for the special prime, at least 4 for these four, at least 2 for the rest) gives the count.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.four_le_factorization_of_mem_mod_exceptions

theorem four_le_factorization_of_mem_mod_exceptions {N q p : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hp : p ∈ (N.primeFactors.erase q).filter fun p => ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) :
  4 ≤ N.factorization p

A prime factor p ≠ q of an odd perfect number with special prime q whose exponent e has 3 ∤ e + 1 has 4 ≤ e: the exponent is even and positive, and e = 2 gives 3 ∣ e + 1.

OddPerfect.four_le_card_ne_two

theorem four_le_card_ne_two {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) :
  4 ≤ ((N.primeFactors.erase q).filter fun p => N.factorization p ≠ 2).card

If 3 ∤ N, at least four prime factors other than the special prime q have exponent different from 2. A superset of the set in four_le_card_mod_exceptions.

OddPerfect.two_mul_omega_add_seven_le

theorem two_mul_omega_add_seven_le {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (h3 : ¬ 3 ∣ N) :
  2 * ω N + 7 ≤ Ω N

If 3 ∤ N, then 2 ω(N) + 7 ≤ Ω(N): the special prime has exponent at least 1, four further prime factors have exponent at least 4 by four_le_card_mod_exceptions, and the rest have exponent at least 2. A formal consequence inside this library; the literature has much stronger results when 3 ∤ N, which are not proved here.

OddPerfect.FiveExceptionCore

OddPerfect/FiveExceptionCore.lean · 870 lines · 47 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeCount

Setting of the five exception result: N odd perfect, 3 not dividing N, special prime 13, and 19 and 31 dividing N. Proves the facts that need no computation: if at most four ordinary primes have an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1, they are 7, 19, 31 and one more prime t; for every other prime s, 1 + s + s2 is a product of powers of 7, 13, 19, 31 and t; exponent classes; the abundancy identity.

Proof idea. σ(13) = 14 forces 7, and 3 not dividing N makes 7, 19 and 31 exceptional, since σ(p2) is divisible by 3 for them. A good prime s has σ(s2) dividing σ(N) = 2N with prime factors that are 1 modulo 3, so they lie among 7, 13, 19, 31 and t, and the exponent vector determines s.

Generated kernel checks: the product of the primes x ≡ 1 (mod 6) with 37 ≤ x < 24500 and the scan of senders s ≡ 5 (mod 6) below 106.

Proof idea. For each candidate fourth prime t in that range the scan lists the good primes s whose 1 + s + s2 is divisible by t; one gcd with the product of all candidates treats them together.

OddPerfect.FiveExceptionThirteen

OddPerfect/FiveExceptionThirteen.lean · 909 lines · 44 public theorems · imports FiveExceptionData0, FiveExceptionData79, FiveExceptionDataT, FiveExceptionScan

If 3 does not divide N, the special prime is 13, and 19 and 31 divide N, then at least five ordinary primes have an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1. This is one case; the same count for every special prime is not proved. Whether the statement is new was not verified.

Proof idea. With only four such primes, 2 ≤ ∏ p/(p − 1) over 13, 7, 19, 31, t and the good primes. The good primes are so sparse (their 1 + s + s2 has at most five prime factors) that the product stays below 2 for every t: by the sender scan for 37 ≤ t < 24500, a square root tail above, and interval tables for t = 17, 67, 79, 307.

OddPerfect.RestrainedTwo

OddPerfect/RestrainedTwo.lean · 793 lines · 4 public theorems · imports Restrained

Two more steps in the restrained case (every prime factor other than the special prime q and one further prime r has exponent exactly 2, and 3² exactly divides N): the case r = 97 with 13² and 61² exactly dividing N is impossible, and the case r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N forces q ≡ 1 (mod 3). Three explicit cases remain when r ≠ 3: r = 13; q = 13 with r = 7; r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N and q ≡ 1 (mod 3). Known mathematics: see RestrainedFive for the published source. The remaining cases with r ≠ 3 are closed in the later modules, up to RestrainedFive.

Proof idea. For r = 97, σ(13²) = 3·61 and σ(61²) = 3·13·97 spend the budget of the prime 3, so q ≡ 1 (mod 3) and every other prime t is ≡ 2 (mod 3) with σ(t²) = 61a97bqc and a ≤ 1. The primes q below 100 are 37 and 73, and both overflow the budget. For q ≥ 100 an exact check of the values 61a97b with b < 6 shows b ≥ 6 when c = 0; then 1/(t + 1) is at most (13/100)a(11/100)b(1/10)c, t determines (a, b, c), and the sum of these weights keeps the abundancy below 2. For r = 61 with q ≡ 2 (mod 3) the same argument runs on the primes 13 and 61.

OddPerfect.RestrainedThree

OddPerfect/RestrainedThree.lean · 909 lines · 2 public theorems · imports RestrainedTwo

In the restrained case with 3² exactly dividing N, the configuration q = 13 with r = 7 is impossible. Two explicit cases remain when r ≠ 3: r = 13; r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N and q ≡ 1 (mod 3). Known mathematics: see RestrainedFive for the published source. The remaining cases with r ≠ 3 are closed in the later modules, up to RestrainedFive.

Proof idea. At most two further primes are ≡ 1 (mod 3), since each sends one factor 3 into σ(N). A kernel check over every z below 10000 with z ≡ 1 (mod 3) shows that such a prime is at least 10000: otherwise the part of σ(z²)/3 coprime to 7 and 13 would have to be the other such prime or its square, and that prime in turn would need σ of its square supported on 7, 13 and z. Every other prime t is ≡ 2 (mod 3) with σ(t²) = 7a13bxcyd, where x and y are the two large primes. If c = d = 0, an exact check of the values 7a13b below 1016 shows σ(t²) ≥ 1016; otherwise 1/(t + 1) is at most 0.378a0.2774b(1/100)c+d. The sum over all t is at most 0.0559, and the known factors give at most 13/9 · 7/6 · 13/12, so the abundancy stays below 2.

OddPerfect.RestrainedFour

OddPerfect/RestrainedFour.lean · 1048 lines · 4 public theorems · imports RestrainedThree

In the restrained case with 3² exactly dividing N, the configuration r = 61 with 13² exactly dividing N is impossible. One explicit case remains when r ≠ 3: r = 13. Known mathematics: see RestrainedFive for the published source. The remaining cases with r ≠ 3 are closed in the later modules, up to RestrainedFive.

Proof idea. By RestrainedTwo, q ≡ 1 (mod 12). The budget of the prime 3 leaves room for at most one further prime x ≡ 1 (mod 3), and σ(x²) = 3·13d61aqb. For each q below 9465 a kernel check lists every such value below a bound and shows that it is not of the form x² + x + 1 with x an admissible prime, so x is large; for q from 9465 on, either q divides σ(x²), which makes x large, or the same check applies. Eight small special primes (37, 73, 97, 109, 181, 1801, 3169, 8269) are refuted by forcing through q + 1, which divides σ(qe): each produces two different primes ≡ 1 (mod 3). For every other prime t, σ(t²) = 61a13bqcxd, and a weighted sum over the exponent vectors keeps the abundancy below 2. The tail lemma is stated for four arbitrary generators.

OddPerfect.RestrainedFive

OddPerfect/RestrainedFive.lean · 1266 lines · 3 public theorems · imports RestrainedFour, Pratt

The last case with r ≠ 3: in the restrained setting with 3² exactly dividing N, r is not 13. Together with the earlier modules this gives restrained_exception_eq_three: if every prime factor other than the special prime q and one further prime r has exponent exactly 2, then r = 3, the exponent of 3 is even and at least 4, q ≡ 1 (mod 3), and neither 5 nor 7 divides N. The case r = 3 itself is not excluded. The conclusion r = 3 is the first half of Theorem 1 of Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 2607.19746), who also prove that the exponent of 3 is at least 23,000,000,000; their proof of this half uses searches to 1010, Nielsen's bound of ten distinct prime factors and results on the Nagell-Ljunggren equation, which the Lean proof does not need. Known mathematics; whether the route is new has not been checked.

Proof idea. Here 13 = σ(3²) divides N with a free exponent. The budget of the prime 3 allows at most two further primes ≡ 1 (mod 3), and at most one when q ≡ 2 (mod 3). If q ≡ 2 (mod 3), such a prime x has σ(x²) = 3·13a, a kernel check makes x at least 106, and the known factors give at most 13/9 · 13/12 · 5/4 < 1.957, so the abundancy stays below 2. If q ≡ 1 (mod 12), forcing trees refute every prime q below 337 and, for larger q, every prime ≡ 1 (mod 3) below 1225: each tree follows the prime factors of σ(p²) and of q + 1 until a third prime ≡ 1 (mod 3) appears. A checker for these trees is proved sound once, and the primes in them are certified by Pratt certificates. A tail lemma with one fixed generator (13) and three split generators (q and the two large primes) closes the bound.

OddPerfect.RankinTailGeneral

OddPerfect/RankinTailGeneral.lean · 462 lines · 3 public theorems · imports RestrainedFour

A general tail bound: for a finite set of numbers t at least x whose rows t2 + t + 1 have all prime factors in a finite set of generators, the sum of σ(t2)/t2 − 1 is bounded by an explicit rational expression.

Proof idea. Rankin's trick with a general exponent 1/k and rational witnesses only. Each known generator g gets a weight a with ak·g ≥ 1; the further generators, known only to be at least x, share one weight. A row n = t2 + t + 1 satisfies n < (t + 1)2, so 1/(t + 1) is below n−1/2, which is at most B−(1/2 − 1/k)·n−1/k for n ≥ B; raising to the power 2k removes every root. Distinct t give distinct exponent vectors, so the weights add up to at most a product of geometric series. The earlier lemmas rankin_tail and rankin_tail3 cover four generators and the exponents 1/2 and 1/4; this one takes any number of generators and any exponent. It is a tool lemma and says nothing about odd perfect numbers by itself.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.rankin_tail_general

theorem rankin_tail_general (T K U : Finset ℕ) {x k M u : ℕ} {α : ℕ → ℚ} {αx mL mM : ℚ}
  (hx : 2 ≤ x) (hk : 3 ≤ k) (hKU : Disjoint K U) (hU : U.card ≤ u)
  (hα0 : ∀ g ∈ K, 0 ≤ α g) (hα1 : ∀ g ∈ K, α g < 1) (hαw : ∀ g ∈ K, 1 ≤ α g ^ k * g)
  (hax0 : 0 ≤ αx) (hax1 : αx < 1) (haxw : 1 ≤ αx ^ k * x) (hUx : ∀ g ∈ U, x ≤ g)
  (hmL0 : 0 ≤ mL) (hmL : 1 ≤ mL ^ (2 * k) * ((x ^ 2 + x + 1 : ℕ) : ℚ) ^ (k - 2))
  (hmM0 : 0 ≤ mM) (hmM : 1 ≤ mM ^ (2 * k) * (M : ℚ) ^ (k - 2))
  (hT : ∀ t ∈ T, x ≤ t ∧ (phi3 t).primeFactors ⊆ K ∪ U ∧
    ((∀ g ∈ U, ¬ g ∣ phi3 t) → M ≤ phi3 t)) :
  ∑ t ∈ T, (fv t - 1) ≤ ((x + 1 : ℚ) / x) ^ 2 *
    (mL * (∏ g ∈ K, 1 / (1 - α g)) * ((1 / (1 - αx)) ^ u - 1) +
      mM * ∏ g ∈ K, 1 / (1 - α g))

General Rankin tail bound with exponent 1/k. Let every t ∈ T satisfy t ≥ x ≥ 2, let the prime factors of phi3 t lie in K ∪ U, and let phi3 t ≥ M whenever no element of U divides phi3 t. Known generators g ∈ K carry weights 0 ≤ α g < 1 with α g ^ k * g ≥ 1; the at most u unknown generators in U are at least x and share the weight 0 ≤ αx < 1 with αx ^ k * x ≥ 1. With mL^(2k) (x^2 + x + 1)^(k - 2) ≥ 1 and mM^(2k) M^(k - 2) ≥ 1, ∑ (σ(t^2)/t^2 - 1) ≤ ((x + 1)/x)^2 (mL G ((1/(1 - αx))^u - 1) + mM G), where G = ∏_{g ∈ K} 1/(1 - α g). This is Rankin's trick; the elements of K and U need not be prime.

OddPerfect.rankin_tail_general_example

theorem rankin_tail_general_example (T : Finset ℕ) {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) (hq53 : 53 ≤ q)
  (hT : ∀ t ∈ T, 53 ≤ t ∧ (phi3 t).primeFactors ⊆ {97, q} ∧
    (¬ q ∣ phi3 t → 10 ^ 30 ≤ phi3 t)) :
  ∑ t ∈ T, (fv t - 1) ≤ 3 / 20

A numerical instance with K = {97}, one unknown prime q ≥ 53, x = 53, k = 4, M = 10^30: if every t ∈ T is at least 53, phi3 t has prime factors in {97, q}, and phi3 t ≥ 10^30 when q ∤ phi3 t, then ∑ (σ(t^2)/t^2 - 1) ≤ 3/20. The witnesses are α 97 = 10^6/3138288, αx = 10^6/2698167, mL = 8/53 and mM = 31622777/10^15; the resulting bound is about 0.13542. When q = 97 the lemma is applied with K empty.

OddPerfect.ProductBound

OddPerfect/ProductBound.lean · 139 lines · 7 public theorems

Two rational upper bounds for a finite product of factors 1 + x with a bounded sum, sharper than 1/(1 − S).

Proof idea. Induction on the finite set with a one step inequality for each rational function; no exponential and no real numbers.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.prod_one_add_le_of_step

theorem prod_one_add_le_of_step (R : ℚ → ℚ) {D : ℚ} (h1 : ∀ S, 0 ≤ S → S < D → 1 ≤ R S)
  (hstep : ∀ x y, 0 ≤ x → 0 ≤ y → x + y < D → (1 + x) * R y ≤ R (x + y))
  {ι : Type*} (s : Finset ι) (x : ι → ℚ) (hx : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ x i)
  {S : ℚ} (hS : ∑ i ∈ s, x i ≤ S) (hSD : S < D) :
  ∏ i ∈ s, (1 + x i) ≤ R S

A generic product bound: if 1 ≤ R S for 0 ≤ S < D and (1 + x) R y ≤ R (x + y) for 0 ≤ x, 0 ≤ y, x + y < D, then ∏ (1 + x i) ≤ R S whenever the x i are nonnegative and ∑ x i ≤ S < D.

OddPerfect.prod_one_add_le_pade11

theorem prod_one_add_le_pade11 {ι : Type*} (s : Finset ι) (x : ι → ℚ) (hx : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ x i)
  {S : ℚ} (hS : ∑ i ∈ s, x i ≤ S) (hS2 : S < 2) :
  ∏ i ∈ s, (1 + x i) ≤ (2 + S) / (2 - S)

The (1,1) Padé bound: if 0 ≤ x i and ∑ x i ≤ S < 2, then ∏ (1 + x i) ≤ (2 + S)/(2 - S).

OddPerfect.prod_one_add_le_pade21

theorem prod_one_add_le_pade21 {ι : Type*} (s : Finset ι) (x : ι → ℚ) (hx : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ x i)
  {S : ℚ} (hS : ∑ i ∈ s, x i ≤ S) (hS3 : S < 3) :
  ∏ i ∈ s, (1 + x i) ≤ (S ^ 2 + 4 * S + 6) / (6 - 2 * S)

The (2,1) Padé bound: if 0 ≤ x i and ∑ x i ≤ S < 3, then ∏ (1 + x i) ≤ (S^2 + 4 S + 6)/(6 - 2 S).

OddPerfect.pade21_le_pade11

theorem pade21_le_pade11 {S : ℚ} (h0 : 0 ≤ S) (h2 : S < 2) :
  (S ^ 2 + 4 * S + 6) / (6 - 2 * S) ≤ (2 + S) / (2 - S)

On 0 ≤ S < 2 the (2,1) bound is at most the (1,1) bound; the cross difference is S^3.

OddPerfect.pade11_le_inv

theorem pade11_le_inv {S : ℚ} (_h0 : 0 ≤ S) (h1 : S < 1) : (2 + S) / (2 - S) ≤ 1 / (1 - S)

On 0 ≤ S < 1 the (1,1) bound is at most 1/(1 - S); the cross difference is S^2. The hypothesis 0 ≤ S is not needed by the proof.

OddPerfect.pade11_nat_eq

theorem pade11_nat_eq {n d : ℕ} (hd : 0 < d) (hn : n < 2 * d) :
  ((2 * d + n : ℕ) : ℚ) / ((2 * d - n : ℕ) : ℚ) =
    (2 + (n : ℚ) / d) / (2 - (n : ℚ) / d)

Natural number form of the (1,1) bound at S = n/d: for 0 < d and n < 2 d, the quotient (2 d + n)/(2 d - n) of naturals (the subtraction does not truncate) equals (2 + S)/(2 - S).

OddPerfect.pade21_nat_eq

theorem pade21_nat_eq {n d : ℕ} (hd : 0 < d) (hn : n < 3 * d) :
  ((n ^ 2 + 4 * n * d + 6 * d ^ 2 : ℕ) : ℚ) / ((6 * d ^ 2 - 2 * n * d : ℕ) : ℚ) =
    (((n : ℚ) / d) ^ 2 + 4 * ((n : ℚ) / d) + 6) / (6 - 2 * ((n : ℚ) / d))

Natural number form of the (2,1) bound at S = n/d: for 0 < d and n < 3 d, the quotient (n^2 + 4 n d + 6 d^2)/(6 d^2 - 2 n d) of naturals (the subtraction does not truncate) equals (S^2 + 4 S + 6)/(6 - 2 S).

OddPerfect.RankinTailPade

OddPerfect/RankinTailPade.lean · 56 lines · 1 public theorem · imports RankinTailGeneral, ProductBound

Product bound for a tail: ∏(1 + xᵢ) ≤ (S² + 4S + 6)/(6 − 2S) when the sum of the xᵢ is at most S < 3.

Proof idea. Same hypotheses as the general tail lemma, with a sharper conclusion: the product of the abundancy factors of the unknown primes is at most (S² + 4S + 6)/(6 − 2S), which is below the older bound 1/(1 − S) for every S in (0, 1) and still finite up to S = 3. The certificate engine tries the older test first and this one second.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSix

OddPerfect/RestrainedSix.lean · 160 lines · 5 public theorems · imports RestrainedFive, ForcingClosed

In the restrained family (every prime factor other than the special prime and one further prime has exponent exactly 2), the exponent e of 3 has 3, 5, 11 and 17 not dividing e + 1, hence e is at least 6. Known mathematics and far weaker than the published bound of Ochem and Zelinsky (2026) for this exponent.

Proof idea. If d divides e + 1 then σ(3^(d − 1)) divides σ(3^e), which divides 2N. For d = 5, 11, 17 this number has a prime factor p ≡ 3 (mod 4): 11, 23 and 1871. Such a prime is not the special prime, so its exponent is 2, and 7 divides σ(p²); but 7 does not divide N by the earlier restrained modules. The case d = 3 follows from the theorem that some ordinary exponent f has 3 not dividing f + 1: all others equal 2. These exclude infinite arithmetic classes of e but leave infinitely many values.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSevenCheck

OddPerfect/RestrainedSevenCheck.lean · 178 lines · 8 public theorems · imports Pratt

The checker for exclusion trees in the restrained family: definitions of the tree check, the row check and the coverage check, with only light imports so that the data modules load quickly.

Proof idea. A tree for a prime p follows primes forced to divide N: a prime t with exponent 2 forces every prime factor of t² + t + 1, and the special prime q forces the odd prime factors of q + 1. A branch ends at a prime already known not to divide N.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSeven

OddPerfect/RestrainedSeven.lean · 174 lines · 7 public theorems · imports RestrainedSix, RestrainedSevenData2, Phi3, SpecialPrime, ForcingClosed

In the restrained family (every prime factor other than the special prime and one further prime has exponent exactly 2), no prime p with 5 ≤ p < 132257 divides N. No novelty is claimed: Ochem and Zelinsky (2026) treat this family in depth and prove that the exponent of 3 is at least 23,000,000,000, which is not proved here.

Proof idea. The exceptional prime is 3 and the special prime is 1 modulo 12 (earlier modules). Each prime below the bound is excluded by a tree of forced primes that ends in a prime already excluded; this module proves the tree checker sound and applies it to the 12342 rows.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.RestrainedSeven.dvd_of_dvd_two_mul

theorem dvd_of_dvd_two_mul {N t : ℕ} (ht : t % 2 = 1) (h : t ∣ 2 * N) : t ∣ N

An odd divisor of 2N divides N.

OddPerfect.RestrainedSeven.at_sound

theorem at_sound {N q : ℕ} (F : Fam N q) {M : ℕ} {t qv : ℕ} {qb ob : Br} (htp : t.Prime)
  (htN : t ∣ N) (ht3 : t ≠ 3) (hqv : qv = 0 ∨ qv = q)
  (hqb : t = q → chk M t (t + 1) qb = true) (hob : chk M qv (t * t + t + 1) ob = true)
  (ihq : ∀ qv src, chk M qv src qb = true → src ∣ 2 * N → (qv = 0 ∨ qv = q) → False)
  (iho : ∀ qv src, chk M qv src ob = true → src ∣ 2 * N → (qv = 0 ∨ qv = q) → False) :
  False

The step at a prime t ∣ N, t ≠ 3: either t = q, and the branch qb closes the source t + 1; or the exponent of t is 2, and the branch ob closes the source t * t + t + 1.

theorem restrained_not_dvd_of_lt {N q r p : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)

**Restrained odd perfect numbers have no prime factor 5 ≤ p < 132257.** With the hypotheses of restrained_exception_eq_three (special prime q, a further prime r ≠ q, every other prime factor with exponent exactly 2), no prime 5 ≤ p < 132257 divides N; together with r = 3 this says that the smallest prime factor of N other than 3 is at least 132257. Each prime is excluded by a kernel checked exclusion tree. No novelty is claimed: Ochem and Zelinsky prove that the exponent of 3 in such N is at least 23,000,000,000, which is not proved here.

Proof idea. Every prime factor other than 3 is at least 132257, so 2 < (3/2)(B/(B − 1))ω − 1 with B = 132257; the comparison of two powers with about 195000 digits is one kernel evaluation. A prime below the cutoff that divides σ(3d − 1) would divide N, so d cannot divide the index of 3.

OddPerfect.LedgerPrime

OddPerfect/LedgerPrime.lean · 294 lines · 8 public theorems · imports Valuation, SpecialPrime, Reciprocity

A conditional statement: if the divisor sum σ(p^e) of every ordinary prime power component of an odd perfect number is prime, then at least five distinct ordinary exponents occur. The hypothesis is a case and is not known to hold. Whether the result is new was not checked.

Proof idea. If σ(p^e) is a prime s, then p has order e + 1 modulo s, so s ≡ 1 modulo e + 1. A prime receives at most one unit from each exponent, and none from a sender with its own exponent, because then e + 1 would divide its own divisor sum. With at most four exponents the special prime has exponent 1, its sender has exponent 2, and a sender into that one has exponent 2 as well, which is the forbidden same exponent pattern.

OddPerfect.LedgerPrimeTwo

OddPerfect/LedgerPrimeTwo.lean · 415 lines · 6 public theorems · imports LedgerPrime, EulerIndexPrimePower, Counting

Under the case hypothesis that the divisor sum of every ordinary component is prime: at least eleven distinct ordinary exponents occur (before: five); there is a forced collision of two distinct ordinary primes with the same prime divisor sum s, where σ of the component of s is the special prime; and N has at least 12 distinct prime factors and at least 185 prime factors with multiplicity. The hypothesis is not known to hold. Whether the results are new was not verified.

Proof idea. With at most ten exponent values the special exponent is 1, 5 or 9 and a prime that receives nothing from the special component has exponent 2, 4 or 6. Residues of q + 1 along a chain of senders (6, 8, 4, then 32 or 58) show that too few senders are available. For the collision: not every sender into q can divide a + 1, and a sender that does not must receive from at least two ordinary primes.

If the full divisor sum σ(p ^ e_p) is prime for every prime factor p ≠ q, then there are an ordinary prime s with σ(s ^ e_s) = q and s ∤ σ(q ^ a), whose exponent is even and at least 2, and two distinct ordinary primes p ≠ r with σ(p ^ e_p) = σ(r ^ e_r) = s and e_p ≠ e_r. No bound on the number of exponent values is assumed. The primality of all these divisor sums is a case hypothesis, not known to hold for a hypothetical odd perfect number. OddPerfect.LedgerPrimeThree

OddPerfect/LedgerPrimeThree.lean · 358 lines · 11 public theorems · imports LedgerPrimeTwo, LedgerOrdersTwo

Structure of the forced collision in the case where every ordinary divisor sum is prime (a hypothesis not known to hold): congruences and size brackets for the three primes involved, which make the collision a solution of the Goormaghtigh equation with odd prime bases and a prime common value. Conditional corollary, with the open statement as an explicit hypothesis: if that equation has no such solution, some ordinary divisor sum of an odd perfect number is composite. Also a capacity bound for prime factors whose index is divisible by a fixed d. Whether these statements are in the literature was not verified.

Proof idea. With σ(pe) = s and e + 1 = m prime, the order of p modulo s is m, so m divides s − 1; the same for the second sender and for s against q. Residues modulo 4 of a geometric sum with an even exponent give the alternative on the exponent of s.

Residues modulo 4 of σ(x ^ E) for an odd prime x and even E: either x ≡ 3 and σ(x ^ E) ≡ 1, or x ≡ 1 and σ(x ^ E) ≡ E + 1 (mod 4).

If σ(x ^ E) = y for primes x, y with prime index E + 1 < y, then x ≢ 1 (mod E + 1): otherwise y ≡ E + 1 ≡ 0 (mod E + 1).

OddPerfect.prime_sigma_collision_structure

theorem prime_sigma_collision_structure {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hP : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → (σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)).Prime) :
  ∃ s p r : ℕ, s ∈ N.primeFactors ∧ s ≠ q ∧ σ 1 (s ^ N.factorization s) = q ∧
    ¬ s ∣ σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q) ∧ Even (N.factorization s) ∧
    2 ≤ N.factorization s ∧
    p ∈ N.primeFactors ∧ p ≠ q ∧ r ∈ N.primeFactors ∧ r ≠ q ∧ p ≠ r ∧
    σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = s ∧ σ 1 (r ^ N.factorization r) = s ∧
    N.factorization p < N.factorization r ∧
    (N.factorization s + 1).Prime ∧ (N.factorization p + 1).Prime ∧
    (N.factorization r + 1).Prime ∧
    Even (N.factorization p) ∧ Even (N.factorization r) ∧ 2 ≤ N.factorization p ∧
    2 * (N.factorization p + 1) * (N.factorization r + 1) ∣ s - 1 ∧
    2 * (N.factorization s + 1) ∣ q - 1 ∧
    q ≡ N.factorization s + 1 [MOD 2 * (N.factorization p + 1) * (N.factorization r + 1)] ∧
    (N.factorization s % 4 = 0 ∨ (p % 4 = 1 ∧ r % 4 = 1 ∧ N.factorization p % 4 = 2 ∧
      N.factorization r % 4 = 2)) ∧
    2 * (N.factorization p + 1) * (N.factorization r + 1) + 1 ≤ s ∧ r < p ∧
    p ^ N.factorization p < s ∧ s < p ^ (N.factorization p + 1) ∧
    r ^ N.factorization r < s ∧ s < r ^ (N.factorization r + 1) ∧
    s ^ N.factorization s < q ∧ q < s ^ (N.factorization s + 1) ∧
    p % (N.factorization p + 1) ≠ 1 ∧ r % (N.factorization r + 1) ≠ 1 ∧
    s % (N.factorization s + 1) ≠ 1

Structure of the forced collision. Let N be an odd perfect number and q its special prime. If the full divisor sum σ(p ^ e_p) is prime for every prime factor p ≠ q, there are ordinary primes s, p ≠ r with σ(s ^ g) = q, s ∤ σ(q ^ a), σ(p ^ e) = σ(r ^ f) = s, e < f (e = e_p, f = e_r, g = e_s, all even, e, g ≥ 2), prime indices m = e + 1, n = f + 1, k = g + 1, and moreover: 2 m n ∣ s - 1, 2 k ∣ q - 1, q ≡ k (mod 2 m n), g ≡ 0 (mod 4) or (p ≡ r ≡ 1 (mod 4) and e ≡ f ≡ 2 (mod 4)), s ≥ 2 m n + 1, r < p, p ^ e < s < p ^ m, r ^ f < s < r ^ n, s ^ g < q < s ^ k, and p ≢ 1 (mod m), r ≢ 1 (mod n), s ≢ 1 (mod k). The primality of all ordinary full divisor sums is a case hypothesis, not known to hold for a hypothetical odd perfect number. Whether this result is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.card_filter_dvd_succ_le_sum

theorem card_filter_dvd_succ_le_sum {N : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) {d : ℕ} (hd : 3 ≤ d) :
  (N.primeFactors.filter (fun p => d ∣ N.factorization p + 1)).card ≤
    ∑ t ∈ N.primeFactors.filter (fun t => d ∣ t - 1), N.factorization t

Capacity for a common index divisor. For an odd perfect number N and d ≥ 3, the number of prime factors p of N with d ∣ e_p + 1 is at most the sum of the exponents e_t over the prime factors t of N with d ∣ t - 1. Whether this is in the literature was not verified.

  ω N - 1 ≤ ∑ t ∈ N.primeFactors.filter (fun t => d ∣ t - 1), N.factorization t

Capacity for the common divisor family. If d ≥ 3 divides the index e_p + 1 of every prime factor p ≠ q of an odd perfect number N, then ω N - 1 is at most the sum of the exponents e_t over the prime factors t of N with d ∣ t - 1. Whether this is in the literature was not verified.

OddPerfect.LedgerOrders

OddPerfect/LedgerOrders.lean · 161 lines · 5 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, ValuationBounds

A counting inequality: for a set A of prime factors, the number of pairs (p, d) with p in A and d a divisor of e_p + 1 divisible by 3 is at most the sum over the prime factors t ≡ 1 (mod 3) of min(e_t, |A|). In particular the number of ordinary primes with 9 dividing e + 1 is at most the sum of the exponents of the ordinary primes that are 1 modulo 3. Whether the result is new was not checked.

Proof idea. For each such divisor d, a prime t of exact order d modulo p divides σ(p^e) (Bang and Zsigmondy), and t ≡ 1 modulo d, hence modulo 3. Different d give different t for the same p, and each pair (p, t) uses one unit of the exponent of t in N.

    ∑ t ∈ N.primeFactors.filter (· % 3 = 1), min (N.factorization t) A.card

Distinct orders inside one sender. For an odd perfect number N and every set A of prime factors of N, ∑_{p ∈ A} #{d ∣ e_p + 1 : 3 ∣ d} is at most the sum of min(e_t, |A|) over the prime factors t ≡ 1 (mod 3) of N.

OddPerfect.sum_card_three_dvd_divisors_sub_one_le

theorem sum_card_three_dvd_divisors_sub_one_le (h : OddPerfect N) (q : ℕ) {A : Finset ℕ}
  (hA : A ⊆ N.primeFactors) :

    ∑ t ∈ (N.primeFactors.erase q).filter (· % 3 = 1),
      min (N.factorization t) A.card

Distinct orders, one prime removed. For an odd perfect number N, any number q (in practice the special prime) and every set A of prime factors of N, ∑_{p ∈ A} (#{d ∣ e_p + 1 : 3 ∣ d} - 1) is at most the sum of min(e_t, |A|) over the prime factors t ≠ q of N with t ≡ 1 (mod 3): the prime q serves at most one order of each component.

OddPerfect.card_nine_dvd_le

theorem card_nine_dvd_le (h : OddPerfect N) (q : ℕ) :
  ((N.primeFactors.erase q).filter (9 ∣ N.factorization · + 1)).card ≤
    ∑ t ∈ (N.primeFactors.erase q).filter (· % 3 = 1), N.factorization t

**Components with 9 ∣ m_p.** For an odd perfect number N and any number q (in practice the special prime), the number of prime factors p ≠ q with 9 ∣ e_p + 1 is at most the sum of e_t over the prime factors t ≠ q of N with t ≡ 1 (mod 3). Each such component has the two orders 3 and 9, and q can serve only one of them.

OddPerfect.LedgerThreeFree

OddPerfect/LedgerThreeFree.lean · 1074 lines · 2 public theorems · imports Abundancy, SpecialPrime, ExponentCap, Phi3, Valuation, Seed.Example

If at most 31 ordinary primes of an odd perfect number have an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1, and each of them is 2 modulo 3, then 3 divides N. There is no restriction on the special prime, and the other primes need only satisfy 3 ∣ e + 1. Whether the result is new was not checked.

Proof idea. Assume 3 does not divide N. Every non exceptional prime p has p² + p + 1 equal to an odd power of the special prime q, so these primes are far apart and contribute little to the abundancy; with the 31 smallest primes that are 2 modulo 3 the total stays below 2 unless q = 109. For q = 109 every prime is exceptional, 5 divides N with exponent at least 4, and a count of the factors 5 supplied by the divisor sums, with a finite check of fifteen small primes and a congruence argument for the 125th cyclotomic value, gives fewer than needed.

theorem three_dvd_of_thirtyone_exceptions_mod_three_of_three_dvd {N q : ℕ} {E : Finset ℕ}
  (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hE : E.card ≤ 31)
  (hE3 : ∀ r ∈ E, r % 3 = 2)
  (h3m : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ∉ E → 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : 3 ∣ N

**Thirty one exceptions that are 2 (mod 3) force 3.** Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q (the prime of odd exponent). If every prime factor p ≠ q of N outside a set E satisfies 3 ∣ e_p + 1, where E has at most 31 elements, all ≡ 2 (mod 3), then 3 ∣ N. Taking E to be the set of prime factors p ≠ q with 3 ∤ e_p + 1: if at most 31 of them have 3 ∤ e_p + 1 and each of those is ≡ 2 (mod 3), then 3 ∣ N. There is no restriction on q.

OddPerfect.LedgerReceiver

OddPerfect/LedgerReceiver.lean · 167 lines · 5 public theorems · imports LedgerOrders, LedgerThreeFree, Counting, SpecialPrime

Conditional family: every prime factor that is 1 modulo 3 is one number q. Then 3 dividing e + 1 forces exponent 2; and if 3 does not divide N and q is the special prime, at least 32 ordinary primes have 3 not dividing e + 1, ω ≥ 33 and Ω ≥ 2ω + 63. Whether this is in the literature was not verified.

Proof idea. The orders 3 and e + 1 of p need two different receiver primes, both 1 modulo 3; only q is available. Then every ordinary prime is 2 modulo 3 and the 31 exception theorem applies.

OddPerfect.LedgerOrdersTwo

OddPerfect/LedgerOrdersTwo.lean · 136 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, ValuationBounds, SpecialPrime

For every odd perfect number: choose for each prime p of a set A some orders d ≥ 3 dividing ep + 1. The number of chosen orders is at most the sum, over all prime factors t, of the smaller of the exponent of t and the number of sources compatible with t. A tool for case analyses.

Proof idea. Each chosen order needs its own receiver prime within one source (Bang's theorem), and each use of a receiver t spends one unit of the exponent of t.

OddPerfect.LedgerParity

OddPerfect/LedgerParity.lean · 200 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Network, Phi3, SpecialPrime

A parity count on the graph of which prime divides which divisor sum: with m the number of pairs (p, r) of prime factors such that r divides σ(p^e), s₂ the number of ordinary primes with exponent 2 and D the number of senders into the special prime, s₂ + D + 2ω(N) ≤ 2m + 2. Whether the result is new was not checked.

Proof idea. For exponent 2 the divisor sum p² + p + 1 is not a square, so it has a prime factor with odd valuation. An ordinary prime has even exponent in N, so a receiver with one odd incoming valuation has a second sender. Counting senders per receiver gives the inequality.

OddPerfect.SquareRow

OddPerfect/SquareRow.lean · 441 lines · 2 public theorems

For an odd prime p and an even exponent e > 0, σ(pe) is a perfect square only for p = 3, e = 4 (σ(34) = 112). Known mathematics: a case of the equation (xn − 1)/(x − 1) = y2 treated in classical work of Nagell and Ljunggren.

Proof idea. A square value gives a solution of p U2 − (p − 1) V2 = 1 with U a power of p. Through the Pell equation for d = p(p − 1), whose fundamental solution is (2p − 1, 2), U is the coefficient of an odd power m of p + √d. The binomial expansion shows that the power of p dividing U is at most the power dividing m (one more for p = 3), while U grows exponentially in m; only p = 3, m = 3 survives.

theorem isSquare_sigma_prime_pow_iff {p e : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hp2 : p ≠ 2) (he : Even e)
  (he0 : e ≠ 0) : IsSquare (σ 1 (p ^ e)) ↔ p = 3 ∧ e = 4

Square rows. For an odd prime p and an even exponent e > 0, the divisor sum σ(p ^ e) = 1 + p + ⋯ + p ^ e is a perfect square exactly when p = 3 and e = 4 (σ(3 ^ 4) = 121 = 11 ^ 2). This is a special case of classical results on (x ^ n - 1) / (x - 1) = y ^ 2 (see Nagell and Ljunggren); the proof here goes through the Pell equation x ^ 2 - p (p - 1) y ^ 2 = 1 and a p-adic valuation count.

  ∃ r, r.Prime ∧ Odd ((σ 1 (p ^ e)).factorization r)

An odd valuation in a non-square row. For an odd prime p and an even exponent e > 0 with (p, e) ≠ (3, 4), some prime r divides σ(p ^ e) to an odd power.

OddPerfect.LedgerParityTwo

OddPerfect/LedgerParityTwo.lean · 178 lines · 4 public theorems · imports LedgerParity, SquareRow

The parity count of LedgerParity without any condition on the exponents: with k = ω(N) and m the number of pairs (p, r) of prime factors such that r divides σ of the component of p, every odd perfect number has 3k ≤ 2m + 3, and 3k ≤ 2m + 2 when the exponent of 3 is not 4. Whether the result is new was not checked.

Proof idea. By SquareRow every ordinary row other than 34 has a prime factor with odd valuation. An ordinary prime has even exponent in N, so a receiver with one odd incoming valuation has a second sender; counting senders per receiver gives the inequality. Every even perfect number satisfies it too, so it excludes nothing by itself.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.exists_odd_sigmaWeight_of_ne_three_pow_four

theorem exists_odd_sigmaWeight_of_ne_three_pow_four (h : OddPerfect N) {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) {p : ℕ} (hp : p ∈ N.primeFactors) (hpq : p ≠ q)
  (h34 : ¬ (p = 3 ∧ N.factorization 3 = 4)) :
  ∃ r ∈ N.primeFactors, Odd (sigmaWeight N p r)

**Every ordinary row except 3 ^ 4 has an odd entry.** If p ≠ q is a prime factor of an odd perfect number N with special prime q, and not both p = 3 and v_3(N) = 4, then some prime factor r of N receives an odd valuation v_r(σ(p ^ e_p)).

OddPerfect.card_rows_add_le

theorem card_rows_add_le (h : OddPerfect N) {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) :
  ((N.primeFactors.erase q).filter (fun p => ¬ (p = 3 ∧ N.factorization 3 = 4))).card
    + (N.primeFactors.filter fun p => q ∣ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p)).card
    + 2 * N.primeFactors.card ≤
  2 * ((N.primeFactors ×ˢ N.primeFactors).filter
    (fun x : ℕ × ℕ => x.2 ∣ σ 1 (x.1 ^ N.factorization x.1))).card + 2

Ordinary rows and parity, all exponents. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q, k = ω(N), m the number of pairs (p, r) of prime factors with r ∣ σ(p ^ e_p), D_q the number of senders into q, and R the set of prime factors p ≠ q with ¬ (p = 3 ∧ e_3 = 4). Then |R| + D_q + 2 k ≤ 2 m + 2.

OddPerfect.three_mul_card_le

theorem three_mul_card_le (h : OddPerfect N) {q : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) :
  3 * N.primeFactors.card ≤
    2 * ((N.primeFactors ×ˢ N.primeFactors).filter
      (fun x : ℕ × ℕ => x.2 ∣ σ 1 (x.1 ^ N.factorization x.1))).card + 3

Corollary, all exponents. For every odd perfect number N with special prime q, 3 ω(N) ≤ 2 m + 3, where m is the number of pairs (p, r) of prime factors with r ∣ σ(p ^ e_p). No condition on the exponents is needed.

OddPerfect.three_mul_card_le_of_factorization_three_ne_four

theorem three_mul_card_le_of_factorization_three_ne_four (h : OddPerfect N) {q : ℕ}
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (h3 : N.factorization 3 ≠ 4) :
  3 * N.primeFactors.card ≤
    2 * ((N.primeFactors ×ˢ N.primeFactors).filter
      (fun x : ℕ × ℕ => x.2 ∣ σ 1 (x.1 ^ N.factorization x.1))).card + 2

**Corollary, e_3 ≠ 4.** For an odd perfect number N with special prime q and v_3(N) ≠ 4, 3 ω(N) ≤ 2 m + 2, where m is the number of pairs (p, r) of prime factors with r ∣ σ(p ^ e_p). This is the exponent free form of three_mul_card_le_of_card_ne_two_le with j = 0.

OddPerfect.PureRows

OddPerfect/PureRows.lean · 227 lines · 8 public theorems · imports LedgerPrime, LedgerParityTwo, Zsigmondy

Rows whose σ value is a power rw of one prime (pure rows). For an odd prime p and an even exponent e > 0: the index e + 1 is prime, r ≡ 1 (mod e + 1), and w is odd except for σ(34) = 112. In an odd perfect number the full components grow along pure rows, so pure rows form no cycle. If every ordinary row is pure, the special component must feed about half of the prime factors.

Proof idea. A composite odd index would give two prime factors of different orders by Bang's theorem, but a pure row has one prime factor. An even weight makes the σ value a square, which happens only for 34. Growth: pe < σ(pe) = rw and w ≤ e_r by the exact count at r. The fan-out inequality |R| + D_q ≤ 2d_q comes from the parity count of LedgerParityTwo, because every pure ordinary row has exactly one receiver. The module excludes nothing: a path of pure rows can end at a row with two receivers.

  (he : Even e) (he0 : e ≠ 0) (hr : r.Prime) (hrow : σ 1 (p ^ e) = r ^ w) :

Prime index. If p is an odd prime, e > 0 is even and σ(p ^ e) = r ^ w for a prime r, then e + 1 is prime.

OddPerfect.receiver_mod_index_of_pure

Receiver modulo the index. If p is an odd prime, e ≥ 2 and σ(p ^ e) = r ^ w for a prime r, then r ≡ 1 (mod e + 1); in particular r ≠ e + 1.

Odd weight. If p is an odd prime, e > 0 is even and σ(p ^ e) = r ^ w for a prime r, then w is odd, except for σ(3 ^ 4) = 11 ^ 2.

The receiver of a pure row. If p is a prime factor of an odd perfect number N and σ(p ^ e_p) = r ^ w for a prime r, then r is a prime factor of N and 1 ≤ w ≤ e_r.

Growth along a pure row. If p is a prime factor of an odd perfect number N and σ(p ^ e_p) = r ^ w for a prime r, then p ^ e_p < r ^ e_r.

No cycle of pure rows. In an odd perfect number no prime factor reaches itself along a path of pure rows.

OddPerfect.card_add_inDegree_le_of_all_pure

theorem card_add_inDegree_le_of_all_pure {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hpure : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → ∃ r w, r.Prime ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = r ^ w) :
  ((N.primeFactors.erase q).filter (fun p => ¬ (p = 3 ∧ N.factorization 3 = 4))).card
    + inDegree N q
    ≤ 2 * (N.primeFactors.filter (fun r => r ∣ σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q))).card

Fan-out when every ordinary row is pure. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q. If σ(p ^ e_p) is a prime power for every prime factor p ≠ q, then |R| + D_q ≤ 2 d_q, where R is the set of prime factors p ≠ q other than 3 when e_3 = 4, D_q the number of senders into q, and d_q the number of prime factors of N dividing σ(q ^ e_q). That every ordinary row is pure is a case hypothesis, not known to hold.

OddPerfect.PureCommonIndex

OddPerfect/PureCommonIndex.lean · 143 lines · 2 public theorems · imports PureRows, EulerPart, EqualExponents

No odd perfect number has every ordinary row a prime power together with one odd prime dividing every ordinary index.

Proof idea. A pure row has prime index, so all indices equal the common prime l, and each receiver is 1 modulo l. No ordinary prime is 1 modulo l, so every receiver is the special prime: every ordinary row is a power of q. Then every prime factor of the Euler index would be q, which does not divide m.

OddPerfect.ordinary_row_pow_special_of_pure_common_index

theorem ordinary_row_pow_special_of_pure_common_index {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2)
  (hidx : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → l ∣ N.factorization p + 1)
  (hpure : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q →
    ∃ r w, r.Prime ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = r ^ w) :
  ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → ∃ w, σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = q ^ w

Under the hypotheses of not_all_pure_common_index, every ordinary row is a power of the special prime: σ(p ^ e_p) = q ^ w for each prime factor p ≠ q.

OddPerfect.not_all_pure_common_index

theorem not_all_pure_common_index {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2)
  (hidx : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → l ∣ N.factorization p + 1)
  (hpure : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q →
    ∃ r w, r.Prime ∧ σ 1 (p ^ N.factorization p) = r ^ w) : False

No odd perfect number has all ordinary rows pure and a common odd prime in every ordinary index. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q. It is impossible that σ(p ^ e_p) is a prime power for every prime factor p ≠ q while one odd prime l divides e_p + 1 for every prime factor p ≠ q. There is no bound on l or on the exponents. This is a restricted subfamily of the open common index family: mixed rows (some ordinary row not a prime power) and pure rows with different index primes are not covered.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThree

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionThree.lean · 569 lines · 7 public theorems · imports ThreeFreeTwo, SpecialPrime, Phi3

Special prime 5 and at most two further primes with an exponent different from 2: then the exponent of 3 is not 4, so it is 2 or at least 6. For exponent 2 the module proves partial results that describe every surviving configuration; that case is closed in TwoExceptionThreeA and TwoExceptionThreeB. Whether these statements are new was not verified.

Proof idea. If the exponent of 3 is 4, then σ(34) = 112 forces 11, and 11 must be the second exception, since exponent 2 at 11 would force 7 and 105 does not divide N. The factor 5 of σ(N) can then only come from σ(11e), so 5 divides e + 1 and σ(114) = 5 · 3221 starts a chain of exact squares 3221, 10378063, 769, 31. The divisor 34 · 5 · 114 · 312 of N is abundant, a contradiction.

  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  N.factorization 3 ≠ 4

Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime 5 in which every prime factor other than 5, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2. Then the exponent of 3 in N is not 4.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_cases

  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  N.factorization 3 = 2 ∨ 6 ≤ N.factorization 3

The clean form: for an odd perfect number with special prime 5 and at most two exceptional exponents r₁, r₂ (every other prime factor has exponent exactly 2), the exponent of 3 is 2 or at least 6.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThree.five_sender_mod

theorem five_sender_mod {p e : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (hp5 : p ≠ 5) (he : Even e)
  (hd : 5 ∣ σ 1 (p ^ e)) : p % 5 = 1 ∧ 5 ∣ e + 1

If 5 ∣ σ(p^e) with p ≠ 5 prime and e even, then p ≡ 1 (mod 5) and 5 ∣ e + 1.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_sixty_one

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_sixty_one {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) :
  ¬ 5 ∣ σ 1 (61 ^ N.factorization 61)

Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime 5 in which every prime factor other than 5, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2, and suppose e₃ = 2. Then the component of 61 does not send the prime 5: 5 ∤ σ(61^{e₆₁}). If 5 ∣ σ(61^e) then 5 ∣ e + 1, so σ(61^4) = 5 · 131 · 21491 divides 2N, and 61 is exceptional. The prime 13 (from σ(3^2)), 17293 = σ(131^2) and 421 ∣ σ(21491^2) are 1 (mod 3); at most one of the chains 13, 131 → 17293, 21491 → 421 can be cut by the second exception, so two of these exact squares send a factor 3, and with 5 this gives three senders against e₃ = 2.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen_sq

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen_sq {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) (h132 : N.factorization 13 = 2) :
  6 ≤ N.factorization 61 ∧ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization 61 + 1 ∧ ¬ 5 ∣ N.factorization 61 + 1

With special prime 5, at most two exceptional exponents and e₃ = 2: if e₁₃ = 2, then 61 is exceptional with e₆₁ ≥ 6, 3 ∤ e₆₁ + 1 and 5 ∤ e₆₁ + 1.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) :
  N.factorization 13 = 2 ∨ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization 13 + 1

With special prime 5, at most two exceptional exponents and e₃ = 2: either e₁₃ = 2 or 3 ∤ e₁₃ + 1.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_shape

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_shape {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) :
  ∃ s, s.Prime ∧ s ∣ N ∧ s % 5 = 1 ∧ 5 ∣ N.factorization s + 1 ∧ s ≠ 61 ∧
    ((N.factorization 13 = 2 ∧
        ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ 61 → p ≠ s → N.factorization p = 2) ∨
      (N.factorization 13 ≠ 2 ∧ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization 13 + 1 ∧
        ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ 13 → p ≠ s → N.factorization p = 2))

The shape of every configuration that survives for e₃ = 2: with special prime 5 and at most two exceptional exponents, e₃ = 2 forces a prime s ≠ 61, s ≡ 1 (mod 5), dividing N with 5 ∣ e_s + 1, and either e₁₃ = 2 and every prime factor other than 5, 61, s has exponent 2, or e₁₃ ≠ 2, 3 ∤ e₁₃ + 1 and every prime factor other than 5, 13, s has exponent 2.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThreeACheck

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionThreeACheck.lean · 145 lines · 6 public theorems · imports Pratt, Phi3

Checker for the table behind TwoExceptionThreeA: for each x that is 1 modulo 10, a divisor of a composite x, or a prime witness dividing x4 + x3 + x2 + x + 1 that forces a third sender of a factor 3. Soundness theorem cover_sound.

Proof idea. A witness t is good if it is 1 modulo 3 itself, or if t2 + t + 1 keeps a factor after 13, 61 and x are removed.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThreeA

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionThreeA.lean · 397 lines · 4 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionThreeAData, TwoExceptionThree, RestrainedFour

Special prime 5, at most two further primes with an exponent different from 2, exponent 2 at 3: the exponent of 13 is not 2. What remains of this case is one branch: the index of 13 is not divisible by 3 and one further prime s that is 1 modulo 5 has index divisible by 5. That branch is closed in TwoExceptionThreeB. Whether these statements are new was not verified.

Proof idea. If 132 exactly divides N the exceptions are 61 and a prime x that is 1 modulo 5. Below 116281 the table gives a third prime sending a factor 3, against exponent 2 at 3; above it the abundancy stays below 2 by the Rankin tail bound.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen_ne_two

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_thirteen_ne_two {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) : N.factorization 13 ≠ 2

Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime 5 in which every prime factor other than 5, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2, and let e₃ = 2. Then e₁₃ ≠ 2.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_sq_branch_b

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_sq_branch_b {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) :
  N.factorization 13 ≠ 2 ∧ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization 13 + 1 ∧
    ∃ s, s.Prime ∧ s ∣ N ∧ s % 5 = 1 ∧ 5 ∣ N.factorization s + 1 ∧ s ≠ 61 ∧
      ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ 13 → p ≠ s → N.factorization p = 2

The corollary: with special prime 5, at most two exceptional exponents and e₃ = 2, the configuration is branch B: e₁₃ ≠ 2, 3 ∤ e₁₃ + 1, and there is a prime s ≠ 61, s ≡ 1 (mod 5), dividing N with 5 ∣ e_s + 1 such that every prime factor other than 5, 13, s has exponent 2.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThreeBCheck

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionThreeBCheck.lean · 240 lines · 6 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionThreeACheck

Checker for the two walks behind TwoExceptionThreeB, and the structure of the branch as a set of rules (Ctx): which primes are forced into N, and which pairs of primes cannot both divide N.

Proof idea. A forcing chain starts at a prime known to divide N and follows prime factors of p2 + p + 1 until it reaches 7 or two primes that are 1 modulo 3; both are impossible in this branch.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionThreeB

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionThreeB.lean · 468 lines · 6 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionThreeBData, TwoExceptionThreeA

Special prime 5 and at most two further primes with an exponent different from 2: the exponent of 3 is at least 6. This closes the case of exponent 2 at 3 that the earlier modules left open. Whether these statements are new was not verified.

Proof idea. In the last branch the exceptions are 13 and a prime s that is 1 modulo 5. At most one further prime t that is 1 modulo 3 divides N, and 7 does not. Small s are closed by forcing chains; for large s the prime t satisfies t2 + t + 1 = 3 · 13a · sb, which a second walk excludes for small t, and beyond that the abundancy stays below 2.

OddPerfect.branch_b_ctx

theorem branch_b_ctx {N s : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (h32 : N.factorization 3 = 2) (hs : s.Prime) (hse : 5 ∣ N.factorization s + 1)
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ 13 → p ≠ s → N.factorization p = 2) :
  Ctx N s

The structure of branch B. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime 5 and e₃ = 2, let s be a prime with 5 ∣ e_s + 1, and let every prime factor other than 5, 13 and s have exponent 2. Then Ctx N s holds: every prime factor of Φ₅(s) other than 2 divides N, every prime factor other than 2 of σ(v^2) for a prime factor v ∉ {5, 13, s} divides N, two distinct prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 3) outside {13, s} do not exist, and 7 ∤ N.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_three_ne_two

theorem two_exceptions_five_three_ne_two {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  N.factorization 3 ≠ 2

Branch B is empty: an odd perfect number with special prime 5 in which every prime factor other than 5, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2 does not have e₃ = 2.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_five_six_le_three

theorem two_exceptions_five_six_le_three {N r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization 5))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ 5 → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  6 ≤ N.factorization 3

An odd perfect number with special prime 5 in which every prime factor other than 5, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2 has e₃ ≥ 6.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFiveIndex

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFiveIndex.lean · 310 lines · 15 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionThreeB, MixedIndexThree, Network, SpecialPrime, Phi3

Special prime 5 with at most two exceptional primes: the exceptions are 3 and a prime s ≡ 1 (mod 5) whose index is divisible by 5; the index of 3 is prime to 105 and has no prime factor up to 31; the exponent of 3 is at least 36.

Proof idea. The exact count of the factors 5 in σ(N) gives a sender s ≡ 1 (mod 5) with index divisible by 5; it is not an exponent 2 row, so it is an exception, and 3 is the other one by the earlier modules. The mixed index theorem then gives a row whose index is prime to 105, and it can only be the row of 3. For each prime l from 11 to 31 dividing the index of 3, a prime factor of σ(3l−1) divides N and starts a short chain of forced primes through rows of exponent 2 and the row of s; every chain reaches 7, which cannot divide N when 3 and 5 do. The exponent of 3 stays unbounded.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFour

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFour.lean · 768 lines · 4 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionFourCheck, TwoExceptionThreeB

Two exceptional exponents with any special prime q. If q ≡ 2 (mod 3) and 9 divides σ of the special component (for example q ≡ 8 (mod 9)), the exponent of 3 is not 2. If the exponent of 3 is 4 and q ≠ 5, then 11 divides N with an even exponent e ≥ 6 such that neither 3 nor 5 divides e + 1, and the two exceptions are 3 and 11. Whether these statements are new has not been checked.

Proof idea. With exponent 2 at the prime 3 and 9 dividing σ of the special component, the ledger of 3 has no room left, so 13 = σ(32) is an exception and every squared prime t has t2 + t + 1 supported on 13 and the other exception. The abundancy then stays below 2 by a tail estimate, a finite table, or an abundant divisor in the few remaining cases.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFourMod

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFourMod.lean · 294 lines · 5 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionFour, TwoExceptionThree

Two exceptional primes and exponent 4 at the prime 3: the special prime q satisfies q ≡ 1 (mod 12).

Proof idea. The exceptions are 3 and 11 by TwoExceptionFour, and the exponent e of 11 is even. Suppose q ≡ 2 (mod 3). A prime that is 2 modulo 3 divides no σ(p2), so no row of exponent 2 feeds q, and 11 is fed by rows of exponent 2 not at all beyond σ(34) = 112. The exact counts of the factors q and 11 give σ(11e) = A·qα and σ(qα) = 2·11e−2·B. Abundancy bounds give 67 ≤ AB ≤ 70, and congruences modulo 3 give A = 23 and B = 3. The closed forms of the two geometric sums then have no common solution. For q ≡ 1 (mod 12) rows of exponent 2 can feed q and the argument stops.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFourChains

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFourChains.lean · 463 lines · 27 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionFourMod, Phi3

Two exceptional primes and exponent 4 at the prime 3: no prime below 79 other than 3 and 11 divides N.

Proof idea. The exceptions are 3 and 11 and q ≡ 1 (mod 12). A prime p of exponent 2 forces the prime factors of p2 + p + 1; those other than 3 are 1 modulo 3, so each is q or a prime of exponent 2 that is 1 modulo 3. At most four such primes exist, because each sends a factor 3 and the exponent of 3 is 4. The special prime forces the odd prime factors of q + 1. Forcing chains exclude each prime from 5 to 73 other than 11, in increasing order: a chain ends at a prime excluded before or at a fifth prime of exponent 2 that is 1 modulo 3. A forced prime that is 1 modulo 12 is split into the cases equal to q and different from q.

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionFourEmpty

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionFourEmpty.lean · 269 lines · 3 public theorems · imports TwoExceptionFourChains, Abundancy, EqualExponentsBound

With two exceptional primes the exponent of 3 is not 4: no odd perfect number has exponent 4 at 3 and exponent 2 at every other prime except the special prime and two more.

Proof idea. After TwoExceptionFourChains every prime factor other than 3 and 11 is at least 79. At most 13 of them have a row that is not a pure power of q: q itself, at most four primes of exponent 2 that are 1 modulo 3, and at most two senders into each of those. The rows that are pure powers of q have distinct exponents, so their primes grow by a factor above 8 and together add at most the factor 401/395 to the abundancy. Then σ(N)/N ≤ (121/81)·(11/10)·(79/78)13·(401/395) < 1.97, which contradicts σ(N) = 2N.

OddPerfect.ThreeSquareCapacity

OddPerfect/ThreeSquareCapacity.lean · 178 lines · 3 public theorems · imports Network, Phi3, SpecialPrime, ForcingClosed

If 32 exactly divides an odd perfect number N, then p4 divides N for some p in {7, 13, 19, 31, 61, 97, 127, 331}.

Proof idea. Call a prime factor p good when it is not the special prime, p ≡ 1 (mod 3) and 3 divides its exponent plus 1. Then p2 + p + 1 divides the divisor sum of the p component, so p sends a factor 3 and every prime factor of p2 + p + 1 divides N. The factors 3 received add up to the exponent of 3, which is 2, so three good primes cannot exist. Now σ(32) = 13 divides N, 13 forces 61 and 61 forces 97. If none of them is the special prime q, that makes three good primes. If q is 13, 61 or 97, the odd part of q + 1 forces 7 or 31 and their rows supply the third prime (19 and 127, or 331). So one of the eight primes, not q, has an exponent e with 3 not dividing e + 1; that exponent is even and not 2, hence at least 4.

theorem false_of_three_sq_of_index_three {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)

  (hA : ∀ p ∈ ({7, 13, 19, 31, 61, 97, 127, 331} : Finset ℕ), p ∣ N → p ≠ q →
    3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1) : False

Core form. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q and v_3(N) = 2. If every prime p among 7, 13, 19, 31, 61, 97, 127, 331 that divides N and differs from q has 3 ∣ v_p(N) + 1, a contradiction follows: three distinct such primes would each send a factor 3, but only two are available.

Headline. An odd perfect number with 3 ^ 2 exactly dividing it is divisible by the fourth power of one of the primes 7, 13, 19, 31, 61, 97, 127, 331.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_three_sq_exception_mod_three

theorem two_exceptions_three_sq_exception_mod_three {N q r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N)
  (hq : q.Prime) (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2)
  (h3 : N.factorization 3 = 2) :
  ∃ r, (r = r₁ ∨ r = r₂) ∧ r ∈ ({7, 13, 19, 31, 61, 97, 127, 331} : Finset ℕ) ∧ r ≠ q ∧
    r ^ 4 ∣ N

Two exceptional primes. Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q and v_3(N) = 2, in which every prime factor other than q, r₁ and r₂ has exponent 2. Then one of r₁, r₂ lies among 7, 13, 19, 31, 61, 97, 127, 331, differs from q, and its fourth power divides N.

OddPerfect.TwoExcEngineCode

OddPerfect/TwoExcEngineCode.lean · 685 lines · 0 public theorems · imports Pratt

The computable checker for certificates of the family with a bounded number of exceptional primes and a fixed exponent at 3 (2 by default): states, certificate trees and the functions check and checkV. Definitions only.

Proof idea. A state lists decided prime factors of N with a role (exponent 2, or a free exponent with recorded divisibility data, either the special prime or an exception) and the factors each one receives from the rows of other decided primes, plus a bound x below which every prime factor is decided. A certificate is a tree of rule applications. The checker derives every state, value and budget itself; the certificate carries only choices and witnesses. The hot paths use the arithmetic that the kernel evaluates fast.

OddPerfect.TwoExcEngineState

OddPerfect/TwoExcEngineState.lean · 162 lines · 3 public theorems · imports TwoExcEngineCode, SpecialPrime

The meaning of a checker state (Holds), the family predicate with a parameter for the number of exceptions, and the root lemma.

Proof idea. Holds says: N is an odd perfect number of the family, every listed key is a prime factor with the stated role, every recorded contribution pw divides the divisor sum of the named component, and every prime factor below x is listed. The family gives the root state, where only 3 is listed, with exponent 2 or, for the entry point checkV, with the exponent fixed by the parameters.

OddPerfect.TwoExcEngineCheck

OddPerfect/TwoExcEngineCheck.lean · 1715 lines · 32 public theorems · imports TwoExcEngineState, Network, ThreeSquareCapacity, TwoExceptionFour, TwoExceptionThreeB, Cyclotomic

Soundness of the checker: an accepted certificate refutes the family (check_sound, and checkV_sound for a fixed exponent at 3), for every rule except the deficiency leaf, which enters as a hypothesis.

Proof idea. One lemma per rule. Rows: the divisor sum of a decided component sends its prime factors, with weights checked by one modular power. Budgets: the weights a prime receives from distinct components add up to at most its exponent. Forcing: a forced prime gets one of an exhaustive list of roles. Receipt: a prime that is 2 modulo 3 must divide the divisor sum of the special prime's or an exception's component, which fixes a multiplicative order condition on the exponent. Abundancy: the decided components already give a ratio above 2. Capacity: the counting rule at 3 from ThreeSquareCapacity. The module also proves the bridge from named exceptions to the family predicate and the table of primes below 4096.

OddPerfect.TwoExcEngineTail

OddPerfect/TwoExcEngineTail.lean · 1374 lines · 1 public theorem · imports TwoExcEngineState, RankinTailPade

Soundness of the deficiency leaf (defSound): when the checker's upper bound for σ(N)/N is below 2, the state is contradictory.

Proof idea. The decided primes contribute a known product. An undecided prime factor is at least x and is one of: the special prime; a new exception; a square prime that is 1 modulo 3, of which the budget of 3 allows at most its exponent minus those already counted; a square prime that is 2 modulo 3 whose row contains a prime with a bounded remaining budget; or a square prime that is 2 modulo 3 whose row is built from finitely many generators. The first four classes have bounded size, so they contribute a bounded factor. For the last class the rows below a limit are enumerated exactly and the rest are bounded by rankin_tail_general.

With at most two exceptional primes, the exponent of 3 in an odd perfect number is not 2, and therefore at least 6.

Proof idea. The top of the certificate tree reaches the 162 subtrees of the data modules, and check_sound turns the accepted certificate into the theorem. The certificate has 12,273 records: 7,341 contradiction leaves, 209 abundant leaves, 3 capacity leaves and 707 deficiency leaves. The certificate uses three earlier theorems on the special prime in this family. The bound 6 follows because 3 divides N, its exponent is even, and exponent 4 was excluded before.

theorem two_exceptions_three_ne_two {N q r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  N.factorization 3 ≠ 2

Let N be an odd perfect number with special prime q in which every prime factor other than q, r₁ and r₂ has exponent exactly 2 (a restricted family with two exceptional exponents). Then the exponent of 3 in N is not 2. This concerns only this restricted family, not odd perfect numbers in general.

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_six_le_three

theorem two_exceptions_six_le_three {N q r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  6 ≤ N.factorization 3

In the same family the exponent of 3 is at least 6. The prime 3 divides N (three_dvd_of_two_exceptions) and is not the special prime (that one is 1 modulo 4), so its exponent is even and positive, and it is neither 2 (two_exceptions_three_ne_two) nor 4 (two_exceptions_three_ne_four).

OddPerfect.TwoExceptionTwoThree

OddPerfect/TwoExceptionTwoThree.lean · 39 lines · 1 public theorem · imports TwoExceptionTwo

With at most two exceptional primes, one of them is 3.

Proof idea. The prime 3 divides N, it is not the special prime, and its exponent is at least 6 by two_exceptions_six_le_three. So 3 is not among the primes of exponent 2, and it must be one of the two named exceptions. For one exceptional prime the corresponding statement is restrained_exception_eq_three.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.two_exceptions_three_exceptional

theorem two_exceptions_three_exceptional {N q r₁ r₂ : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q))
  (hsq : ∀ p ∈ N.primeFactors, p ≠ q → p ≠ r₁ → p ≠ r₂ → N.factorization p = 2) :
  r₁ = 3 ∨ r₂ = 3

With at most two exceptional primes r₁ and r₂ (every other prime factor except the special prime has exponent 2), one of the two is 3.

OddPerfect.SpecialIndexWitness

OddPerfect/SpecialIndexWitness.lean · 283 lines · 7 public theorems · imports Zsigmondy, EqualExponents

A budget inequality that ties the exponent of the special prime to the exponent of any odd prime l.

Proof idea. Let a be the exponent of the special prime q and v the exponent of l in a + 1. For each j from 1 to v, both lj and 2lj divide a + 1, and a primitive prime factor of σ(qa) exists for each of these orders (module Zsigmondy). These 2v primes are distinct prime factors of N, different from q and 1 modulo l. Each one whose exponent e has l dividing e + 1 sends a factor l into σ(N) = 2N, and σ(qa) itself contributes its own factors l. Counting the factors l gives special_index_witnesses. For l = 3 the remaining witnesses have exponent at least 4.

Public theorems

OddPerfect.two_mul_special_index_le_card

theorem two_mul_special_index_le_card {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2) :
  2 * padicValNat l (N.factorization q + 1) ≤
    (N.primeFactors.filter fun p => p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1).card

The witness step: an odd perfect number has at least 2 v_l(a + 1) prime factors other than the special prime q (of exponent a) that are 1 modulo the odd prime l.

OddPerfect.special_index_budget

theorem special_index_budget {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2) :
  padicValNat l (σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) +
      (N.primeFactors.filter fun p =>
        p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1 ∧ l ∣ N.factorization p + 1).card ≤
    N.factorization l

The budget of an odd prime l: the special prime q pays v_l(σ(q ^ a)), and every prime factor p ≠ q with p ≡ 1 (mod l) and l ∣ v_p(N) + 1 pays at least one factor l.

OddPerfect.special_index_witnesses

theorem special_index_witnesses {N q l : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (hl : l.Prime) (hl2 : l ≠ 2) :
  2 * padicValNat l (N.factorization q + 1) +
      padicValNat l (σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) ≤
    N.factorization l + (N.primeFactors.filter fun p =>
      p ≠ q ∧ p % l = 1 ∧ ¬ l ∣ N.factorization p + 1).card

The special index inequality: 2 v_l(a + 1) + v_l(σ(q ^ a)) ≤ v_l(N) + #{p} over the prime factors p ≠ q of N with p ≡ 1 (mod l) and l ∤ v_p(N) + 1, for every odd prime l.

OddPerfect.special_index_three

theorem special_index_three {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) :
  2 * padicValNat 3 (N.factorization q + 1) +
      padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (q ^ N.factorization q)) ≤
    N.factorization 3 + (N.primeFactors.filter fun p =>
      p ≠ q ∧ p % 3 = 1 ∧ 4 ≤ N.factorization p ∧ ¬ 3 ∣ N.factorization p + 1).card

The case l = 3: a counted prime has exponent at least 4.

theorem padicValNat_three_succ_le_sigma {q a : ℕ} (hq : q.Prime) (hq3 : q ≠ 3) (ha : Odd a) :
  padicValNat 3 (a + 1) ≤ padicValNat 3 (σ 1 (q ^ a))

For a prime q ≠ 3 and an odd a, v_3(a + 1) ≤ v_3(σ(q ^ a)).

theorem three_mul_special_index_le {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)

3 v_3(a + 1) ≤ v_3(N) + #{p ≠ q : p ≡ 1 (mod 3), v_p(N) ≥ 4, 3 ∤ v_p(N) + 1}.

theorem four_exceptions_of_three_sq_of_nine_dvd {N q : ℕ} (h : OddPerfect N) (hq : q.Prime)
  (hodd : Odd (N.factorization q)) (h3 : N.factorization 3 = 2)
  (h9 : 9 ∣ N.factorization q + 1) :
